Folk Strings (Worldwide)

Orientation

This is the pilot file for the Sub-$150 Instrument Build Catalog series. It covers folk string instruments of the world: from the simplest one-string musical bow through developed regional lutes, fiddles, zithers, and harps. The cigar-box-guitar / diddley-bow cluster is in, but it is a small slice. The anti-default pass was run deliberately: the file is organized to put Africa, Asia, the Middle East, and Central Asia first.

Price note: All prices are research snapshots (June 2026). Prices drift; verify before acting. Price bands (~$X-Y) are used throughout. Confidence flags per source: [ESTABLISHED] well-documented; [PLAUSIBLE] reasonable inference, not directly verified; [UNCERTAIN] limited or contested evidence; [UNKNOWN] no reliable path found.

URL note: Only URLs confirmed live or appearing in multiple credible search results are included. A few are flagged [PLAUSIBLE link] where the site's existence is established but the specific page was not directly fetched.

PART ONE: SUB-SAHARAN & EAST AFRICA

1. Kora (West African Harp-Lute)

Origin: Mandinka / Mande tradition, The Gambia, Senegal, Guinea-Bissau; griot instrument; 21 strings in two banks.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: 21-string layout, two-bank bridge, thumb-and-index-finger playing style, drone-over-melody texture. What the cheap build trades away: the large natural calabash resonator (swapped for a bowl or substitute), exact tonal darkness, and the skin head tone. A IKEA-bowl kora sounds close; it is not the same as a 50-year-old Senegalese kora.

Large calabash gourds (42-48cm diameter, 12-16mm wall) are the traditional target and genuinely hard to source in the US north; grow your own in a warm climate or use the bowl workaround. Note: the five variants are five creative paths from one builder, not five independent sources.

2. Akonting (Gambian Folk Lute, Banjo Ancestor)

Origin: Jola/Diola tradition, The Gambia, Senegal, Casamance. Three strings, gourd body, skin head. Widely cited as a direct ancestor of the American banjo.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: three-string fretless gourd/skin lute played with downstroke picking; thumb drone on a short string; pentatonic vocabulary. What the build trades away: the specific tonal character of a large Gambian calabash (bowl gourd substituted). Technique is genuinely close.

Bushel gourds are available on Etsy or from gourd farmers at craft fairs (~$10-20 for the right size). Cedar or any straight-grained softwood for the neck. Total cost confirmed under $50.

3. Ngoni / Kamale Ngoni (West African Lute)

Origin: Mandinka/Bambara tradition, Mali, Guinea, Burkina Faso. The ngoni is a plucked lute with a calabash or skin-covered wooden body and a neck passing through the body. The kamale ngoni is a modern youth version with more strings.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: plucked calabash/skin lute, neck-through-body construction, similar picking approach to the akonting. What the build trades away: exact calabash acoustics (substitutable), specific string arrangement of the traditional form.

The neck-through-gourd construction is the key technique; the YouTube references show it.

4. Berimbau (Afro-Brazilian Musical Bow)

Origin: Central and West African musical bow traditions transplanted to Brazil; foundational instrument of capoeira.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: single-wire-string over a flexible stave, gourd resonator for amplification, struck with a stick and modulated with a coin (dobrao) to produce two pitches plus overtones. The $20 scratch build with a substitute stave and grown-or-bought gourd produces the instrument's core technique completely. What the build trades away: exact biriba-wood resonance (substituted well by ash, locust, or bamboo) and the precise tonal darkness of a hand-seasoned cabaça.

Arame (wire string) is available as a 3-pack on Amazon (~$5-8) or recycled from a bicycle spoke. Capoeira Connection in Austin is the US supplier for awkward-to-source parts.

5. Musical Bow / Uhadi (Nguni / South African)

Origin: Nguni tradition (Xhosa, Zulu), South Africa. A flexible stave strung with a single string; a gourd resonator is attached to the bow. The player hums or sings near the gourd opening to amplify specific harmonics. The San people use a mouthbow (bow against the lips as the resonator) without an attached gourd.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: single-string bow, resonator amplification, harmonic manipulation technique. The basic construction is essentially the same as the berimbau minus the cultural context and minus the stick-and-coin playing technique (the uhadi is plucked or struck with a stick and the gourd swung). The mouthbow version needs no attached gourd at all.

6. Masenqo / Masenko (Ethiopian / Eritrean Spike Fiddle)

Origin: Amhara/Tigrinya tradition, Ethiopia and Eritrea. One-string spike fiddle with a diamond-shaped skin-covered resonator box. The defining instrument of the azmari (wandering musician-bard) tradition.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: single-string spike fiddle bowed with a horsehair bow; fretless; the left hand pinches the string to change pitch. What the build trades away: the exact diamond-shaped hardwood resonator (substituted with any small wooden or gourd box) and the specific horsehair string (substituted with nylon monofilament). The technique transfers; the tone is related but different.

7. Goje / N'ko (Hausa Spike Fiddle, West Africa)

Origin: Hausa tradition, northern Nigeria, Niger, Ghana. A one-string spike fiddle with a gourd or wood resonator and an animal-skin soundboard. Central to Hausa praise-music traditions. The n'ko refers to closely related instruments in neighboring traditions.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: one-string spike fiddle played with a horsehair bow; fretless continuous pitch. What the build trades away: exact gourd acoustics and the specific snakeskin soundboard (snakeskin sourcing is complex in the US; rawhide substitutes acoustically).

8. Krar (Ethiopian / Eritrean Bowl Lyre)

Origin: Tigrinya/Amhara tradition, Ethiopia and Eritrea. A 5 or 6-string bowl lyre, plucked with a plectrum or fingers, with a gourd or wooden bowl resonator and sometimes a skin face.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: pentatonic/heptatonic plucked lyre played with a plectrum, bowl resonator + yoke + crossbar structure, similar to ancient Greek kithara family. What the build trades away: skin-covered bowl tone if you use a wooden bowl substitute, and exact traditional tunings.

9. Valiha (Malagasy Tube Zither)

Origin: Malagasy tradition, Madagascar. A tube zither where strings run longitudinally along the surface of a bamboo tube, raised by small carved bridges. One of Africa's most distinctive chordophone forms; the national instrument of Madagascar.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: tube zither form -- strings along a tube, plucked with both thumbs and fingers, using the body of the tube as the resonator. Traditional strings are strips of the bamboo skin itself raised on small bridges; modern versions use guitar or nylon strings. What the build trades away: the specific resonance of a large-diameter dried bamboo culm (substitutable with ABS pipe, losing some warmth).

PART TWO: MIDDLE EAST / WEST ASIA

10. Saz / Baglama (Turkish / Central Asian Long-Neck Lute)

Origin: Turkish and broader Anatolian tradition; the baglama/saz family is the national folk instrument of Turkey and central to Greek, Kurdish, Azerbaijani, and Central Asian related traditions. Three double-courses, movable (tied) frets in a quartertone-capable layout.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: long-neck fretted lute with movable frets; plucked with a plectrum or fingers; three double courses. What the build trades away: the specific mulberry/juniper tonal character (substituted with linden/maple) and the quartertone fret layout (requires a specific calculator; standard Western fretting will not produce the correct scale).

11. Folk Oud (Simplified)

Origin: Arab/Ottoman tradition, broadly the Middle East and North Africa. A 5-double-course (11-string) fretless lute with a deep bowl back. The premier melodic instrument of the Arab world.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: fretless plucked lute, right-hand plectrum technique, deep resonant bowl body. What the build trades away: an authentic bowl-back oud is a major luthiery project requiring stave bending. The guitar-conversion route gives a fretless lute with oud strings and partial oud feel, but the body shape and response are a cousin, not an equivalent.

PART THREE: SOUTH ASIA

13. Ektara (South Asian One-String Drone Lute)

Origin: Bengali, Rajasthani, and broadly South Asian folk tradition. Used by Bauls and other wandering musicians. A single-string lute with a gourd or coconut body, skin head, and bamboo neck. The name means "one string."

Close-enough bar: What transfers: single-string drone lute plucked repeatedly; the player typically sings over a continuous drone. The cheap build has the same fundamental function. What the build trades away: the tonal qualities of a large seasoned gourd vs. a coconut or small bottle gourd.

14. Gopichand / Khamak (Bengali Percussion-String)

Origin: Bengali folk tradition, Bangladesh and West Bengal, India. A one-string instrument where two bamboo tongs attached to a drum-like resonator are squeezed to vary the string tension and produce a sliding pitch. Used by Bauls. The khamak is essentially the same instrument played differently (shaken/struck).

Close-enough bar: What transfers: the sliding pitch effect (squeezing the tongs tightens the string) and the drone/percussion role. What the build trades away: nothing significant -- the bamboo-tong mechanism is fully reproducible from the chandrakantha.com plans.

20. Erhu Substitute Builds (Tin-Can / Coconut Erhu)

Origin: Chinese tradition; the erhu is the most prominent instrument of the huqin (spike fiddle) family. The tin-can and coconut-body DIY versions are a maker-community adaptation, not a traditional form.

PART SIX: SOUTHEAST ASIA

23. Dan Bau (Vietnamese Monochord)

Origin: Vietnamese tradition. A one-string instrument with a flexible bamboo wand that bends the string to produce microtonal glissandos. Played with a plectrum while the other hand deflects the wand. The modern form uses an electric pickup; the original form used a bamboo tube or long wooden box as a resonator.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: single-string microtonal instrument where the left hand bends the string for pitch (using the wand's flex) while the right hand plucks. This is a unique technique without close parallels in Western instruments. What the build trades away: the modern amplified tone (the original bamboo tube form is acoustic and much simpler to build).

PART SEVEN: OCEANIA / PACIFIC

24. 'Ukeke (Hawaiian Musical Bow)

Origin: Hawaiian tradition; Hawaii's only indigenous string instrument. A flat wooden bow (traditionally koa, 16-24 inches long, 1.5 inches wide) with 2-3 strings tied at both ends. One end is held to the open mouth, which acts as the resonating chamber. Related to Marquesan and other Polynesian mouth bows.

Note on Oceanic string instruments generally: String instruments were comparatively rare in pre-contact Oceanic traditions. The 'ukeke and related Polynesian mouth bows represent the primary documented indigenous string tradition in the Pacific. Tube zithers exist in Melanesia and SE Asian borderlands but are extremely thinly documented for DIY builds.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: mouth-bow technique (one end to open lips, harmonics changed by shaping the mouth cavity). What the build trades away: specific koa wood resonance (any flat, resonant hardwood substitutes).

29. Jouhikko / Tagelharpa (Nordic Bowed Lyre)

Origin: Finnish/Scandinavian tradition; the jouhikko is the Finnish form, tagelharpa the broader Scandinavian term (also strakharpa, talharpa). A bowed lyre with 2-4 strings and an arm-hole cutout that lets the left hand reach through to stop strings from behind.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: bowed lyre, each string producing a different note; the bow works through a gap in the yoke. Playing technique (bow tilts to contact individual strings; left hand reaches through the arm hole) is unique to this instrument family. What the build trades away: the precise sound of aged spruce and horsehair if using substitute materials.

30. Welsh Crwth (Simplified)

Origin: Welsh folk tradition; one of Europe's oldest bowed instruments, combining a flat fiddle fingerboard with a lyre-style body. 6 strings (4 fretted, 2 open drones), flat bridge, played with a horsehair bow.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: bowed rectangular lyre/fiddle hybrid; the fingerboard allows chromatic playing. What the build trades away: the exact rectangular resonator acoustics and the specific open-string drone interplay.

32. Scheitholt / Hummel (German / Scandinavian Drone Zither)

35. Hurdy-Gurdy (Simplified)

What transfers: the mechanical concept (wheel, key mechanism) works and produces the characteristic sound. What the build trades away: the tonal richness and key responsiveness of a properly set up hurdy-gurdy.

38. Charango (Andean, Wood Body Only)

Origin: Andean tradition, Bolivia, Peru, Chile, Argentina. A small 10-string (5 double-course) lute. Traditionally made from armadillo shell (illegal and unethical; all modern plans use carved wood). Scale ~370mm.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: 10-string double-course lute, re-entrant tuning, finger-and-plectrum technique, Andean musical traditions. What the build trades away: armadillo shell sound (wood is now the standard; not a meaningful loss ethically or practically). The scratch build is essentially miniature-guitar lutherie.

Bottom line: One hardware-store trip. A metal washtub or garbage pail (~$8-15), a broomstick, and a dacron or nylon string. Total under $25. Havlena's plans (online for ~25 years) are the canonical reference. No kit needed; no lumber yard needed.

PART TEN: NORTH AMERICA

43. Cigar Box Guitar (CBG)

Origin: American folk tradition, with roots in Depression-era and post-Civil War improvised instrument building. Three or four-string slide or fretted guitar built in a cigar box resonator. Electric CBGs with piezo or magnetic pickups are central to the tradition.

Note: This is the deepest kit market in the catalog -- multiple distinct US vendors, Amazon, and Etsy builders. Full detail in the AAAAAAA worker file (Cigar Box and Primitive String Kits and Plans.md); this entry surfaces the distinct vendor landscape.

44. Diddley Bow

Origin: African-American folk tradition, the American South. The simplest possible string instrument: one string under tension over a board, played with a slide. Blind Willie Johnson and many other blues artists started on this instrument.

45. Canjo (Tin-Can Banjo)

Origin: American folk tradition. A one-string, diatonically fretted banjo using a tin can as the resonator/head. The diatonic fretting means wrong notes are essentially impossible.

46. Apache Fiddle / Tsii' Edo'a'tl (Note: Ethical Flag)

Origin: Western Apache tradition (White Mountain Apache, San Carlos Apache), Arizona. A one-or two-string bowed instrument made from an agave or mescal stalk. The name means "wood that sings." Used in social dances and storytelling contexts. This is a LIVING Indigenous tradition, not a historical artifact -- it was actively suppressed during the US assimilation era and is undergoing cultural revival.

Ethical consideration: The AMIS 2022 presentation "Apache Fiddles: Tradition, Forced Assimilation, Commerce, and Museums" directly addresses the tension between non-Apache commercial interest and cultural stewardship. Non-Apache builders should research this context carefully before proceeding. This entry is included for completeness of the survey; Mark should determine whether building this instrument aligns with his personal ethics and the respect he wishes to show to Apache cultural heritage.

Group What Body/Materials Price Band US Source Link

Structural note (for reference only): The instrument uses a dried agave or mescal stalk as the body (split in half, hollowed, rejoined), pine pitch as a sealant, horsehair strings, and horsehair bow. Agave stalks are freely available in the US Southwest after the plant has bloomed and died.

Bottom line: [UNKNOWN] for build plans. [ETHICAL FLAG] for non-Apache builders. This entry is documented but not recommended as a build project without engaging with the Apache cultural revival community first.

PART ELEVEN: SMALL LEVER-LESS FOLK HARP (Cross-Regional)

47. Small Folk Harp / Lap Harp (Lever-Less, 22-String)

Origin: European harp tradition broadly; the lever-less folk harp is associated with Celtic, Paraguayan, and global folk traditions. Covered here as a separate entry because the kit options are distinct from the Paraguayan harp section and deserve their own treatment.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: full diatonic harp technique; all basic melody and chord playing. A 22-string lever-less harp gives a 3-octave range and enables folk and traditional repertoire. What the build trades away: the ability to change keys without retuning (sharping levers, at $10-25 each, can be added later).

The Backyard Music Fireside Folk Harp kit is the cheapest complete one-stop assembled kit but is currently $289 (well over budget); the Kovac hardware kits at $145 plus $20-30 in materials are the realistic under-$175 path.

MATERIAL SOURCING ACROSS THE CATALOG

Goatskin / rawhide: Amazon (pre-cut rounds $7-20), Centralia Fur & Hide (furandhide.com), Etsy (drum head sellers). No CITES issues with domestic or imported goat/elk rawhide.

Gourds (calabash, bushel, bottle): Etsy gourd sellers, The Gourd Place (thegourdsplace.com), Martha's Gourds (marthasgourds.com), craft fairs. Large gourds (42-48cm) for a full kora are genuinely hard to find; grow your own in warm climates or use Havlena's IKEA bowl workaround.

Bamboo: Garden centers (thin to medium diameter), Asian grocery stores (some types), bamboo farms (search "bamboo nursery + your state"). Arundo donax (giant reed) is free to forage in California (invasive) but not well-stocked as tube cane.

Berimbau parts (verga, arame, cabaça): Capoeira Connection, Austin TX (capoeiraconnection.com).

Zither pins / tuning pins: Musicmakers/harpkit.com ($0.55 each), Folkcraft, elderly.com (21-pin packs).

Violin friction pegs: Amazon, StewMac, elderly.com (set of 3-4, $5-15).

Erhu / bowed instrument bows: Chinese erhu bows, Amazon ($10-15, pre-threaded between strings; required for erhu-family instruments).

Cheap violin bow: Amazon ($15-20); works for masenqo, goje, rebab, morin khuur, jouhikko.

Music wire / zither strings: Musicmakers, elderly.com, Amazon.

Luthier woods (spruce, mahogany, cedar): StewMac.com, Luthiers Mercantile International (lmii.com), Woodcraft, local hardwood dealers.

Harp hardware (strings, eyelets, tuning pins): John Kovac Harps (johnkovac.com), Musicmakers/harpkit.com.

Coconut shells: Amazon, Etsy ($3-8 each).

COVERAGE GAPS AND HONEST VOIDS

These instruments were researched and no viable US build path was found:

[UNKNOWN] paths confirmed absent: - Begena (Ethiopian large bass lyre): No English-language plans or kit; specialized religious instrument. - Afghan robab/rubab: Double-chambered body; no plans; no kit; complex enough that no accessible path found. - Dan tranh (Vietnamese zither): No English plans; related to guzheng which also has no plans. - Kobza (Ukrainian folk lute): No English plans in accessible form. - Domra (Russian round-body lute): No plans or kit found. - Nyckelharpa (Swedish keyed fiddle): Full instrument is $500-2000+ to build properly; over budget; Instructables and plans exist but materials well over $150.

Thin coverage (non-English sources likely richer): - Dutar, dombra, komuz: Build paths are plausible but documentation in English is very thin. Non-English YouTube (Kyrgyz, Kazakh, Uzbek) almost certainly has more. - Goje / masenqo: No written plans in English. Spike fiddle YouTube covers the construction family generically. - Mvet / ngombi (Central African bow-lute family): Not documented for DIY in English. - Pacific/Melanesian tube zithers and musical bows: Documented in museums; no DIY builds in English found.

REPORT-BACK

Cigar Box Guitar

Orientation

The cigar box guitar is the deepest kit market in the entire Sub-$150 series. There are at minimum 15 distinct vendor families, a free-plans ecosystem with multiple canonical sources, a community hub (Cigar Box Nation, 13,000+ members) that has been active since 2008, and a body of instructional books and video series that no other instrument in this catalog comes close to matching. This file reflects that reality: it has sections, not just rows, and each section goes wide.

How to read this file: Section 1 covers kits with the full vendor field. Section 2 covers configuration (string count, fretted/fretless, scale). Section 3 covers acoustic vs electric and the pickup aftermarket. Section 4 covers free plans, books, and from-scratch BOMs. Section 5 covers video build series. Sections 6-8 cover the immediate siblings: diddley bow, canjo, washtub bass.

Source confidence notation: [ESTABLISHED] well-documented, high confidence. [PLAUSIBLE] reasonable inference, not directly verified at the URL level. [UNCERTAIN] limited or contested. [UNKNOWN] outside reliable knowledge; no fabrication.

Price note: All prices are research snapshots (June 2026). Prices drift; verify before ordering. Price bands (~$X-Y) are used throughout.

StewMac note: StewMac's 3-string CBG kit (item #101512-C, $129.99) is listed as "no longer available / sold out" as of the research date [ESTABLISHED]. It is documented here because it may return or be useful as a reference point for what premium spec looks like.

SECTION 1: KITS -- The Full Vendor Field

The CBG kit market has more distinct commercial sources than any other instrument in this catalog. The entries below are organized by vendor, not by product, because vendor identity matters here: C.B. Gitty is the hub of the entire ecosystem, and the other vendors are genuinely distinct. Counting storefronts as separate sources would be misleading; counting a single vendor's 15 kits as 15 sources would be equally wrong.

Source-counting rule used here: Every distinct independent business or maker is one source. C.B. Gitty plus all its retail distribution channels (Amazon, Reverb, eBay, Guitar Center, Musician's Friend, Walmart, Etsy) is ONE source. MGB Guitars' entire 20-kit catalog is ONE source. Etsy as a marketplace with dozens of individual makers is counted as a category, not a single source.

Source 1: C.B. Gitty Crafter Supply (THE HUB)

Who they are: The central supplier of the modern CBG revival. Based in Rochester, NH. Founded by Ben "Gitty" Baker. Also runs: American Canjo Company (canjo kits), and has sub-brands/kit lines including Hubcap Howler, Red Barn, Tin Pan Alley, Reso-Plate, Rodeo King. All Gitty storefronts (cbgitty.com, Amazon, Reverb, eBay, Guitar Center, Musician's Friend, Walmart, Etsy) are the same company and the same SKUs. ONE source.

SECTION 2: Configuration Guide

3-String vs 4-String vs 6-String

3-string (dominant form): The canonical CBG. Three strings over an open tuning (GDG, DAD, GBD) make slide playing and barred chords easy without music theory. Approximately 85% of CBG community builds and all kit entry points are 3-string.

4-string: More chords, more familiar to anyone who plays ukulele or banjo. Standard tuning for a 4-string CBG is typically DGBD (same as guitar's four middle strings) or CGBD (related to banjo). MGB offers most kits in 3 or 4-string options at the same price. Gitty's kits also have 4-string variants for several models.

6-string: Rare in the CBG context. Uses standard guitar scale (24.75"-25.5"), standard guitar tuning EADGBE; the cigar box becomes a resonator body for a conventional guitar-scale neck. Plans exist (Amazon: full-scale print plans for 6-string acoustic and 6-string electric CBG). No complete 6-string kit found in the US sub-$150 range at the time of research [PLAUSIBLE -- the component approach works: standard guitar neck + cigar box body + bridge + hardware is within range if parts are sourced carefully].

Fretted vs Fretless

Fretless (slide-focused): The original form. Played with a glass bottle neck, brass tube, or machined slide. No frets means the entire fingerboard is available. Open tuning (GDG or DAD) means the open strings form a chord. This is the slide guitar tradition. Most from-scratch builds start here.

Fretted: Adds conventional fretting -- typically 17-22 frets. Allows both slide and conventionally fretted notes. Gitty, MGB, Catoctin, Chickenbone John all do fretted kits. The fretted CBG plays like a simplified guitar.

Scale Lengths

Scale Who Uses It Notes
22.75" Chickenbone John Short scale; lower string tension; easier for smaller hands; slightly warmer tone
24" MGB Easy Neck, Gitty most kits Most common CBG scale; splits the difference between Fender and Gibson
24-5/8" (625mm) StewMac Guitar-equivalent scale; same fret spacing as a standard electric guitar
25.5" MGB Super Neck, some builds Full Fender-scale; brighter, higher tension; most "guitar-like"
30" Gitty G-Bass Short-scale bass territory

Standard Tunings

Tuning Strings Common Use
GDG (Open G) 3-string Most common; open G chord; natural for slide; easy for beginners
DAD (Open D) 3-string Second-most common; open D chord; slide and fretted both work
GBD (Open G partial) 3-string Same as guitar's G, B, D middle strings; easier transition from guitar
DGBD 4-string Guitar's four middle strings; instant familiarity for guitarists
EADGBE (partial) 6-string Standard guitar tuning on a CBG scale

SECTION 3: Acoustic vs Electric -- Pickups and the Aftermarket

Acoustic CBG

A plain cigar box guitar body produces a small, raw, primitive acoustic sound. The wooden cigar box resonates but is not a large acoustic body. Acoustic CBGs are best heard in quiet settings or close-mic'd recording. Most kit builders add at least a basic pickup. Pure acoustic builds (the slide tradition) are valid but expect less volume than a resonator.

Piezo Pickup (Most Common Entry Point)

Piezo disks are inexpensive ($3-15), require no routing, and install inside the box lid. The piezo responds to mechanical vibration -- a trebly, bright, acoustic-forward tone with high-frequency presence. Most Gitty kits with "acoustic/electric" in the name use a piezo disk + 1/4" jack.

Magnetic Pickup Options

Magnetic pickups respond to string movement (like a guitar pickup), not box vibration. They give a rounder, more "guitar-like" electric tone. Require ferromagnetic strings (standard guitar strings work; nylon will not).

Resonator CBG

A resonator cone (aluminum, chrome, or brass) mounted in the box top gives significantly more volume and a dobro-like tone character. Two bridge types: biscuit (round wood disk in the cone well) and spider (metal spider over the cone bowl). Biscuit is far more common in CBG builds.

SECTION 6: Diddley Bow (Sibling)

Origin: African-American folk tradition, the American South. One string under tension on a board or fence post, played with a slide. Blind Willie Johnson, Jimi Hendrix, and many other significant players started on or referenced this instrument. One of the absolute cheapest and simplest instruments in this entire catalog.

Kit market verdict: Genuinely thin. C.B. Gitty is essentially the only commercial kit source in the US. Etsy has a handful of handmade diddley bows and one or two kit-adjacent listings. Twister Strums makes finished instruments but not kits. The diddley bow's natural habitat is the free scrap-lumber build; the $39 Gitty kit is the packaged version.

SECTION 7: Canjo (Sibling)

Origin: American folk tradition. A one-string diatonically fretted banjo using a tin can as the resonator/head. The diatonic fretting means wrong notes are essentially impossible -- the frets are spaced for the major scale only. Played with a pick or finger.

Kit market verdict: Thin but coherent. The American Canjo Company is Gitty's own brand, so Gitty is effectively the only commercial kit source (sold via cbgitty.com and Amazon). The CanJoe Company (canjoe.com) is a distinct long-running maker of finished canjos since 1994, but sells finished instruments only.

Bottom line: $45 kit from Gitty or under $15 from scratch (a tin can, a stick, a string). The diatonic fretting is a genuine advantage for non-players: wrong notes are not on the instrument. Kit market is essentially one source.

SECTION 8: Washtub / Gutbucket Bass (CBG-Adjacent)

Origin: African-American folk tradition, the American South. A single string stretched from a washtub (the resonator) to a pole, played upright by varying string tension for pitch. Used in jug bands, skiffle, and early string band traditions. The instrument is CBG-family by philosophy (found-object, primitive string, cheap) but not by construction.

Kit market verdict: No commercial kits exist. The washtub bass is entirely a free-plans/from-scratch instrument. Multiple documented free plans; total cost $15-40.

Critical Context: The 2025–2026 Import Duty Situation

This affects every kit that ships to you directly from outside the US. Read once before using any price in this file.

De minimis exemption: suspended. The US $800 duty-free threshold was first suspended for China-origin goods (2 May 2025), then extended to all countries by Executive Order (29 August 2025), and explicitly continued by a second EO on 20 February 2026 [ESTABLISHED] (NAMM Tariff Explainer, Apr 2026). There is no duty-free floor. Every imported parcel, regardless of value, now faces customs processing and applicable duties.

IEEPA tariffs: struck down. The US Supreme Court ruled 6–3 on 20 February 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs [ESTABLISHED] (NAMM, Feb 2026). The broad reciprocal tariffs of 10%+ that had applied to most trading partners — and the "drug trafficking" tariffs on Canada, Mexico, and China — are invalid. Refunds for IEEPA duties already paid are being processed via the CBP CAPE portal (60–90-day timeline, not automatic).

Section 122 tariffs: 15%, all countries, temporary. Following the Supreme Court ruling, President Trump immediately imposed a 15% global tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 [ESTABLISHED] (NAMM, Feb 2026). Section 122 is capped at 15% for 150 days without a Congressional extension; 150 days from 20 February puts the expiry at approximately 19 July 2026. As of the date of this file (5 June 2026), these are active.

Section 301 tariffs on China: intact. Section 301 tariffs, imposed for unfair trade practices, were not affected by the IEEPA ruling and remain in place [ESTABLISHED] (NAMM, various). For HTS Chapter 92 (musical instruments, including electric guitars under 9207.10), the Section 301 rate for Chinese-origin goods is approximately 7.5% [PLAUSIBLE — rate confirmed by Dutify.com tariff table as "USA: 5.0%" base, Section 301 China adds ~7.5% per 2019 rulemaking; exact rate should be verified at trade.cbp.gov for 9207.10.00].

Country of origin vs. shipping origin. Harley Benton kits are manufactured in China and stocked in Germany by Thomann. For US customs purposes, the country of origin is China, not Germany. This means HB kits are subject to Section 301 China tariffs even though they ship from Germany. Solo Music Gear (Canada) assembles in Canada but uses Chinese-sourced components; USMCA preferential rates require meeting rules of origin that kits built from Chinese parts may not satisfy — [UNCERTAIN], verify with customs broker. Pit Bull Guitars (Australia) assembles in Australia; Australian-origin goods are not subject to Section 301 but face the Section 122 global tariff.

Net tariff stacking for a direct import from Germany (HB kit), June 2026: - MFN base (HTS 9207.10): ~5% - Section 301 China surcharge: ~7.5% - Section 122 global: 15% - Approximate total: ~27.5% of customs value (kit price + shipping)

Section 122 tariff expires ~19 July 2026; after that, stacking drops to ~12.5% for non-China and ~12.5% for Canada (or 0% if USMCA-qualifying), reducing but not eliminating the gap.

Practical implication: Under June 2026 tariff conditions, no kit shipped directly to you from Thomann (Germany), Solo Music Gear (Canada), or Pit Bull (Australia) appears to land under $150. The sub-$150 market in the US is currently the US-stocked kit pool on Amazon and domestic storefronts. This is a real, recent change from the market described in the prior survey.

Post-July 2026 the import options may re-open partially.

Section 1: Electric Guitar Kits Under $150

Origin and scope

Electric guitar as a commodity instrument: US, 1950s (Leo Fender's bolt-on designs, Gibson's carved-top tradition). The body styles cataloged here all derive from those roots. The global manufacturing reality is that virtually every sub-$150 kit is Chinese-made, regardless of which brand name or country it's sold through. This is not a default; it is the actual supply chain. There is no meaningful non-Western kit tradition for electric guitars at this price point — the instrument and the DIY-kit market are both Western-origin commercial categories that happen to be manufactured in China. The closest non-Western contribution is the Japanese Hosco (noted below), which was historically significant but is no longer a primary sub-$150 source in the US.

What transfers at this tier: Six-string fretted electric, bolt-on neck, standard 25.5" scale, SSS/HH/HSS/P90 pickup configurations. You are building a playable instrument, not a boutique one. The wood is poplar, basswood, or paulownia; the hardware is generic; the pickups are ceramic. All of that is fine and expected. The builder's effort — cleanup lutherie and finish — determines the final result far more than the kit quality does.

What the cheap version trades away: Fit and finish from the factory. Expect: fret ends that need dressing, a nut cut too high, off-drilled pilot holes, cheap strings, and instructions ranging from "minimal" to "absent." Budget $20–50 in finishing supplies and a few afternoons of setup work for any kit in this section.

These kits are already in US warehouses. You pay the listed price; no customs transaction falls on you. The seller absorbed import costs (or sourced domestically). These are the genuinely sub-$150 options under current tariff conditions.

Group 3: Plans and Scratch Builds Under $150

Solid-body electric guitar is among the most buildable from scratch because the body is simple flat woodwork — no bending, no joining under tension. A body template, a router, and poplar or pine from a lumber yard can make a playable body for $15–25.

Free plans (confirmed live, Jun 2026): - eGuitarPlans.com — $8 PDF plans with full measurements, wiring diagrams, construction tips. Multiple styles (ST, TL, LP, offset). [ESTABLISHED — site confirmed live] - Electric Herald (electricherald.com/guitar-templates/) — free downloadable templates at 1:1 scale for multiple body styles. [ESTABLISHED] - John Anthony Guitars (johnanthonyguitars.com/free-plans.html) — free solid-body plans. [ESTABLISHED — site confirmed live] - GenOne Luthier Services (genone-luthier-supply.com/collections/free-plans) — free specialty plans including bridge layouts and neck profiles. [ESTABLISHED] - MyMyDIY (mymydiy.com) — aggregator listing 11 free guitar plans from various sources. [ESTABLISHED]

BOM estimate for a scratch solid-body S- or T-style (US materials):

Part Source Approx. cost
Body blank (poplar/pine, 1.75" × 13" × 18") Local lumber yard or Home Depot $10–20
Neck blank (maple, ~1" × 3" × 26") Local lumber yard or online $12–20
Fretboard (rosewood or maple strip) Stewart-MacDonald or eBay $15–25
Fretwire (nickel, ~3 ft.) StewMac or Amazon $8–15
Truss rod (double-action) StewMac, Amazon, or eBay $8–15
Bridge (hardtail or trem) GFS, Amazon generic $15–30
Tuning machines (6-inline) GFS or Amazon generic $10–20
Pickups (loaded pickguard or 2-pickup set) GFS XGP, Amazon $25–45
Pots, switch, jack, wiring GFS or electronics kit $10–20
Nut (pre-slotted plastic or bone) StewMac or Amazon $3–8
Neck screws, string trees, strap buttons Amazon $5–10
Finish (spray lacquer or tru-oil) Hardware store $10–20
Total ~$131–248

A lean build targeting the low end of each category (poplar body, cheap maple neck, generic hardware, basic paint) can hit $130–150 in the US. It is not guaranteed and requires sourcing discipline. The fretboard and fretwire are the hardest to cheapen without hurting playability; do not cut corners there. [PLAUSIBLE]

Key BOM gatekeepers: The neck is the problem. A scratch neck requires: truss rod installation, fret slots, fret installation, nut slot, tuner holes, finishing, truss access. If you skip scratch-building the neck and buy a budget replacement neck (Amazon: ~$25–45 for generic bolt-on maple necks with pre-installed frets), the total comes down and removes the highest-skill step. A pre-fretted generic neck + scratch body + GFS electronics can land around $110–145. [PLAUSIBLE]

Plans-only resources: eGuitarPlans has the most complete package for $8. Electric Herald's free templates are better for routing guides than full build instructions. For video walk-through: search "build electric guitar from scratch" on YouTube — several full-length documented builds exist with supplier links in descriptions (independent builders, not kit companies). No single dominant video series emerged from this research pass; the field is scattered. [PLAUSIBLE]

Group 4: Close-Enough Cousins (and why they are cousins, not equivalents)

These are instruments that share playability with electric guitar but differ in key ways. Plucked, fretted, right-hand pick/fingers technique transfers. Tone, electronics, and setup differ.

Instrument Why it counts Why it's only a cousin Sub-$150 kit path
Cigar Box Guitar (3- or 4-string electric) Same fretted, plucked, plugged-in interface; many are tuned like partial guitar chords Reduced string count; slide-dominant playing; often open tuning C.B. Gitty (cbgitty.com) has the deepest kit and parts catalog; complete CBG kits from ~$30–80 US-stocked [ESTABLISHED]
Lap Steel (electric) Same single-coil pickup chain; same signal path Horizontal play, slide-only, no frets in use; requires different technique entirely Guitar Fetish sells $30–50 lap steel kits; scratch builds well-documented online [ESTABLISHED]
Resonator (acoustic-electric) Fretted, six-string, plug-compatible if fitted with pickup Cone-resonator acoustic tone; requires different build skill (metal cone, biscuit or spider bridge) Budget resonator kits exist (~$120–150) but are at the upper edge; [UNCERTAIN on US stock under $150]

Bottom Line: Electric Guitar

The cheapest real path under $150 in the US right now: Glarry GST DIY at $89.99 from US warehouse with free shipping — no import exposure, no customs paperwork, ships in 3–5 days. Solderless. Mahogany body and maple neck are better specs than the prior-generation basswood-only wave. Second-best in this band: Fistrock ST (~$109–119) and Leo Jaymz ST/TL (~$89–119), both on Amazon with US-based fulfillment and return rights.

Best build: Any Harley Benton kit (especially the JA offset at $95 list, or the ST at $77) once the tariff situation normalizes or if you can absorb the landed cost around $180–205. The JA's praise-consistent neck and the deeply documented HB community (1,175+ verified Thomann reviews for the ST alone) make these the most information-rich kits in the under-$200 world. They are just not sub-$150 to your door in June 2026.

Offset coverage: HB JA ($95 list, over $150 landed) and FretWire Offset (several variants, US-stocked, ~$100–149, exact price unconfirmed). The FretWire offset is the most accessible US-stocked offset kit. HB JA is the one with the most documented build experience.

Semi-hollow coverage: Batking, DBL, and FretWire ES on Amazon are the accessible options; exact prices were not confirmed in this research pass — check Amazon directly.

Key trade: Pay less ($90–120 US-stocked generics) and do more cleanup lutherie. Import a better-documented kit (HB, Solo, Pit Bull) and pay more once duties are factored. There is no budget kit under $150 that arrives with frets dressed, nut slotted, and action set — that work is on you.

Section 2: Electric Bass Kits Under $150

Origin and scope

Electric bass: US, 1951 (Leo Fender, Precision Bass). Four-string fretted electric bass, standard 34" scale, split-coil P or J pickup configurations dominate the budget market. Five-string and fretless options exist but are scarce under $150. Origin is Western, supply chain is Chinese, same as electric guitar above. No distinct non-Western kit tradition exists for electric bass.

What transfers: The same fretted, plucked, plugged-in technique as electric guitar. Playing technique is plucked (fingers or pick), long-scale neck (34"). Bass body kits are uniformly heavier than guitar kits — paulownia is the lightweight exception (Fistrock).

What the cheap version trades away: Same as guitar: fret ends, nut height, strings, instructions. Additionally, bass neck geometry is more demanding — higher string tension, longer scale — so a neck that is merely close-enough on guitar becomes a real problem on bass. Neck pocket fit and truss rod accessibility matter more.

Fistrock P-bass specifics (best-documented US option): Paulownia body is the lightest in this price range (6 lb 8 oz completed, per AxeKit build). Pre-assembled pickguard with pre-wired split-coil pickup; all electronics connect without soldering. Maple neck with dyed poplar fretboard. Common issues: fret ends need filing (expected at any price), slight neck pocket play (does not affect string alignment once correctly seated), butterfly-style tuners (not Fender-style). Group 3: Plans and Scratch Bass Builds Under $150

Precision and Jazz bass body shapes are simple, flat, contoured routes — easier than some carved-top guitar bodies. The neck is the hard part (same truss rod + fret challenge as guitar, but longer scale).

BOM estimate for scratch P-bass (US materials):

Part Cost
Body blank (alder, 1.75" × 14" × 19") $15–30
Neck blank (maple, 1.25" × 3" × 35") $15–25
Fretboard $15–25
Bass fretwire $8–12
Truss rod (45" or standard) $10–18
Split-coil P-pickup (GFS or Amazon) $15–30
Bridge (top-load hardtail) $12–25
Tuners (4-inline) $12–20
Electronics (1V/1T pot, jack, wiring) $8–15
Nut, pickguard, misc hardware $10–18
Finish $10–20
Total ~$130–238

The floor (lean sourcing, common woods, Amazon generic hardware): ~$130–155. Staying under $150 requires either very cheap wood sourcing or a pre-fretted replacement bass neck. Budget bass necks (bolt-on, 4-string, pre-fretted) are available on Amazon and AliExpress for ~$35–55, which is the single biggest line item to economize. [PLAUSIBLE]

Free plans for P- and J-bass: Electric Herald and eGuitarPlans both have bass plans. John Anthony Guitars has bass templates. BOM estimates above apply.

Bottom Line: Electric Bass

The cheapest real path under $150 in the US right now: Fistrock P-bass at $109.99 from Amazon — US-warehoused, solderless, pre-assembled pickguard, paulownia body (lightest in class), strongly reviewed. Best beginner kit in this section. Second option: Leo Jaymz J-bass (~$99–129) or Ktaxon (~$80–100), though these have lighter review coverage.

Best build: Harley Benton P-bass ($98 list) — best-documented budget bass kit at this price point, with 500+ Thomann verified reviews. Not currently sub-$150 landed. Same post-July 2026 tariff opportunity as guitar kits.

5-string / fretless / exotic: Genuinely thin market under $150. Pit Bull Guitars is the only maker with depth here, but all their options land over $150 to US buyers. If you want a 5-string DIY bass, expect to spend $200+ landed. If you want fretless, buy the cheapest P-bass kit above and do not install frets — the body and neck blank work the same way.

Key trade: Bass kits reward simplicity. The P-bass is mechanically the easiest: one split-coil, one volume, one tone, hardtail bridge. The Fistrock P-bass executes this formula at $109.99 with the additional advantage of paulownia weight savings. Nothing else in the US-stocked pool touches it at that price for build ease.

Section 3: Acoustic Guitar Kits — Brief Note

No acoustic guitar kit exists under $150 in the US in June 2026. The cheapest credible acoustic kit is the Solo ACK-10 Classical at $159.99 on sale (solomusicgear.com; prior survey, verified Apr 2026). Standard acoustic dreadnoughts start at $199.99 (Solo ADK-10). Acoustic building requires: go-bar deck or substitute, radius dishes, clamping jigs, brace shaping, and glue-up of a closed box — fundamentally more tool-intensive than bolt-on electric. This scope is documented in "Guitar and Bass Build Kits.md" (the parent file); it is out of scope here.

Same-Kit, Different-Label (OEM Rebranding)

The sub-$150 market is a shared OEM catalog. Key confirmed patterns:

Confirmed same-kit or same-maker: - Glarry GST DIY: same kit appears on Temu (Temu-fulfilled, different price), Amazon, and Glarry's own site — three storefronts, one product [ESTABLISHED per AxeKit]. - Bogart = Fistrock: same maker, name change. Individual components still appear under Bogart. [ESTABLISHED]. - Muslady = Ametoys: same factory, shared neck/body CNC origin, documented across multiple kits including the "children's LP" short-scale [ESTABLISHED per AxeKit].

Probable OEM family (same factory pool, not identical SKUs): - Leo Jaymz, Fesley, Ktaxon: one builder who purchased all three documented near-identical poplar-glued CNC bodies, solderless connectors, and identical pictorial manuals. Same factory pool, different QC pull and surface prep [PLAUSIBLE per AxeKit]. - "LeoTone": named in earlier research, produced no credible US DIY-kit footprint. Likely a conflation with Leo Jaymz. [UNKNOWN] — do not use as a distinct source.

The Hosco exception: Hosco (Japan) is a historical budget kit maker, still available in the US via Solo and Amazon. In the under-$150 electric guitar band, Hosco does not appear to have in-stock US-priced electric kits below $150 independently; their catalog under Solo is acoustic. Their historical significance is their origin work on budget kit manufacturing; they are the reason why "budget Japanese kit" has different connotations than "budget Chinese kit," though the practical distinction has blurred. [ESTABLISHED as historical note; current Hosco US-stocked electric selection under $150: UNKNOWN]

General mechanism: Budget kits are sold under many brand names from the same China factories. Bodies are uniformly poplar, basswood, or paulownia; CNC-cut; some with veneer tops. The defensible claim is a shared OEM pool with overlapping but not always identical models. Count vendors, not listings, when judging how many options exist.

Summary

The under-$150 electric guitar and bass kit market in the US in June 2026 splits cleanly into two pools.

Pool 1 — US-stocked, genuinely sub-$150: Glarry ($90, US warehouse, solderless), Fistrock ($110, Amazon, solderless, highly reviewed), Leo Jaymz ($89–149, Amazon, solderless), ammoon ($56–105, Amazon/Walmart), Ktaxon ($80–100, Amazon). Covers S-style, T-style, LP, SG, V, Explorer, offset (FretWire), semi-hollow (FretWire, Batking, DBL), P-bass, J-bass, Explorer bass. This pool is the actual $150-and-under market right now.

Pool 2 — Better kits, over $150 landed under current tariffs: Harley Benton ($77–$109 list, ~$180–210 landed), Solo ($120–130 list, ~$180–210 landed), Pit Bull ($119–146 list, ~$200+ landed). These are the most-reviewed and most-documented kits in the world at this price band and should be considered seriously after the Section 122 tariff expires (~July 19, 2026), when the calculation may shift to closer to $145–165 landed for the cheapest HB kits.

Parts builds are possible under $150 with careful sourcing (pre-fretted Amazon neck + scratch poplar body + GFS electronics), but the floor is genuinely $130–150 and requires buying discipline. Not obviously better than buying a kit.

Acoustic guitar is out of scope: no acoustic kit under $150 exists in the US market.

Bass is thinner but covered: Fistrock P-bass ($110) is the standout US-stocked option. Everything over that — Solo, HB, Pit Bull — lands at $200+ under current conditions.

Ukulele

Origin tag

Hawaiian instrument, late 19th century, derived directly from Portuguese immigrants' braguinha (machete) and rajão from Madeira. Standardized by Hawaiian makers (Nunes, Santo, Dias) in the 1880s-1890s. Four nylon strings, re-entrant tuning (gCEA standard, dGBE baritone), fingerpicked or strummed with a felt or thumbnail plectrum. Four standard sizes: soprano (13" scale, ~20.9" total), concert (15" scale, ~23" total), tenor (17" scale, ~26" total), baritone (19" scale, ~30" total). Body construction is side-bent and glued, closer to classical guitar than to folk carved-box instruments.

Close-enough bar

For kit builds: the articulation is fingerpicked/strummed, four nylon strings, re-entrant tuning on soprano/concert/tenor, linear tuning on baritone. A "close enough" build must hit those: plucked/strummed, nylon strings, four courses. Box-body and cigar-box variants trade resonance chamber geometry for simplicity; they play the same way but sound more nasal and quiet. Banjolele and guitalele are close cousins with distinct characters (see Group 4). The braguinha/cavaquinho family is the ancestral lineage, not a substitute.

Anti-default note

The ukulele kit market is genuinely and almost entirely Western-oriented -- specifically US/Hawaiian market. This is not a research gap: Japan (Hosco) is the only non-Western commercial kit supplier. The instrument's non-Western lineage runs through Portuguese Madeira (braguinha, machete, rajão) and is alive as a distinct family of instruments, but no DIY kits for those exist in the US. The honest anti-default result for this family: Western kit market dominates; non-Western lineage documented in Group 4. Hosco (Japan) is the outlier within the kit tier.

Tiple (Colombian or US 10-string) Colombia / early US Ten strings in four courses; plucked/strummed; GAL has Plan #51. The US Martin tiple was made as a uke successor. BOM under $150. GAL Plan #51 (Colombian Tiple) ~$15-35 estimated Plan ~$15-35 + BOM ~$60-100 luth.org [ESTABLISHED plans; PLAUSIBLE price]

Same kit, different label

Commodity Guangdong lineage. Kmise, Aklot, and roughly a dozen other "brands" on Amazon and AliExpress at $15-40 are commodity output from a small number of Guangdong factories: laminate basswood body, plastic nut and saddle, open-gear tuners. These are one OEM source, not competing designs. Kmise is a real registered brand. Most of the others are Amazon storefronts with a sticker on the same kit. IMPORTANT: do not confuse the bare "DIY build kit" (unassembled body + neck + hardware, $15-40) with the same brands' "starter kit bundle" (a finished assembled ukulele sold with a bag, tuner, strap, and picks for $30-60). Both exist on Amazon under similar product names. The DIY build kit is the unassembled one.

Harley Benton is Thomann's house brand. It is commodity basswood spec like the Guangdong OEM kits but it ships from Germany with a proper return path, a 3-year Thomann warranty, and a returns process that actually works. That is the practical reason to choose it over an anonymous Amazon listing at the same price point, not a different instrument.

StewMac general ukulele kits vs. Walnut Tenor. StewMac's general ukulele kits page (soprano, concert, mahogany versions) is showing "out of stock while we work to update the materials" as of June 2026. The Walnut Tenor Kit page (item 5383/5384) is a separate listing and shows IN STOCK. These are distinct products; the OOS notice does not apply to the Walnut Tenor. Verify on the day before ordering.

Hosco is a credible Japanese OEM luthier parts supplier (established 1969). The UK-KIT-5 and UK-KIT-35 soprano kits reach the US only through gray-market Amazon/eBay/Reverb resellers. No US direct storefront. Price and availability are volatile; the instrument is real and well-regarded in Japanese luthier circles but the US supply chain is informal.

Stock and discontinuation alerts (as of 2026-06-05)

  • StewMac general ukulele kits (mahogany soprano/concert/baritone): OOS as of June 2026. StewMac statement: "out of stock while we work to update the materials." No return date given. Email notification available on product page. The walnut tenor kit is a separate listing and is IN STOCK.
  • StewMac Walnut Tenor: In stock as of June 2026 at $95.28 (walnut top) / $100.28 (spruce top). Prices reflect a sale; original $120/$125. Verify current price before ordering.
  • Harley Benton Soprano: $14.70 through June 10, 2026 (promotional price); expect it to return to ~$17-18 after that date.
  • Ohana TK-KIT Tenor: $149 MSRP puts it exactly at the $150 ceiling; some retailers list it below MSRP (~$99-109 at Aloha City Ukes, per prior research). Verify retailer price.
  • Hosco kits: Gray-market reseller supply; check eBay/Amazon/Reverb listings day-of. Inventory is not stable.
  • Commodity OEM kits: Amazon/AliExpress listings come and go under rotating brand names. Price and exact spec vary. The OEM behind them is stable but specific listings are not.

Bottom line

The ukulele is the deepest kit market in the fretted folk instrument space, and almost everything is under $150. The tiers sort clearly:

Cheapest real path: Harley Benton Soprano ($14.70-18) or Commodity Guangdong ($15-40). Both work and both have the same core issue: the bridge placement in printed instructions (HB explicitly, commodity implicitly) is wrong and must be set by measuring 2x the nut-to-12th-fret distance. Treat the instructions as assembly guidance, not as intonation guidance.

Best overall kit for traditional construction: StewMac Walnut Tenor ($95-100). Pacific walnut laminate back/sides, choice of solid walnut or solid spruce top, 10-part free video series by Dan Erlewine, proper instruction book, fits together cleanly. It is genuinely the standard by which others are compared. Only tenor size is currently available.

Best size range coverage: Ohana SK/CK/TK-KIT ($79-149). Soprano through tenor in one product family, consistent spec, consistent instructions, video tutorial on the Ohana site. The pineapple concert (PKC-KIT) is a bonus variant not in most competitor lines. These are decorate-and-play kits more than luthier kits -- the basswood is optimized for painting, not for acoustic performance.

Best US-made option: CB Gitty Gittylele Soprano ($55) or Tenorlele ($95). Laser-cut birch plywood in New Hampshire. The Tenorlele is the only kit in the under-$150 band that ships with a pickup installed.

Baritone situation: Nothing complete under $150 with body. The MGB partial kit ($42.50) gives you a quality neck + hardware; you source or build a wooden box body separately (craft store wooden boxes run $10-25). Plans are cheap and plentiful (GenOne $22, Folkcraft ~$15-20). A scratch baritone BOM lands at $75-120.

Scratch build floor: $50-90 for a soprano from Woodgears or McDonald Strings free plans. GenOne PDFs ($22) cover all four sizes and include Kasha-braced variants for the adventurous.

Confidence audit: Evidence quality: Strong for all kit prices/specs confirmed from seller pages (StewMac, Ohana, CB Gitty, Grizzly, Amahi, Harley Benton, MGB). Moderate for Hosco (reseller pricing only). Moderate for GAL plan prices (range from prior survey, not from direct page fetch). Weak for Hana Lima (page did not render). Biggest confidence limiter: Price volatility and sale pricing in flux (StewMac sale, Harley Benton sale both time-limited). Stock status on StewMac general kits may change. Verify before acting: Current stock and price on StewMac Walnut Tenor (confirm it's still in stock); Ohana TK-KIT retailer pricing (MSRP is $149 but street price varies); Hosco US reseller availability day-of.

Mountain Dulcimer

Orientation

The mountain dulcimer kit market is genuinely deep and well under the $150 cap. This is one of the strongest kit markets in the full catalog: multiple distinct vendors, multiple construction styles, and a rich plans ecosystem. The brief called for an exhaustive sweep, and the field rewards it.

Price note: All prices are research snapshots (June 2026). Verify before acting. Price bands (~$X-Y) used throughout. Confidence flags per source: [ESTABLISHED] confirmed live; [PLAUSIBLE] reasonable inference; [UNCERTAIN] limited evidence; [UNKNOWN] no reliable path found.

URL note: Only URLs confirmed live or appearing across multiple credible sources are included.

Instrument

Origin: Appalachian US folk tradition, early 19th century. The dulcimer was developed in the Shenandoah Valley / southwestern Pennsylvania Appalachians out of a blending of British musical traditions with immigrant European drone-zither forms: primarily the German scheitholt, also the French épinette des Vosges, Swedish hummel, and Norwegian langeleik. Those European ancestors are covered in detail in Build Catalog - Folk Strings Worldwide (entries #25-27, #32). The Appalachian form developed its distinctive hourglass waist, elongated fretboard running the full length of the body, and diatonic noter-and-drone playing style in the mountain communities.

Instrument form: A fretted diatonic zither, 3-4 strings, played flat on the lap. One melody string is fretted chromatically (standard layout) or played with a wooden noter (traditional style). One or two drone strings run unfretted and provide continuous accompaniment. Scale length typically 26-27". Body shapes: hourglass (traditional curving waist), teardrop (single curved end, no waist cut, easier to build), and box/trapezoid (simplest).

Close-enough bar: What transfers completely: the diatonic noter-and-drone playing style; all melody and chord techniques; tuning (D-A-A or D-A-d). The cardboard and plywood builds produce fully playable dulcimers with the same fret spacing and string gauges as a solid-walnut instrument. What the cheap build trades away: tonal richness, sustain, and warmth compared to a solid-walnut or solid-mahogany body. The cardboard builds are acoustically lively and community reports confirm they last decades with care. The laser-cut plywood (Jaromin) body produces noticeably better sustain than cardboard. The trade is real but not a technique or learning barrier.

Group 1: Kits (buy and assemble)

Construction style context

Three distinct kit body styles exist under $150:

Cardboard-box-on-fretboard (Backyard Music, Folkcraft cardboard): Pre-cut corrugated cardboard soundbox glued and assembled onto a pre-fretted solid hardwood fretboard. No woodworking tools; 60-120 minutes to finish. Fully playable and durable. Community consensus: the fretboard is the acoustically important part, and both vendors use real wood fretboards with properly installed metal frets. Cardboard is acoustically different from solid wood (brighter, less sustain) but not inferior for learning and playing.

Laser-cut plywood (Jaromin): 1/8" Baltic birch plywood body with box-jointed press-fit assembly, combined with a fretted hardwood neck (oak, cherry, or walnut). Intermediate between cardboard and solid wood in construction permanence and tone. About one hour assembly.

Solid wood kits exist but are all over budget: Folkcraft Black Walnut Hourglass ($395), Musicmakers Hourglass ($399, also SOLD OUT June 2026). These are noted at the bottom for context.

Group 2: Plans and Written Tutorials (BOM under $150)

BOM note

A teardrop body avoids side bending entirely (single gentle curve at one end only; the sides are bent once, with no waist cut). A box/trapezoid body requires no bending at all. An hourglass body requires bending the sides at the waist -- two curved bends per side. Bending iron rental or purchase (~$40-100) is an additional cost for hourglass builds. The GenOne plans include a heated side bender you build yourself from scratch; the Musicmakers hardware kit pairs with their plan download.

BOM estimate (typical Folkcraft-hardware-based build):

  • Folkcraft hardware kit (configured): ~$57-65
  • Folkcraft plan (teardrop or hourglass): $20
  • Wood (pine, poplar, or hardwood): $20-50 from hardware store or StewMac
  • Glue, finish, sandpaper: $10-20
  • Total: ~$107-155. Stays under $150 with careful sourcing and inexpensive domestic woods.

Book canon (plans + text)

All four are genuine references used by the community. None are over budget.

  • Dean Kimball "Constructing the Mountain Dulcimer" -- Standard beginner luthiery reference; full construction plans included. Borrowable free on Internet Archive (prefer lending copy). Used copies $10-30.
  • Howie Mitchell 1966 booklet -- Early how-to pamphlet; historically important. Limited print run; community scans exist.
  • Robert Force "In Search of the Wild Dulcimer" -- Free PDF from Force's own site (robertforce.com). Covers construction and playing.
  • Foxfire 3 (1975) -- Chapter on Appalachian dulcimer building in traditional context. Prefer the Internet Archive lending copy over unvetted scans.

Key Notes: Community and Sourcing

Live community: Friends of the Mountain Dulcimer (fotmd.com). Everything Dulcimer, the longtime community hub, went down ~2023; its successor for active builder discussion is FOTMD. The FOTMD builders forum is active and responsive for build questions.

Fretboard sourcing for box builds: Backyard Music (Willimantic CT) sells a pre-fretted fretboard with all hardware (tuners, strings, nut, bridge, end pins) for $50 via direct email (backyard.music.instruments@gmail.com, ask for "the Mandy Fretboard"). This is the key component for anyone building a wooden body from scratch without wanting to source and install frets themselves.

Folkcraft hardware: The Folkcraft hardware kit (folkcraft.com, ~$57-65 configured) is the community's preferred go-to parts source. Machine heads available in two styles (open-gear bone or chrome), two nut/bridge widths; choose at checkout. 96 reviews, 96% five-star.

Fretting a scratch build: Fret wire from Folkcraft ($12/4 feet) is a standard material. Fret spacing for a 26.5-27" VSL dulcimer can be calculated at strothers.net (free online diatonic fret calculator) or taken directly from any of the plans listed above.

Bottom Line

The dulcimer kit market is the deepest and best-documented kit market in the Sub-$150 series. Three genuinely distinct kit types exist under $150, plus a plans ecosystem with both paid and free options, and a video build library that goes back a decade.

Cheapest real kit: Backyard Music Simplicity at $69. Cardboard soundbox, real wood pre-fretted board, plays as a proper diatonic dulcimer from day one. The community is explicit: the fretboard is the acoustically critical part, and this fretboard is spot-on. Decades of documented community builds confirm durability.

Best wood-body kit under $100: Jaromin at ~$90. Laser-cut birch plywood body, hardwood neck (choose oak/cherry/walnut), Corian fittings, one-hour assembly. Significantly better sustain than cardboard, under $100.

Best plans path: Mandy Tyner free box build (~$70 all-in, includes the $50 Backyard Music pre-fretted fretboard) is the cheapest all-up wood dulcimer build in the catalog. WJC001 (Woodworker's Journal, free PDF) is the best free plan for a traditional teardrop/hourglass build.

Folkcraft plans + hardware route: $20 plan + $57-65 hardware kit + $20-50 wood = $97-135 all-in for a traditional solid-wood scratch build.

The key trade across all cheap builds: Cardboard lasts, but solid wood sounds better. Plywood is the middle path. All three play the same technique identically; the trade is tonal depth, not playability.

REPORT-BACK

Mandolin & Banjo

Orientation: the honest-ceiling problem

These two instruments have the thinnest under-$150 kit market in the fretted-folk family. The acoustic mandolin kit that everyone points to (Saga AM-10) costs $249.95. The 5-string banjo kit everyone used to point to (Saga RK-2/OK-2) is gone from Saga's own kit page. This catalog is honest about that: where only one or two live options exist after a full search, it says so rather than padding.

The anti-default check was run for both instruments. Mandolin is Italian in origin; a pass through Chinese (liuqin), Greek (bouzouki), Turkish (saz), Andean (charango), and other plucked-chordophone traditions found no US-accessible kit market at under $150 for those instruments as of June 2026 -- the field is genuinely absent, not missed. For banjo, the West African gourd-lute ancestry (akonting, ngoni, xalam) is documented below; it is also the most interesting cheap-build path in this entire catalog.

MANDOLIN

Origin tag: Italy, late 17th c., Neapolitan bowl-back style; A-style (oval hole) and F-style (scroll, f-holes) American descendants dominant in bluegrass and old-time traditions. Instrument carried into North American folk music via Italian immigration and adapted by country and bluegrass musicians.

Close-enough bar: 8-string (4 paired courses), fretted neck, plectrum-played, GDAE tuning. Arched carved top and back are the structural and sonic signature of the "real" mandolin; a flat-top box body produces a different tone (woodier, less sustain, less projection). A flat-top or box-body build transfers the fingering and plectrum articulation fully but trades away the arched-top resonance that defines the classical mandolin sound. Label those builds plainly as flat-top or box-body mandolins.

Group 1: Kits

The confirmed under-$150 kit field for mandolin is thin. The two traditional-body A-style kits (Saga AM-10, IVC MK0) both run over $150 for a retail buyer. One partial kit and one electric kit qualify on price; the traditional acoustic kit market sits above the ceiling.

OEM note: The Saga AM-10 and the International Violin MK0 are the same Chinese-OEM kit under different labels. Mandolin Cafe build threads have confirmed this identity repeatedly. Folkmusician, Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, and Zoro all resell at $228-$270; IVC sells the same kit at $135 to dealers only. Do not count these as separate sources.

What the MGB kit actually is: This is the only confirmed in-stock under-$150 mandolin kit for a retail buyer. It is a partial kit: neck, fretboard, bridge, tailpiece, tuners, and 8 strings (GDAE). You provide the body -- a cigar box works, but the box needs significant reinforcement because 8 mandolin strings create real tension. MGB's own description recommends a top surface close to 3/8" thick where the neck joins. Reviews (16 reviews, 100% positive) consistently praise the neck quality and value; builders note that the fret ends benefit from light dressing. The result is a flat-top box-body mandolin, not an arched-top A-style. Tone is different: warmer, woodier, less sustain. Fingering and plectrum articulation are identical.

What the MT-10 electric actually is: Pre-mounted pickup and volume/tone controls, no soldering required. Bolt-together solid body. Mixed Amazon reviews; noisy electronics at this price point. Stock is erratic; check Saga's page and Amazon/eBay for resale. If it comes back in stock it is the cheapest route to an electric mandolin build at under $150. [ESTABLISHED on spec, UNCERTAIN on availability]

The AM-10 at $249.95 does not qualify under $150. It is documented here because it is the dominant mandolin kit reference and the IVC MK0 trade route requires clarification.

Group 2: Plans + Written Tutorials

For a from-scratch A-style mandolin, the plan itself is the cheap part. The BOM (wood + hardware) is where the cost lives. A typical A-style BOM:

  • Spruce top blank: ~$20-30 (StewMac, Exotic Woods, or similar)
  • Maple back + sides: ~$25-45
  • Maple neck blank: ~$15-25
  • Rosewood or equivalent fretboard: ~$12-20
  • Fretwire (18-fret set): ~$5-12
  • Economy 8-peg tuner set: ~$15-30
  • Bridge, nut, tailpiece, strings: ~$20-35
  • Binding, finish, glue: ~$15-25

Total BOM: roughly $130-220 depending on wood quality and hardware grade. Landing under $150 requires deliberate economy: the cheapest credible tonewoods, economy tuners, and DIY finishing with oil or wipe-on poly. It is achievable but not guaranteed and requires careful sourcing. [PLAUSIBLE]

For the flat-top cigar-box variant: MGB kit ($60) + reinforced cigar box ($5-15 from CB Gitty or a tobacco shop) + finish materials (~$10) = ~$75-85 total. Easily under $150. [ESTABLISHED]

An F-style from scratch is a 200-400+ hour project and the BOM for quality carved wood almost certainly exceeds $150.

Mandolin Bottom Line

Cheapest real path: MGB partial kit ($60) + reinforced cigar box (~$10) = ~$70-85. Flat-top box-body mandolin; real fingering, real plectrum technique, different tone.

Cheapest traditional-body path: From-scratch A-style using economy tonewoods and a $23-35 plan set. BOM can land under $150 with disciplined sourcing; more likely to run $140-170. Requires full lutherie skills including neck carving, fretwire installation, and setup.

Electric path: Saga MT-10 at $129.95 when in stock. The only sub-$150 electric mandolin kit in the US; currently OOS.

Key trade: The AM-10 at $250 is the real traditional-body kit. Under $150, you are either building a box-body instrument (MGB route, easy, different tone) or a from-scratch acoustic (hard, right tone, tight budget). No middle ground exists in the current US market.

BANJO

Origin tag: American, with West African roots. The banjo descends from gourd-body, skin-head lutes brought to the Americas by enslaved West Africans: the Jola akonting (Senegal/Gambia/Guinea-Bissau), the Mande ngoni, the Wolof xalam, and related instruments. Early American banjos were gourd-body tackhead instruments; the modern 5-string open-back descends from those traditions via 19th-century minstrel banjo. The resonator bluegrass banjo is a 20th-century development. The gourd banjo build is therefore not a "folk" alternative -- it is the ancestor.

Close-enough bar: The canonical 5-string banjo has a short drone string (the 5th) anchored partway up the neck, a floating bridge on a tensioned membrane head, and is played with finger picks (three-finger bluegrass) or bare fingers (clawhammer/frailing old-time). The 4-string (Irish tenor, plectrum) uses a plectrum and a different tuning (CGDA tenor or GDAE). A box-body or fretless instrument transfers the overall technique but changes the acoustic character fundamentally: the floating-bridge-on-membrane is what gives the banjo its sound. Label any box-top banjo as such.

Honest ceiling statement

After a complete search of the US kit market in June 2026, there is one in-stock under-$150 banjo kit. The traditional round-pot 5-string kit market has effectively collapsed at this budget level: Saga has discontinued its BJ-10/RK-2/OK-2 line (gone from their kit page as of 2026), Backyard Music has paused all production ("until further notice"), and Gold Tone's MC-KIT line was discontinued earlier. The CB Gitty Country Roads kit at $144.99 qualifies on price and is in stock, but it is a box-top instrument, not a round-pot banjo. The most compelling under-$150 banjo paths are the from-scratch gourd and tackhead builds -- which happen to be the most historically authentic ones.

Akonting note: This is not a curiosity addition -- it is the most direct ancestor of the American 5-string banjo, with the same stroke/frailing technique and the same short drone-string concept. Building one from Havlena's free plans costs roughly $30-60 in materials (mostly gourd + neck + tuning pegs + skin or drum head). It is simultaneously the cheapest build in this catalog and the most historically significant one. Anyone interested in old-time clawhammer banjo should know about it.

Banjo Bottom Line

Only confirmed in-stock under-$150 kit (June 2026): CB Gitty Country Roads at $144.99. Box-top, 3 or 4 strings. Correct fretted technique; different acoustic character from a round-pot banjo.

Best under-$150 5-string banjo path: From-scratch gourd banjo using Havlena's free plans. BOM ~$65-115. This is the instrument's ancestral form, plays with clawhammer articulation, and costs less than any kit.

Best historical depth: Akonting from Havlena's free plans at ~$30-60. Technically a cousin but more authentic to the banjo's origins than any commercial kit.

Plans if you want a conventional open-back: Folkcraft's $20 mailed plans (5-string open-back or fretless mountain are the best entry points) + economy hardware. BOM ~$110-150. Rim lamination or stave construction is the gating skill.

5-string kit market status: Effectively gone below $150. Backyard Music (best-reviewed option historically) is paused and OOS. Saga's traditional kits are discontinued. This is not a gap to fill with substitutes -- it is the honest ceiling of this market segment.

Same-OEM / Relabel Watch

  • Saga AM-10 = International Violin MK0. One Chinese-OEM kit, two labels, two very different price tiers ($250 retail vs. $135 dealer-only). Mandolin Cafe has confirmed the identity. Do not count as separate options.
  • The CB Gitty Country Roads Banjo Kit is CB Gitty's own product, made in their New Hampshire shop. It is not a relabeled import.
  • Backyard Music banjos are designed and built by the company in Connecticut. Not a relabeled import.
  • The generic "cheap mandolin kits" on Amazon ($30-50) at this budget are fully assembled beginner mandolins, not build kits. They do not appear in this catalog as kits.

Confirmed OOS / Discontinued as of June 2026

  • Saga RK-2 and OK-2 banjo kits: gone from Saga's kit catalog; resale-only
  • Backyard Music all banjo kits: production paused, all OOS; could resume
  • Saga MT-10 electric mandolin: OOS at Saga direct; resale on Amazon/eBay at variable prices
  • Gold Tone MC-KIT resonator and open-back: previously discontinued (prior survey)

Lyre & Harp

Orientation

Lyres and harps are related but distinct instrument families that span cultures from Ethiopia and Eritrea to Scandinavia to the Middle East. Both use strings stretched over a resonating body; the key structural difference is that lyres have a yoke and two arms framing the strings (all strings roughly the same length), while harps have a soundboard-column-neck triangle with strings of graduated length. For building purposes, this matters: lyres are generally simpler and cheaper to build from scratch; harps require more precision, more hardware, and (if you want key-changing) sharping levers that are a separate budget entirely.

Lyre anti-default note: Lyres are routinely defaulted to the ancient Greek or Anglo-Saxon form in English-language instrument-making content. They are not. The krar (Ethiopia and Eritrea), the kinnor (Hebrew/Middle Eastern), and multiple other bowl-lyre and box-lyre forms exist globally and some have build paths. This file covers the full spectrum.

Lyres vs. finished Amazon "lyres": The mass-market "7-string lyre" sold on Amazon and AliExpress is typically marketed as a "DIY kit" but is better understood as a pre-cut, pre-drilled assemble-and-string kit (no woodworking skill required, just assembly). Fully finished identical instruments also exist at the same price point. For the purposes of this catalog, the 7-string and 16-string Amazon lyres are listed under Group 1 (Kits) because they require assembly, but with a note that finished versions are interchangeable at the same price.

THE HARP LEVERS CALLOUT (read before the harp section)

Sharping levers are the single biggest hidden cost in harp building and the main reason most harp builds blow the $150 budget even when the kit does not. They are rarely included in any harp kit or plan; they are a second project installed after the harp is finished, strung, tuned to pitch, and stable.

  • Approximate per-lever costs (2026): Loveland ~$17-18 each, Truitt ~$26 installed, Camac ~$34 installed. [ESTABLISHED on order of magnitude; PLAUSIBLE on exact figures]
  • Fully levering a 34-string harp: ~$600-1,150+ on top of any kit cost.
  • The under-$150 harp path is either (a) lever-less or (b) plans-only where levers are deferred indefinitely.
  • String sets are model-specific and not interchangeable. A generic 34-string nylon set runs ~$50-60; maker-specific wound bass string sets are higher. [PLAUSIBLE]
  • New strings on any harp or lyre require 1-2+ weeks of repeated retuning before holding pitch.

PART ONE: LYRES (WORLDWIDE)

1. Generic 7-String Assemble-and-String Lyre (Modern; floor entry)

Origin: Modern; manufactured in China, marketed globally. Design draws loosely on ancient Greek lyre aesthetics. Sold under many brand names on Amazon, AliExpress, and Etsy worldwide.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: plucked 7-string lyre, basic finger-plucking technique, diatonic or re-entrant tuning. What the build trades away: any tonal depth or sustain compared to a properly built wooden instrument; QC consistency varies significantly between units. This is the floor entry, not a fidelity claim.

Kit note (per the brief): These are assemble-and-string kits (insert posts, set bridge, tension strings -- an evening's work), not woodworking projects. Fully finished versions of the identical instrument also exist in the same $25-60 price band; the distinction matters only if you want to say you "built" it.

3. Ancient Greek Lyra / Kithara (Mediterranean)

Origin: Ancient Greek tradition (1200 BCE to late Antiquity); the lyra (bowl-resonator, arm-yoke-crossbar construction) and kithara (box resonator, larger, professional form). Revived by the modern ancient-music scene.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: plucked multi-string lyre with arms and crossbar; finger-or-plectrum plucking; diatonic or re-entrant tuning. What the build trades away: traditional tortoiseshell bowl resonator (legally off the table; a wooden or IKEA bowl is the standard substitute), the specific tonal character of an authentic kithara soundboard. The playing technique (plectrum strumming with simultaneous left-hand damping) is fully achievable on a scratch build.

Under $30 total materials for any of these. The Getty cardboard version is a genuine under-$5 proof-of-concept. Luthieros is the reference modern-Greek-lyre maker but sells only finished instruments; their "full package" accessory bundle (bridges, plectra, strap, gut strings) is NOT a build kit.

4. Kinnor / Biblical Lyre (Middle East / Hebrew tradition)

Origin: Hebrew/Israelite tradition; the kinnor is the biblical instrument associated with King David. A bowl or box lyre, 10 strings traditionally, plucked with fingers or a plectrum. Played across the ancient Near East; modern reconstructions range from simple to highly ornate.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: multi-string plucked lyre, plectrum or finger technique. What the build trades away: the specific tonal character of a traditional kinnor, which is debated among scholars (the exact original form is uncertain).

Kit gap note: A true kinnor build kit essentially does not exist. The cheap 7-string Amazon lyres are sometimes marketed as "King David lyres" or "kinnor" and are the closest thing in kit form. Dedicated kinnor kit makers do not appear to exist.
