5. Krar (Ethiopian / Eritrean Bowl Lyre)

Origin: Tigrinya/Amhara tradition, Ethiopia and Eritrea. A 5- or 6-string bowl lyre, plucked with a plectrum or fingers. The resonator is traditionally a wooden bowl or gourd covered with skin; modern forms use a wooden box resonator. One of Africa's primary surviving lyre traditions. Closely related to the ancient Greek lyre family.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: plucked pentatonic/heptatonic bowl lyre, plectrum technique, yoke-and-arms structure. What the build trades away: the skin-covered bowl resonance if substituting a drum-head-and-hardware assembly (audible difference; the JOS design below uses this substitution intentionally and considers it a functional trade). Full gourd or wooden bowl versions are more traditional.

6. Begena (Ethiopian Large Bass Lyre; Build Path Status)

Origin: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church tradition; a 10-string large bass box-lyre used in sacred music and meditation. Associated with King David in Ethiopian cultural tradition. A living sacred instrument, not just a historical artifact.

Build path: [UNKNOWN] No English-language DIY plans found. The begena is a large instrument (approximately 1 meter frame height) with a complex wooden box resonator, stretched skin soundboard, 10 strings arranged in two banks of five, and tuning toggles. The Folk Strings Worldwide file also flags this as a confirmed [UNKNOWN] path.

If you want to attempt it anyway: The construction is a scaled-up box-lyre (similar logic to the kinnor or Anglo-Saxon lyre, entry 7). You would need a large wooden box resonator, stretched rawhide soundboard, two vertical wooden arm pillars, a crossbar, 10 tuning toggles (wooden pegs or metal tuning machine heads), and gut or nylon strings (~$20-40). The total materials cost is potentially under $150, but the plans gap is real: no English-language source exists that documents begena construction dimensions or construction sequence. [UNKNOWN on the build path; [PLAUSIBLE] that raw materials could be under $150 if you derive dimensions from museum photographs and academic documentation]

7. Anglo-Saxon / Germanic Round Lyre (Sutton Hoo, Trossingen, Snape types)

Origin: Anglo-Saxon and Germanic tradition, 5th-10th century CE. A rounded-rectangle box lyre with a hand-hole cutout; 6 strings; one surviving intact instrument is the Trossingen lyre (Merovingian grave, 6th century). Associated with bardic and court music in early medieval Northern Europe.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: 6-string plucked box lyre with hand hole; one hand strums all strings while the other damps the strings not wanted, producing a form of polyphonic melody. The scratch build replicates this completely. What the build trades away: the carved decorative surface of the Trossingen lyre (skip it; it has no acoustic function) and exact aged-wood resonance.

8. Kravik Lyre / Norse Round Lyre (Norwegian tradition)

Origin: Norwegian tradition; the Kravik lyre is a 7-string round lyre surviving from the 16th century in a style continuous with earlier 12th-14th century forms. Associated with Norwegian folk revival musicians including Einar Selvik (Wardruna). A "giant hand-carved spoon" in cross-section -- more three-dimensional and complex to build than the flat Anglo-Saxon lyre.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: 7-string plucked round lyre; the playing technique (similar to the Anglo-Saxon form, but the additional string and curved profile affect voicing). What the build trades away: the warm tonal character of a well-seasoned wood body; the exact rounded-spoon profile (requires gouge work).

PART TWO: HARPS (UNDER $150 AND CONTEXT)

Harp section orientation

Honest reckoning upfront: most harps exceed $150 to build. A 22-string lever-less harp in kit or plans-plus-hardware form lands at $140-180 before wood; a 34-string lever harp kit runs $1,500-1,750 before levers ($600-1,150+ extra). The under-$150 harp is real but narrow: it is the small lever-less lap harp in plans form or the lowest-end hardware kits. Cardboard harps also exist but are over $150. This section documents the genuine under-$150 (or very near) paths and gives honest context for the over-budget options.

Musicmakers (harpkit.com, Stillwater MN) vs. Stoney End (Red Wing MN): These are two different companies. The brief notes they are sometimes conflated. Musicmakers is the kit-and-plans maker covered here. Stoney End is a finished harp maker whose kit status is unconfirmed. Keep them separate. [ESTABLISHED]

10. Musicmakers Shepherd Lap Harp (Plans + Hardware + Strings, Verified June 2026)

Origin: Musicmakers (Stillwater, MN); a 22-string 3-octave walnut lap harp, one of the most documented beginner plans-based harp builds in the US. Design is in the Celtic/folk harp tradition.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: full basic harp technique across 3 octaves (G3-G6); all standard folk harp playing. What the build trades away: sharping levers (not included, deferred; the harp is lever-less unless you buy and install them separately). A lever-less harp locks you into one key per tuning but otherwise plays exactly as a harp.

Verified prices (harpkit.com, observed June 2026): - Shepherd Harp Plan (PDF download): $14.50 (on sale from $29.00) [ESTABLISHED] - Musical Hardware Pack (22 tuning pins, 22 bridge pins, 22 brass eyelets, L-handle wrench; strings NOT included): $59.45 [ESTABLISHED] - Shepherd Harp String Set: $39.00 [ESTABLISHED] - Total from Musicmakers (plans + hardware + strings): $112.95 [ESTABLISHED] - Plus wood: walnut body lumber (hardware store) + soundboard. If you use local birch plywood for the soundboard (~$20-30) and walnut lumber ($20-40), total all-in is approximately $155-185. If you source the Musicmakers Small Soundboard Blank ($69), total climbs to ~$182. Under $150 is achievable only with careful wood sourcing.

13. Paraguayan Folk Harp (Build Path Summary)

Origin: Paraguayan and Venezuelan plains tradition; the harpa paraguaya / harpa llanera is a diatonic lever-less harp, 32-36 strings, lighter and more portable than concert harps. The national instrument of Paraguay.

Close-enough bar: Full folk harp technique; diatonic range; lever-less. The 22-string version gives 3 octaves (reduced from traditional 36+ string range) but the same playing technique.

Build paths (consolidated):

The Kovac kits (entry 12) are the primary hardware kits. The Sligo Waldorf free plan (entry 11) and Kovac's "Harpmaking Made Simple" book are the primary plans resources. An Instructables build (Building a 35-String Paraguayan Harp, 24 steps) exists as a detailed video-adjacent tutorial.

The two commercially established cardboard educational harp kits are:

Owner reports on Harp Column forums are consistently warm: sturdy, light, low tension, travel-proof, quiet, repairable. They are real instruments, not toys; they are simply not under $150. If budget flexibility exists to ~$185-290, these are the easiest complete one-stop harp build.

MATERIAL SOURCING NOTES

Zither pins / tuning pins for lyres: elderly.com (small packs, ~$0.55-0.75 each), Musicmakers (harpkit.com), Folkcraft.

Harp hardware (tuning pins, bridge pins, eyelets, strings): Musicmakers (harpkit.com), John Kovac Harps (johnkovac.com).

Harp strings (model-specific): Musicmakers (Shepherd set $39), John Kovac (included in kits), generic nylon replacement sets on Amazon/eBay (~$50-60 for 22-34 strings unconfirmed on quality).

Hardwood for lyres (maple, oak, ash, walnut): Hardware stores for dimensional lumber; Woodcraft; local hardwood dealers; StewMac (small pieces). For the Anglo-Saxon lyre, Friedman specifically notes 1/8" hardwood plywood (available at Home Depot in 4'x8' sheets for ~$10) works as a soundboard substitute.

Lyre strings: Nylon guitar strings (pairs of G, B, E) work well per Friedman's plans. Fishing line (monofilament 40-60 lb) is a traditional substitute per Havlena. Full string sets for 7-string lyres on Amazon: ~$5-10.

Friction pegs (for bowl lyres like krar): Amazon (violin-style friction peg sets, $5-15); StewMac; elderly.com.

ANTI-DEFAULT CHECK: WESTERN VS. NON-WESTERN SPLIT

Instruments / build paths covered:

Non-Western origins: - Generic modern lyre (Chinese manufacture, global): 2 entries (7-string kit, 16-string finished) -- neutral/global - Ancient Greek lyra/kithara (Mediterranean): 1 - Kinnor / Biblical lyre (Middle East / Hebrew): 1 - Krar (Ethiopia / Eritrea, East Africa): 1 - Begena (Ethiopia, East Africa, no build path): 1 - Paraguayan folk harp (Latin America): 1 (consolidated with entries 11-12)

Western / Northern European origins: - Anglo-Saxon / Germanic round lyre: 1 - Kravik / Norse round lyre: 1 - Michael J. King comprehensive plans (covers both Western and non-Western lyre types): 1 - Musicmakers Shepherd Lap Harp (Celtic/folk tradition): 1 - Sligo Harps Waldorf (European pedagogical): 1 - John Kovac kits (Paraguayan form, but US maker): 1 (overlaps with Paraguayan above)

By instrument count (excluding duplicates and the "over budget" context section): roughly 6 non-Western and 5 Western origins, with the generic lyres and Kovac kits being cross-regional.

Anti-default verdict: PASS with caveats. Lyres as a family are genuinely global and the catalog reflects this (Greek, Ethiopian, Middle Eastern, Anglo-Saxon, Norse all covered). The harp under-$150 market is thin and predominantly US/European in its surviving kit and plans infrastructure -- that reflects the actual market, not a research default. The krar (East Africa) and kinnor (Middle East) are both documented fully, including the genuine kit gap for both. Begena is confirmed [UNKNOWN] rather than omitted.

CONFIDENCE AUDIT

  • Evidence quality: Strong for all Musicmakers Shepherd prices (fetched from harpkit.com, June 2026), Sligo Harps Waldorf plan (confirmed live), Kovac kit prices (confirmed in Folk Strings file June 2026), David Friedman lyre plans (live fetch June 2026), King's Kravik plans price (live fetch from payhip June 2026), all Amazon lyre listings. Moderate for Joy of Sound krar materials costs (UK design, US materials estimates). Weak for begena build BOM (no plans exist), Etsy Anglo-Saxon kit price range ($200-400 is an estimate).
  • Biggest confidence limiter: The harp under-$150 market is genuinely thin. The two Kovac kits at ~$145 are confirmed near-budget but their all-in cost with materials is ~$165-175. The Sligo Waldorf free plan is the cleanest under-$150 path but requires local wood sourcing that varies in cost. No harp kit under $150 with wood included exists in the US market.
  • One thing to verify externally before acting: For the Musicmakers Shepherd, confirm the sale price ($14.50 for plans) is still active before ordering -- sale prices on harpkit.com have a history of returning to full price. For Backyard Music Fireside, verify the current kit price (discrepancy between $189 and $289 in research files).

CORRECTIONS AND FLAGS FOR MARK

  1. Musicmakers vs. Stoney End: Different companies. Musicmakers = harpkit.com, Stillwater MN (kit maker). Stoney End = Red Wing MN (finished harp maker, kit status unconfirmed). The brief calls this out; confirmed kept separate throughout.

  2. Backyard Music price discrepancy: Prior research showed $189 (May 2026); Folk Strings file shows $289 (June 2026); brief says ~$289. Discrepancy is real; verify live at backyardmusic.com.

  3. Waring Harp Kit price in the brief (~$185): The brief says "Waring/Fireside ~$185 is OVER." Waring's Mini kit is indeed ~$185; the Standard is ~$225. The $185 figure is accurate for the Mini.

  4. Amazon lyre "finished not kit": The brief says to note this. Clarification: 7-string Amazon lyres are marketed as "DIY kits" (assemble-and-string); they are not woodworking builds. Fully identical finished (pre-assembled, ready-to-play) versions also exist in the same price band. For the 16-string Amazon lyres, most are sold as finished instruments. Both are noted throughout.

  5. Musicmakers Shepherd plans "bundle": Not a single bundle SKU. Three items bought separately. Confirmed total $112.95 + wood.

REPORT-BACK

Bowed Strings

Price and Confidence Notes

All prices are research snapshots (June 2026). Prices drift; verify before acting. Price bands (~$X-Y) are used throughout. Confidence flags: [ESTABLISHED] well-documented; [PLAUSIBLE] reasonable inference, not directly verified; [UNCERTAIN] limited or contested evidence; [UNKNOWN] outside reliable knowledge.

De minimis note (repeated from prior survey): The US duty-free de minimis exemption remains fully suspended for all countries as of June 2026 (suspended for China/HK May 2025, all other countries August 2025, continued February 2026). Every imported package now faces formal customs entry and full duty. This matters because several white-instrument sources are Romanian, German, or Chinese. US domestic sources (Saga/Anton Breton, StewMac, Metropolitan Music, Old World Tonewood) have a real price advantage now.

Orientation: The Master Structural Fact

The under-$150 reality for bowed strings is overwhelmingly on the electric side. Here is why.

Acoustic bowed instrument building is hard at every tier because the arched carved top, the bass bar, the soundpost, the graduation, and the varnish are all acoustically load-bearing. A wrong graduation can produce an unplayable top; a poorly fit soundpost can collapse the instrument or kill the tone. The result is that every serious acoustic violin kit currently retails above $150 (the StewMac Fiddle Kit is $265.82; the Saga/Anton Breton white violins start at $139.95 for the body but completing one adds $70-100+ in finishing supplies). There is no acoustic cello kit at any price point. There is no acoustic double-bass kit in the ordinary sense.

Electric solid-body bowed building inverts the difficulty almost entirely. No soundpost. No bass bar. No arched-plate carving. No f-holes. The body shape matters almost nothing for acoustic resonance, because you are amplifying via a pickup. The result: a working electric violin can be built from a 3D-print file and a cheap piezo for around $70-100. A working EUB can be built from free plans and a hardware-store mahogany board for under $150. The DIY electric bowed scene is not a footnote; it is the main event at this budget.

This catalog is structured accordingly: electric sections lead, acoustic sections follow with honest treatment of where things actually land on the $150 ruler.

SECTION 1: Electric Solid-Body Violin and Viola

Origin: Western violin/viola as the playing-technique substrate (Italian Baroque tradition, fully developed by the 17th century), applied to a solid-body electric form pioneered by 20th-century electric violinists and the modern open-source maker community.

Close-enough bar: What transfers completely: standard violin technique (GDAE tuning, shoulder rest, chin rest, left-hand stopping, right-hand bowing, all of it). Viola transfers completely on CGDA. What the solid-body electric trades away: acoustic projection without an amp (you need a cable, headphone amp, or PA); tonal warmth (a piezo in a 3D-print body sounds like a thin electric, not a carved maple-and-spruce violin). For practice and exploration it is fully functional. For unplugged performance it is not.

Pickup note, relevant throughout this section: For a DIY electric bowed instrument, pickup choice determines most of the character. The cheapest path is a raw piezo disk ($2-5 on Amazon) wired to a 1/4" mono jack ($2-5) -- this works, it has hum and impedance issues, but a builder can troubleshoot. The next step up is a guitar saddle-style piezo transducer with a shielded lead ($5-15). Above that, a commercial bridge-mount transducer intended for violin/viola ($30-100) produces a noticeably more balanced result. Unless a build note specifies otherwise, the price figures below include a $10-20 budget piezo + jack as the pickup.

1a. 3D-Print Designs (Files Free or Low-Cost; Materials Under $150)

These are the clearest under-$150 electric bowed builds. Files are free or nearly free; cost is filament plus purchased hardware plus a pickup.

Printer notes: All of the above require a standard FFF/FDM printer (PLA or PETG recommended; PLA degrades in heat). Bed size needed varies: Hovalin needs ~200x300mm across two prints; the Modular Fiddle is designed to print in sections on a smaller bed. None require supports on most sections. A borrowed or makerspace printer brings the filament-only cost to ~$15-20 per print.

Bottom line for 3D-print electric violin: Hovalin is the safest bet for a first acoustic/electric printable violin ($70 including electrification, massive community, actively maintained). The Modular Fiddle is the better long-term platform if you want to explore viola/5-string/electric-acoustic configurations and want a community around the build. JAx/Mina is a second option if you want the wiring-channel feature. The F-F-Fiddle exceeds budget.

1d. Mislabeled (Don't Buy These as Build Kits)

Any "$50-$200 electric violin kit" on Amazon or AliExpress (Cecilio CEVN-1, NAOMI, unbranded) is a finished instrument with accessories in a box, not an unassembled build. "Kit" in this market means "outfit with a bow, headphone amp, and a case." There is no budget unassembled electric violin kit at that price point.

SECTION 2: Electric Upright Bass (EUB)

The deepest, most active single DIY corner in the whole bowed-string family. The EUB scene lives in free plans and a rich TalkBass community build culture, not in commercial kits, because no EUB kit exists at any price.

Origin: Upright bass, Italian origin (double bass emerged from the viol family in the 16th-17th century); the electric upright is a 20th-century spinoff. Standard arco technique transfers fully from double bass; pizzicato players who have never bowed can learn arco on a well-set-up EUB.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: upright bass playing posture, left-hand technique, right-hand bowing (for arco-capable builds). What the EUB trades away: the resonant boom of an acoustic double bass (even a good EUB with a large piezo bridge is thinner acoustically; it works through an amp). For rehearsals, practice, recording, and gigging with PA support, a well-built EUB is a real instrument. For an orchestral acoustic section, it is not.

Critical arco note on the Libellula (read this first): The standard Libellula (35" scale, 7.25" fingerboard radius, 0.75" string spacing at bridge) is designed and documented as a pizzicato-only instrument. The fingerboard radius is too large and the string spacing too narrow for a bow to clear adjacent strings cleanly. Mottola explicitly says so on the instrument page. The 3/4 beta plan (41" scale per the plan filename) has "fingerboard and bridge dimensions suitable for arco playing" and is the version to build for bowing. Both plans are free downloads on the same page.

Group 1: Commercial Kits

No EUB kit exists at any price point. The Pulga/Moscha (below) would be the first if released.

Community Build Scene: TalkBass

The TalkBass EUB subforum is the deepest single DIY resource for bowed-string builders anywhere. Key threads:

  • Homebuilt EUB megathread -- 546+ replies, 43,000+ views, active through 2026. The go-to place for build questions, setups, material sourcing, and photos of completed instruments.
  • "Baby Bass" sticky -- 369,000+ views; DIY builds of baby bass / EUB style instruments.
  • "34-inch scale EUB build" thread -- for those who want bass-guitar ergonomics on an upright body.

All at https://www.talkbass.com/forums/ (search "homebuilt EUB" and "DIY EUB").

Planned-But-Not-Yet-Released: Pulga / Moscha Batch Kit

As of May 2026, a TalkBass community member was developing a batch kit in two scale lengths: "Pulga" (35") and "Moscha" (41"). This kit is not for sale as of the research date. No price, no release date, no SKU. Watch the TalkBass EUB subforum for updates. Included here because the brief specifically calls it out as a notable development to flag.

Folk Cousin: Havlena Washtub Upright Bass

Dennis Havlena (dennishavlena.com/db.htm) documents a 4-string upright bass built on a washtub resonator, using electric bass tuners, a wooden neck, and commercially available bass strings. This is primarily a plucked (pizzicato) instrument by design, but the setup with proper bridge curvature and string height could support arco playing -- the plans do not preclude it. It is closer to a folk bass than a professional EUB.

Havlena says "well under $100" but that was before inflation and assumes no-cost sourcing for some parts. Scale is adjustable. The washtub resonator gives actual acoustic projection -- louder than a typical EUB without amplification. http://dennishavlena.com/db.htm

Bottom line for EUB: Build the Libellula 3/4 beta for a real arco EUB under $150. Build the standard Libellula if pizzicato is sufficient. Both are free plans, one source, well-documented. The TalkBass community is where you go when you have questions. The Havlena washtub bass is a viable folksy alternative if acoustic projection matters more than EUB posture.

SECTION 3: Electric Cello

The electric cello DIY scene is real but thin and uncoordinated. No electric cello kit exists at any price. The from-plans community has two main documented resources. Unlike the EUB scene, there is no community hub equivalent to TalkBass specifically for DIY electric cello builds.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: full cello technique (CGDA, seated posture, bow hold, left-hand stopping). What the solid-body electric trades away: acoustic projection and the characteristic resonant tone of a carved instrument. For amplified playing, a well-built solid-body electric cello is a real instrument.

Under-$150 caveat: Electric cello is the hardest bowed instrument to land cleanly under $150 from scratch. The fingerboard, tuners, endpin, and even a cheap pickup add up faster than for violin. A careful sourcer with some parts already on hand can hit $140-150; a builder starting cold is likely $160-220. Both paths are described.

SECTION 4: Acoustic Violin and Fiddle (Honest Treatment)

The acoustic violin is the ONLY bowed instrument in the family with a real kit market -- and even here, most options are over $150. Here is the honest picture.

Origin: Italian; Brescia and Cremona workshops, mid-16th century. The violin form has been essentially stable for 350+ years. The bowed Western violin transferred across folk traditions globally (Celtic fiddle, Appalachian fiddle, Nordic fiddle, etc.), all using identical or near-identical instruments.

Close-enough bar: For a kit or white-instrument build, the resulting instrument IS a violin (or fiddle) -- technique, tuning, posture all identical. What a cheap white instrument trades away versus a master instrument: tonal complexity and projection. A well-set-up VW-1 white violin or a StewMac kit violin is a real playable instrument; it is not a Stradivarius.

4a. White Instruments (Assembled-In-The-White, Buyer Finishes and Sets Up)

A "violin in the white" is a complete instrument -- carved, boxed, bass bar in, purfling inlaid, neck set -- but raw and unvarnished. The buyer applies varnish/finish, fits and sets the soundpost, fits and carves the bridge, cuts the nut, fits the pegs, and strings up. This is finishing-and-setup work, not from-scratch lutherie.

Zero independent buyer reviews. Romanian origin now attracts US import duty post-de-minimis. https://luthierboutique.com

Bottom line for white violins: The VW-1 at $139.95 is the only white violin body currently available under $150 in the US. It is a real instrument with spruce and maple, not a basswood craft object. BUT completing it to playable condition pushes the total project to roughly $200-240. Honest categorization: the body clears the $150 bar; the project does not. Whether you count it as under-$150 or not depends on whether you already own a bow, peg tools, and finishing supplies.

4b. Assembly-Plus Kit (Over Budget; Most Notable Option)

Kit Price What Notes Link
StewMac Fiddle Kit (#5342) $265.82 [ESTABLISHED] Carved + boxed spruce top/maple back+ribs (in white), machine-shaped neck, ebony fingerboard, nut + saddle, boxwood tailpiece + fine tuner, chinrest, endpin, pegs, maple bridge blank, purfling, bass bar, soundpost blank, instructions The best-documented hobby violin kit in English. You fit the neck, install purfling, fit soundpost, carve bridge, finish. FiddleForum/Fiddle Hangout consensus: "a pretty decent fiddle and real knowledge of how they go together." Over budget at $265.82. Included because it is the name kit in this space and useful context. Add bow + strings + varnish for full completion. https://www.stewmac.com/kits-and-projects/instrument-kits/violin-kits/fiddle-kit/

4c. Craft-Grade Mass-Market Kits (Under $150; Not Real Instruments Acoustically)

Source Price Band What Honest note
Amazon/AliExpress basswood "DIY violin kit" (TUOREN, Jiayouy, Zimo, Shsyue, unbranded) ~$25-80 Basswood body pre-sanded; all hardware included (sometimes bow + strings). Assemble in an afternoon, decorate/paint it Basswood has no acoustic future. The spruce-and-maple structure that gives a violin its voice is completely absent. This is a craft/school project, not an instrument. If you want a painted display object or a first-soldering-adjacent project, it qualifies. If you want a violin that plays in tune and produces a musical sound, it does not qualify. Dismissed universally on lutherie forums for this reason.

Name trap to avoid: Cecilio/Mendini/Cremona "violin kit" ($60-200) is a finished student outfit (case, bow, rosin, extra strings) labeled "kit." It is not a build project.

4d. From-Scratch Plans (Tier 3; Materials Far Over $150)

Included for completeness. A from-scratch acoustic violin requires carved plates, arching, graduation, purfling, and varnish from raw tonewood. The tonewood alone ($150-350 for a violin set) consumes the entire budget before a single cut is made, and the full lutherie tool kit runs $800-2,500.

Plans Cost Notes Link
The Strad technical posters (violin, viola, cello; multiple models) GBP 22.95 flat-rolled (~$29) / GBP 14.95 folded (~$19) Full-size photo + measured outline + arching sections. Gold-standard dimensional reference. No bass poster. https://thestradshop.com
Henry Strobel "Violin Making Step-by-Step" $29.50 (Metropolitan Music) The standard English starting point for amateur violin makers; written for accessibility https://www.metmusic.com

Bottom line for acoustic violin: The only under-$150 acoustic violin body is the VW-1 at $139.95, but the full project runs $200+. There is no under-$150 complete acoustic violin build from scratch -- tonewood alone consumes the budget. The cheapest complete playable violin is the StewMac kit at $265.82. For a builder prioritizing cost, the 3D-print or wood-body electric routes in Section 1 are the real answer.

SECTION 5: Acoustic Viola

The viola has no kit market at any tier equivalent to the violin. No StewMac viola kit exists. The under-$150 picture is essentially nonexistent.

  • White viola bodies: Luthier Boutique (Romania) offers white violas at EUR 550-600 (~$595-660 + import duty; three sizes: 40.5, 41, 41 cm). International Violin lists white violas behind their trade login. No US-domestic under-$150 white viola body was found.
  • From-scratch plans: Strobel's "Viola Making Step-by-Step" ($25) and H.S. Wake's viola plans (Tertis model included) exist. Viola tonewood sets run ~$200-450. Same situation as violin -- materials alone exceed $150.
  • Electric viola: Covered by the OpenFab Modular Fiddle (viola configuration available) and the Barbera guide in Section 1. The electric path is the same as violin; under $150 via 3D-print or wood-body plan.

Honest finding: If you want an acoustic viola, your budget options are extremely thin. If you want an electric viola under $150, the Modular Fiddle viola configuration is the clear path (same plans, Patreon tier for viola files, same hardware kit).

SECTION 6: Acoustic Cello

The cello has no packaged kit at any price. The white-body trade exists but is intermittent and gated.

  • White cello bodies: Available through International Violin's trade channel (~$150-600 per body, price ranges vary by source and quality; login required), from Chinese workshops, or occasionally on Alibaba. Quality varies batch to batch; TalkBass and Maestronet consensus is "usable starting point but expect remediation" (re-graduation of top, bass bar reshaping, bridge fitting, soundpost setup). This is intermediate-to-advanced lutherie work.
  • Tonewood for from-scratch cello: A figured maple back alone runs $675-1,165+ at Old World Tonewood. Cello spruce top ~$300. Full set ~$800-1,800. Build time 350-600 hours. Far over budget.
  • From-scratch plans: Strobel "Cello Making Step-by-Step" ($29.50) is one of the only affordable English cello texts. Multiple Strad cello posters (Montagnana "Farina," "De Munck" Strad, Brothers Amati, Gofriller, Nicolo Amati) at GBP 22.95 each. H.S. Wake cello plans exist.
  • Electric cello under $150: See Section 3.

Honest finding: No acoustic cello build qualifies under $150. The cheapest acoustic path involves a white body from the trade channel at $150-600 plus setup materials. Electric cello (Section 3) is the only path close to $150, and even that is tight.

SECTION 7: Acoustic Double Bass

The acoustic double bass is the least-served instrument in the entire bowed family. There is no kit, there is no stocked white body at any mainstream US retailer, and the from-scratch tradition is better supported by plans than by any kit source.

  • White bass bodies: Found occasionally on eBay or Alibaba. No mainstream supplier stocks them as a retail item. TalkBass characterizes them as "mediocre, needs a lot of work" but salvageable starting points for someone who understands what they are getting into.
  • Tonewood: Bass tonewood is the most expensive in the family. A spruce top ~$340-390; figured maple back ~$550-1,450; neck block ~$320. Total set ~$1,200-2,500+. Build time 500-800+ hours. No path to $150.
  • The one standout from-plans resource: Roger Hargrave's "Making a Double Bass" is a free PDF (~24,000 words, 371 photographs, CC NC-ND) from one of the world's most respected luthiers. It is the definitive free bass-building text in English and TalkBass-endorsed. Available at roger-hargrave.de. H.S. Wake's "To Make a Double Bass" is one of the only other dedicated bass plans. The Strad does not make a double-bass poster. Strobel has no bass title.
  • The Canotto bass (Mottola): Liutaio Mottola's instruments page includes the "Canotto" bass, another free plan from the same source as the Libellula. Worth reviewing alongside the Libellula if a full acoustic upright appeals.

Honest finding: There is no acoustic double bass build anywhere near $150. The cheapest complete path involves a white body at $150-600 (trade/Alibaba, intermittent, remediation required) plus setup materials. The from-plans route with Hargrave is the better starting point philosophically but requires skills and tools far beyond a first-timer. For a bowed bass under $150, the Libellula 3/4 beta EUB (Section 2) is the real answer.

SECTION 8: Pickup Conversions (Electrify What You Already Own)

If you already have an acoustic violin, viola, cello, or bass, the cheapest path to amplification is not to build an electric instrument but to fit a pickup. This is a mature, well-reviewed product market.

Hardanger Fiddle (Hardingfele): Norwegian folk fiddle with sympathetic strings beneath the fingerboard. No English-language kit or under-$150 build plan found. Luthier Boutique offers white hardanger bodies at EUR 800+ (over budget, far over). From scratch is advanced (requires a second set of sympathetic string slots, specialized tuning, different neck angle). A documented under-$150 hardanger build does not appear to exist in English. [UNKNOWN as under-$150 build]

Nyckelharpa: Swedish keyed fiddle. Keys press against the strings to produce notes; bowed with a short bow. A functioning Nyckelharpa requires complex key mechanism + resonant box + fiddle setup. No under-$150 kit or plan was found. Estnord and similar Scandinavian shops sell kits at EUR 500+. [UNKNOWN as under-$150 build]

Pochette / Kit Violin: Tiny 16th-18th century dance master's pocket violin. No kit or commercial plan found. A scratch build from scrap hardwood is feasible: very small body, simple f-holes or round holes, short scale. Could be built from a single hardwood offcut. A builder with the Strobel violin reference and a set of Strad-poster dimensions could scale down to pochette dimensions. Genuine under-$150 path exists in principle, but no documented build was found. [PLAUSIBLE as scratch build; UNKNOWN as published plans]

Hard Scope Notes: What Doesn't Exist

Claim Reality
"Under-$150 acoustic violin kit" Does not exist in the assembled-and-playable sense. The VW-1 white body is $139.95 but adding finishing materials + bow = $200+. The StewMac kit (the real kit) is $265.82.
"Under-$150 acoustic viola/cello/bass kit" Does not exist at any tier. No viola kit exists at any price. No cello kit exists at any price. No bass kit exists at any price.
"Electric violin kit under $150" Does not exist as a commercial boxed unassembled kit. Every "$50-200 electric violin kit" on Amazon is a finished instrument with accessories. The only true commercial electric violin kit is EVL Dragonfly at $600. The under-$150 electric violin paths are 3D-print files and from-scratch wood plans (both covered in Section 1).
"Electric cello kit" Does not exist at any price anywhere. Plans-only path (Carolyn Matthews + Instructables), tight at $150.
"Electric upright bass kit" Does not exist at any price. The planned Pulga/Moscha kit is in R&D, not for sale. Plans-only path (Libellula).
LMII (Luthiers Mercantile International) Closed permanently (announced August 2023, wound down through 2024). Do not cite as a current source. StewMac absorbed some product lines.
Fishman C-100 cello pickup Out of stock; superseded by C-200. Older recommendation lists are stale.
LR Baggs cello pickup No cello model was found in current catalog. Violin model ($189) exists.

Confidence Audit

Evidence quality: Strong for all prices fetched directly from live pages (VW-1 $139.95, VW-3 $319.95, StewMac $265.82, EVL Dragonfly $600, Hovalin $70 BOM, all pickup prices from Gollihur/K&K/Fishman/Schatten). Moderate for OpenFab Modular Fiddle hardware kit price (JS-rendered; prior survey estimated ~$60-100; check at checkout). Plausible for Libellula BOM (~$100-145), Carolyn Matthews electric cello BOM (~$130-200), and Havlena washtub bass BOM (~$75-125) -- all are builder estimates based on publicly known materials, not confirmed purchase receipts.

Biggest confidence limiter: OpenFab hardware kit price and Carolyn Matthews electric cello final BOM are the two entries where the under-vs-over-$150 question is genuinely uncertain. For OpenFab, verify price at the shop page before assuming; for the electric cello, budget to $175 and see where careful sourcing lands.

One thing to verify before acting on any price: Check the Anton Breton VW-1 at $139.95 at a current Saga dealer (not direct from Saga.com, which says "Find a Dealer"). Dealer pricing may vary from the MSRP on the Saga product page.

Non-Western Art Strings

Orientation

This file covers the art-tier plucked lutes and zithers that the master series Non-Western Instrument Kits and Plans survey (Worker GGGGGGG, 2026-05-29) flagged as either "no kit, no plan" or material-blocked. The directive here: confirm the void honestly where it is real, and surface every substitute / synthetic / student / cheap-buy path the void hides.

The dominant finding matches GGGGGGG: for most of these instruments, the wall is material sourcing, not money or skill. Python skin, rare gourds, aged mulberry, and CITES-restricted tonewoods are the recurring gates. Where synthetic skin, hammered dulcimer plans, or sub-$150 factory instruments break the wall, those paths are the value of this entry.

Path-state tags used throughout (each entry leads with one):

  • PLAN - free or low-cost plans exist; build is achievable under $150 in materials
  • SUBSTITUTE - no authentic build path under $150, but a functionally equivalent or close cousin build/buy exists under $150
  • BUY-FINISHED - no build path documented; cheap finished instruments exist under $150 (or close to it)
  • GENUINE VOID - no build, no buy, no sub under $150; honest absence documented

Price note: All prices are research snapshots (June 2026). Bands (~$X-Y) used throughout. Verify live before acting. [ESTABLISHED] = confirmed; [PLAUSIBLE] = reasonable inference; [UNCERTAIN] = not directly confirmed; [UNKNOWN] = no reliable path found.

PART ONE: SOUTH ASIAN ART STRINGS

1. Sitar (Indian Classical)

Path state: GENUINE VOID (build under $150) | BUY-FINISHED: cheapest ~$300

Origin: North Indian Hindustani classical tradition. Long-necked lute with movable metal frets, multiple resonance strings (tarb), a large carved tumba gourd resonator, and the characteristic jiwari buzz.

Close-enough bar: What must transfer: movable frets for micro-pitch adjustment, resonating sympathetic strings, the jiwari buzz tone. What cheap versions trade away: the tumba gourd (US scarce), the carved teak/toon neck joint, the bone bridge for jiwari, and years of precise setup. A "sitarcaster" conversion captures some of the tone but none of the resonance.

The tumba gourd (large calabash, Miraj GI-tagged 2024) is the first material wall, toon/tun wood is the second. Cheapest real instrument is a student Kolkata sitar at ~$300; buy at Musicians Mall USA or Old Delhi Music. The sitarcaster conversion is a creative project, not a sitar substitute. Digital sitar tones: GarageBand's sitar patch or apps like iTabla Pro are free and give the sound but not the playing experience.

2. Tanpura / Tambura (Drone Lute)

Path state: SUBSTITUTE (electronic box ~$90-130 or free app; build is impossible under $150)

Origin: North and South Indian classical music; the foundational drone instrument providing tonal center for vocal and instrumental performance. 4 strings tuned to a root-fifth-octave pattern, plucked in a continuous cycle. No melodic content, no fingering -- all drone.

Close-enough bar: The tanpura's function is purely drone. Any device that produces an accurate continuous harmonic drone in the correct pitch serves the musical function completely. The physical tanpura playing experience (the large resonant body, the ringing overtones) is not reproducible under $150, but the musical function is.

Material wall for build: The physical tanpura requires the largest tumba gourd in the entire Indian instrument family (Miraj gourd, now with a 2024 GI tag that tightly controls the variety to a specific region of Maharashtra). Toon/tun wood neck. Total impossible to source under $150 in the US, and no build documentation exists even at higher cost. The Raagini electronic box is the genuinely sufficient substitute -- it fully serves the musical function at the lower end of its price range.

Bottom line: Buy the Raagini on Amazon or use a free app. The physical build path is a genuine void and it doesn't matter -- the drone function is completely served by electronics. Verify the Raagini PDI-DG base model price before purchasing; the entry-level model has historically been in the $90-120 range but drifts.

3. Sarod (Indian Classical)

Path state: GENUINE VOID (build under $150) | BUY-FINISHED: cheapest ~$276

Origin: North Indian Hindustani classical tradition. Short-necked lute with a metal fingerboard (no frets), goatskin-covered wooden body, steel main strings, and sympathetic resonance strings. The metal fingerboard producing gliding, unfretted pitch is the instrument's defining characteristic.

Close-enough bar: What must transfer: fretless metal fingerboard for smooth gliding, resonant skin body, sympathetic string ringing. What cheap versions lose: the precision metal plate, the goatskin tone, the sympathetic string system.

Build walls: No English or widely available plans exist for the sarod. The metal fingerboard (traditionally a steel plate precision-ground to a concave profile) requires metalworking equipment beyond basic shop tools. The goatskin body and sympathetic string system require specialist fitting. Experimental builders have used maple and walnut as body substitutes with partial success, but no complete Western build documentation exists. Cheapest real sarod is ~$276 from Musicians Mall or similar Kolkata-sourced retailers.

4. Santoor / Santoori (Indian Hammered Dulcimer)

Path state: SUBSTITUTE (build a hammered dulcimer, tune it to Indian/Kashmiri layout; plans abundant under $150)

Origin: Kashmiri classical and folk music, now prominent in Hindustani classical. Trapezoid wooden box, 25-30 courses of 4 strings each, struck with light walnut hammers. Structurally a hammered dulcimer -- the same family as the Persian santur and Western hammered dulcimer.

Close-enough bar: What transfers directly: both hands mallet technique, drone-over-melody texture, the struck-string articulation. What the substitute trades away: the precise Kashmir course layout (different from a Western dulcimer) and the specific wood tonal profile of a traditional santoor. The playing technique and finger articulation transfer completely.

5. Veena (Saraswati Veena, South Indian Classical)

Path state: GENUINE VOID (build under $150) | BUY-FINISHED: ~$350-600

Origin: Carnatic classical tradition, South India. Large carved jackfruit-wood body (kudam), 24 metal frets on a curved fingerboard, additional gourd resonator (kuzhal) attached to the neck, 7 strings (4 main + 3 drone). One of the most complex construction challenges in Indian lutherie.

Close-enough bar: What must transfer: curved fingerboard with specific fret heights for Carnatic gamaka ornaments, two-level string layout (main + drone), gourd resonator acoustics. No sub-$150 instrument or build comes close.

The gourd resonator (kuzhal) adds a separate sourcing challenge. Total build cost even with substitute woods would likely exceed $150 and requires advanced woodworking capacity. The documentation on Scribd and gaatha.org is valuable for understanding construction but falls short of a hobbyist build plan.

PART TWO: CHINESE ART STRINGS

6. Guzheng 古筝 (Chinese Zither)

Path state: PLAN (free, advanced build, genuine path -- ARCHIVE NOW: site sunsetting)

Origin: Chinese zither tradition, 2,500+ years. 21-string (standard modern) movable-bridge zither, curved paulownia soundboard, played with finger picks on the right hand, bends with the left. Related to the Japanese koto, Korean gayageum, and Vietnamese dan tranh.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: right-hand picking with picks, left-hand pressure bends, pentatonic-rooted tuning, movable bridge key changes. What the build trades away: the quality of aged paulownia and precise sound-chamber tuning of a factory instrument. A student-grade build is a fully playable guzheng.

URGENT NOTE: GuzhengAlive is definitively sunsetting. Creator JB has announced the end of the site due to sustained brain injuries, and is paying hosting costs through at least end of 2028. After that, the site may go offline without warning. Archive the How to Make, Build Keys, 3D Model, and Community Builds sections now via the Wayback Machine or local save. The URL to submit for archiving: https://guzhengalive.com/how-to-make-guzheng. Do this before the information is gone. This is the single most complete free English-language build reference for any traditional East Asian zither and it will not be replaced.

Bottom line: The clearest real build path in this catalog. The GuzhengAlive plans give exact dimensions and construction method, community builds confirm it is achievable, paulownia is US-obtainable, and the total BOM is under $150. The soaked-and-pressed soundboard curve is the key technical challenge; a steam-press jig or improvised form handles it. Build this before the site closes.

7. Guqin 古琴 (Seven-String Zither)

Path state: PLAN (scattered sources, advanced build, genuine path)

Origin: Chinese literati tradition, 3,000+ years. 7-string fretless zither (no movable bridges), played flat on a table, with harmonics, slides, and open strings fundamental to technique. UNESCO Intangible Heritage. One of the most philosophically loaded instruments in Chinese culture.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: 7-string open-tuned zither, left-hand slides and harmonics, right-hand plucking. What the build trades away: the tonal character of aged paulownia and the lacquer surface (genuine guqin lacquer -- "deer antler powder and raw lacquer" -- is a multi-year process; substitute lacquer finishes are used by modern builders).

Paulownia sourcing: Available in the US as ornamental/building lumber (Paulownia tomentosa and elongata are common plantings). Specialty instrument wood suppliers stock it. Boards large enough for a guqin top (approx 125cm x 25cm) are available from acoustic instrument suppliers for ~$25-40.

Traditional rule: Chinese luthiers say a guqin takes 18 months minimum (allowing for lacquer curing). A hobby build with oil finish can proceed faster. The structural join (hollow chamber from two boards) and surface finishing are the key challenges, not the basic woodwork.

8. Pipa 琵琶 (Chinese Lute)

Close-enough bar: What transfers: pear-body short-lute playing position, plucked-with-nails right hand technique. What the build trades away: the precision multi-height fret arrangement and the specific tonal character of hard-carved wood.

CITES warning: Python skin is CITES Appendix II (requires documentation for import). US Customs has seized instruments at the border. Before buying any cheap sanxian from overseas, verify the skin material with the seller. Chinese factory instruments may use legally sourced farmed python or legal substitute skins, but documentation is often absent. Build with a synthetic membrane (banjo head) sidesteps this entirely -- the structural challenge is minimal; the membrane-sourcing challenge is solved. No Western builder has publicly documented this approach for sanxian, but the erhu community has proven synthetic skin works for the same instrument family.

Cross-reference: Erhu and jinghu (also snakeskin-membrane family) with full synthetic-skin substitute documentation are in Folk Strings Worldwide (Worker LLLLLLL, 2026-06-03).

PART THREE: JAPANESE AND KOREAN ART STRINGS

13. Koto 琴 (Japanese Zither)

Path state: GENUINE VOID (build under $150) | COUSIN: guzheng build at GuzhengAlive

Origin: Japanese classical and folk tradition. 13-string movable-bridge zither, hollowed from a single paulownia (kiri) log. Played with finger picks (tsume) on the right hand, bends and pressure with the left. Tuning changed by moving elephant-shaped bridges (ji).

Close-enough bar: What transfers to the guzheng cousin: right-hand picking with picks, movable bridge key changes, left-hand pressure technique. What the koto specifically trades: the single-log construction gives a different tonal character, and the 13-string layout and ji bridge shape differ from the guzheng's 21-string design.

PART FOUR: WEST AND CENTRAL ASIAN ART STRINGS

17. Qanun / Kanun قانون (Middle Eastern Plucked Zither)

Path state: GENUINE VOID

Note: "Qanun" (Arabic) and "kanun" (Turkish) are two transliterations of the same instrument. Single entry.

Origin: Arab, Turkish, Persian, and broader Middle Eastern classical tradition. Large flat zither with 26 courses of 3 strings each (78 strings), fish-skin soundholes, and a mandal mechanism (72 individual brass levers per string course for microtonal adjustment). Played with two plectra worn on the index fingers.

Close-enough bar: What must transfer: flat-body plucked zither with the mandal microtonality system -- there is no substitute for the mandal mechanism in authentic maqam playing. That mechanism alone is a significant engineering challenge.

Build notes: The circular body is structurally simple (thin hardwood rim + spruce or mahogany top and back), similar to a tenor guitar in basic construction. The challenge is the movable fret system (Vietnam uses different fret arrangements per mode) and the specific proportions. No plan exists. A confident luthier could reverse-engineer from Wikipedia dimensions (30cm diameter body, 100cm neck) but without a dedicated source the fret placement is the unknown. Closest cousin: a mandolin-family instrument with circular body or a heavily modified tenor guitar body.

Early Music (European)

Master spec: Workers/Briefs/MASTER SPEC - Sub-150 Instrument Build Catalog.md Governing constraint: under $150 total, US-available. All tools and skills assumed. Price in bands with confidence flags.

Orientation

This file covers Western European early music instrument families from approximately 1350–1750: the lute family (Renaissance lute, Baroque lute, theorbo, archlute), plucked hybrids (gittern, cittern, mandore), the viol family (viola da gamba), the recorder consort, and early wind instruments (crumhorn, gemshorn, cornetto). Instruments from this period already covered elsewhere in the series are cross-referenced rather than duplicated.

Anti-default check: This is one of the few catalog files in this series where Western European scope is genuinely the correct and complete scope. The instrument families named in the worker brief are historically specific to European courts, churches, and households. The deliberate non-Western pass was run: the oud is the most significant related instrument (direct ancestor of the lute, staved-bowl construction skills transfer directly) and is cross-referenced in the lute Group 4 below; rebab/rabab appears as a viol cousin; duduk and shawm families are crumhorn-adjacent but are covered in Build Catalog - Other Winds. No scope failure. Confirmed genuinely Western-specific.

1. Lute Family

The named gap. Fullest treatment per worker brief.

Renaissance Lute (6–10 course)

Path-state: NEAR-VOID. No kit under $700. No finished lute under $500. Plans exist; materials with standard commercial sourcing push the total build to $175–280+. A scrounged-materials build from free or reclaimed tonewoods is theoretically possible under $150 but not reliable.

Origin: Europe (Italy, Germany, France primarily), 15th–17th century. Descended from the Arabic oud brought to Europe via Moorish Spain; became the dominant plucked instrument of Renaissance courts and household music.

Close-enough bar: The lute's defining construction feature is the staved bowl back: 7–13 narrow hardwood strips (typically figured maple, yew, or ebony) bent over a mold and edge-glued into a hemispherical bowl. A flat-back body loses the tonal projection and resonance that define the instrument; if the bowl is absent, it is a cousin. Fretted with tied gut. Multi-course with re-entrant tuning. The stave-bending and bowl assembly is the specific construction challenge that has no shortcut; this is not an entry-level build.

Baroque Lute (13-course)

Path-state: NEAR-VOID. Same as Renaissance lute on all paths. More complex due to 13 courses, swan-neck extension, and different tuning. No kit at any price. Plans exist. Materials over $150 with standard sourcing.

Origin: Europe (Germany primarily), late 17th–early 18th century. Dominant solo instrument of German Baroque music (Bach, Weiss, Falckenhagen). 13 courses with a distinctive double-headed pegbox: a standard neck pegbox plus a swan-neck extension carrying the bass courses.

Close-enough bar: The swan-neck extension (an angled second pegbox carrying courses 10–13 alongside the neck) is the defining construction feature. Without it, the instrument is not a Baroque lute regardless of stringing. The construction challenge exceeds the Renaissance lute.

Group 1: Kits — VOID. No kit found at any price.

Theorbo / Archlute

Path-state: VOID. Larger and more complex than a standard lute on every dimension. Plans exist. Materials would be even heavier than a standard lute. No path under $150 exists.

Origin: Italy, late 16th–18th century. Long-necked bass continuo instrument, typically 6+ feet in total length. The theorbo has a re-entrant tuning with re-entrant top courses; the archlute (chitarrone) carries more courses. Used as continuo bass in chamber and operatic ensembles.

2. Gittern / Cittern / Mandore

Three distinct instruments sharing a broad period (13th–18th century). Unlike the lute, none requires staved-bowl construction: the gittern and mandore are typically carved from a solid block (neck and body in one piece), and the cittern has a flat back with built or bent sides. This makes material sourcing considerably more accessible than the lute, and all three are plausible under-$150 builds from historical documentation.

Gittern (Medieval / Early Renaissance)

Path-state: PLAUSIBLE under $150 from historical documentation and from-scratch build. No commercial kit confirmed at any price. Solid-body carve construction is simpler than lute staving; materials are modest.

Origin: Europe, 13th–15th century. Small plucked instrument with gut strings; body and neck were typically carved from a single block of hardwood, creating a distinctive waisted pear shape with a carved-out body cavity. Played with a plectrum. Precursor to both the Renaissance lute and guitar families.

Close-enough bar: The carved-in-one-piece neck/body construction is authentic but not strictly required for function. Playing technique (plectrum, small neck, re-entrant tuning) is the practical bar. A gittern with a separate neck and carved body is functionally adequate.

Cittern (Renaissance / Baroque)

Path-state: PLAUSIBLE under $150 from documentation and from-scratch build. Flat-back construction is more accessible than lute or carved gittern. No commercial kit confirmed at any price.

Origin: Europe, 16th–18th century. Wire-strung plucked instrument with a flat back and carved or built sides. Pear-shaped outline. Played with a plectrum. Common tavern and household instrument of the Renaissance and Baroque periods; sometimes called the English guitar in later forms.

Close-enough bar: Wire strings (steel or brass) on a flat-back body produce the characteristic bright, sustained cittern sound. Nylon strings work for playing but significantly change the tone character. Fretted.

Mandore

3. Viol Family (Viola da Gamba)

Treble Viol

Path-state: NEAR-VOID. No kit under $1,595. Plans exist (GAL #40). Materials for a viol typically run $150–300+ even with careful sourcing. No finished student instrument under ~$500.

Origin: Europe (Italian/Spanish origin, spread widely), 15th–19th century. Bowed chordophone played da gamba ("at the leg"), held between or below the knees. Distinguished from violin family by: flat or slightly vaulted back (often flat), sloped shoulders, tied gut frets, 6–7 strings in thirds/fourths tuning, C-holes or flame holes, thinner and lighter construction. The delicate, reedy tone is specific to the lighter construction and gut strings; it cannot be approximated by a violin.

Close-enough bar: Gut strings and gut frets are essential to the sound. Bowed, fretted. The flat or vaulted back construction matters acoustically. A student treble viol with tied gut frets and appropriate setup plays authentic early music even if the wood is modest.

Bottom line: The Low-Cost Bass Viol design (GAL #29, $32–37 [ESTABLISHED]) is specifically intended to bring construction cost and complexity down. It is the best available entry point for viol building and the plan price is confirmed. With aggressive wood scrounging (free spruce, reclaimed maple), a sub-$150 total is possible but difficult. This is a major project at any materials budget; the "low cost" makes it more reachable, not cheap.

4. Recorder Consort

Path-state: BUY PATH ALIVE at $30–50 for a working soprano+alto consort. Build-from-blank has no commercial kit currently available (post-LMII closure). 3D-printing is viable if equipment is available.

Origin: Europe, 14th–20th century (modern revival from 1920s). End-blown fipple flute with finger holes; the windway is internal (no embouchure control needed). Standard consort: soprano (C), alto (F), tenor (C), bass (F). "Recorder consort" refers to playing these together in polyphonic early music.

Close-enough bar: The fipple/windway construction produces the recorder's characteristic gentle, direct tone. Plastic recorders made by Yamaha and Aulos are genuine instruments used in professional early music education and amateur consort work worldwide; they are not toys. A plastic soprano or alto plays in tune, responds consistently, and is completely adequate for consort music. Upgrading to wood is a choice about tone color and tactile feel, not functional capability.

Group 1: Kits — No recorder kit currently available. (The closest category is "from blank" in Group 2.)

5. Early Wind Instruments: Crumhorn / Gemshorn / Cornetto

Crumhorn

Path-state: NEAR-VOID. No confirmed active kit under $150 from any source. No finished crumhorn under ~$200. Build-from-scratch documentation is thin at the hobbyist level.

Origin: Europe (primarily German-speaking), 15th–16th century. Windcap double-reed instrument with a cylindrical bore. The windcap entirely encloses the double reed; the player cannot affect reed pressure, which fixes the dynamic level to a loud, buzzy tone. The characteristic covered, buzzy sound is inseparable from the windcap design.

Close-enough bar: The windcap covering the double reed is the defining construction feature. Without the windcap, the instrument is a shawm or bagpipe chanter. The cylindrical bore (as opposed to conical for most woodwinds) is also essential to the crumhorn sound.

Gemshorn

Path-state: ALIVE. ABS polymer soprano confirmed at $69.90 US-domestic (Kelischek/Susato, Brasstown NC). DIY-from-actual-horn path plausible at ~$15–50 total.

Origin: Europe (primarily German-speaking), medieval. Made from animal horn (typically ox or cow), end-blown with an internal fipple block, with finger holes drilled into the tube. The natural conical bore of the horn produces a soft, mellow, slightly reedy tone. The name means "chamois horn" or "gem horn" in German.

Close-enough bar: The conical bore from actual horn produces the characteristic soft tone. The ABS plastic version approximates this well. Playing technique is similar to a recorder (fipple, finger holes) but the narrower conical bore gives a different range and softer, less focused tone.

Cornetto (Cornett)

Path-state: VOID. No kit at any price. Finished instruments start ~$200+ even for the simplest straight designs. Complex construction.

Origin: Europe, 15th–17th century. Lip-vibrated instrument made from two carved wooden halves joined and wrapped in leather, with a cup mouthpiece carved from wood or bone. Conical bore, finger holes. Sound falls between a recorder and a small trumpet. Used in the highest voice of Renaissance and early Baroque wind bands and church music (the loud choral cornett voice in Monteverdi, Schütz, etc.).

Close-enough bar: Playing technique is fundamentally like a brass instrument (lip vibration into a cup mouthpiece), not a woodwind. There is no affordable substitute that shares both the technique and the range. The construction (split-carved wood block, steam-bent or pressure-bent to shape, leather-wrapped, cup mouthpiece with narrow conical bore) is specialized.

Group 1: Kits — VOID. No kit found.

Group 2: Plans + tutorials — No hobbyist-accessible build documentation found. This instrument appears in specialist lutherie literature but not in accessible hobbyist form at the standard search depth. [UNKNOWN — specialized workshops exist but are not cheap]

Bottom line: Complete void. EMS sells simple straight cornetti from ~£150–200+ (~$200–260 USD) and mute cornetti higher. No kit, no accessible plans, no under-$150 path of any kind. The cornetto is a specialist workshop instrument; a determined builder would need to find specialist instruction (workshops exist in Europe) rather than commercial kits or free plans.

Report-back

Native American Flute & Cheap Winds

Cultural Note (read before anything else)

The Native American flute — also called the North American flute, the love flute, or the courting flute — is an Indigenous instrument with living ceremonial, cultural, and healing significance across dozens of nations. Scholars such as Kevin Locke (Smithsonian) prefer "North American Indigenous Flute" to acknowledge the full geographic and tribal breadth. This catalog uses "NAF" as shorthand and "Native American style flute" when referring to instruments made by non-tribal makers, following the usage of the instrument's own maker community.

Legal dimension: The Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990 (IACA-1990) is federal law. It prohibits representing a handmade item as "Indian produced" or "Native American made" unless the maker is a member of a federally or state-recognized Indian tribe. Applied to flutes: a flute made by a non-tribal maker cannot legally be marketed as a "Native American Flute" or "American Indian Flute." The terms "Native American Style Flute," "Native Flute," and "North American Flute" are legally and community-accepted for non-tribal-made instruments. All kits and plans in this catalog produce a "Native American style" flute by that distinction. Non-tribal makers selling finished flutes should verify their labeling against IACA-1990. Source: Flutopedia, flutopedia.com/tradition.htm.

Community posture: The NAF kit and teaching market is notably welcoming to non-Indigenous learners, and the major kit vendors (Stellar, Blue Bear) have explicitly partnered with tribal programs, schools, and rehab centers. The tradition asks for respect and acknowledgment, not exclusion of learners. Buying kits from Indigenous-owned vendors or supporting Indigenous flute makers directly when purchasing finished instruments is the commonly stated community preference.

1. Native American Flute (NAF / North American Indigenous Flute)

Origin: Indigenous North America. Documented traditions span Plains, Great Lakes, Southwest, and many other nations. The "love flute" / courting flute form most associated with the contemporary kit market traces primarily to Plains traditions. Not a single monolithic tradition; each nation and maker carries distinct forms. Living tradition, not historical artifact.

What must transfer for the instrument to be the instrument: - Two-chambered bore (slow-air chamber + melody chamber, divided by the nest/block sound mechanism). This is the defining acoustic feature. - External block (totem/bird) tied over the sound hole, creating the fipple-plus-splitting-edge mechanism. The block is adjustable, which is how you tune the air gap. - Pentatonic-optimized fingering: the standard six-hole NAF in the "A pentatonic minor" tuning (holes 1-2-3 / gap / 5-6) produces the Native American pentatonic minor without requiring accidentals. The gap hole (hole 4) is left uncovered or covered for specific notes. - Wood construction is traditional; cedar (western red, eastern red) is by far the dominant timber in the kit market. PVC builds are a substitute, acknowledged as such below.

What the pre-tuned kit trades away: Shape work. A pre-tuned square blank arrives with bore, fipple holes, and finger hole positions already set; you carve, sand, and finish. The cheapest kits are assembly + finishing, not lutherie.

Bore ratio rule of thumb (from Flutopedia): Bore length from splitting edge to end = bore diameter × 18. Standard 7/8" bore → ~15.75" bore length → F# range. Standard 3/4" bore → ~13.5" → A range. Sound hole width ≈ 1/2 bore diameter. These are starting points; undercutting and block gap adjustment are the actual tuning levers.

Group 4: Close-Enough Cousins

The NAF is a specific acoustic design: two-chamber end-blown fipple flute, external block, pentatonic-minor tuning. These are adjacent instruments worth knowing about, but each trades something real.

What Why it counts / why it's only a cousin Cost Link
PVC NAF-style flute (from Blue Bear free plan or NAFlutomat) Acoustically identical design in PVC instead of wood. The two-chamber mechanism works in PVC. Sound is brighter, sustain shorter, no wood warmth. The grain of cedar contributes to tone in ways PVC doesn't replicate; experienced players notice. Legitimate substitute for learning the playing technique and fingering pattern, clearly a substitute not an equivalent for aesthetic/tonal experience. BOM: ~$5-15. ~$5-15 BBF PVC plan
Bamboo NAF-style flute (from Blue Bear bamboo plan) Bamboo is used in some traditional contexts; acoustically closer to cedar than PVC. The grain is hollow-not-solid so splitting-and-gluing is different. Blue Bear's plan documents a workable approach. Sound is warm but bamboo tonal variability is high. ~$0-20 (foraged or purchased culm) BBF bamboo plan
Anasazi-style flute (end-blown, no block) A different branch of North American Indigenous flute: end-blown without a block mechanism, using embouchure only. Harder to play consistently. Documented on Flutopedia. If you want the sound without the block mechanism, this is the direction. Different tradition, different technique requirement. ~$15-40 (from wood or clay) flutopedia.com

Bottom line: The pre-tuned cedar kits from Stellar Flutes ($55-$60) are the clearest on-ramp in this whole catalog: arrive fully tuned, carve and finish, and it plays when you're done. The Blue Bear Single A ($40) is slightly cheaper and requires you to assemble and tune yourself, with a massive video ecosystem for support. The Pre-Bored kit from Stellar ($35) is the cheapest but puts real woodworking skill back into the equation. For a scratch build with your own timber, the Flutopedia NAFlutomat plus the Shands or Goss PDFs are free and complete. The whole kit field is essentially Western-cedar-focused; if you want the playing feel and pentatonic tuning without the wood work, the PVC plan from Blue Bear is a legitimate skill-builder but not the same experience. The NAF is the richest true-kit wind market in this entire series.

2. PVC Transverse Flute and Low Whistle

Origin: No single cultural origin; the PVC/copper-tube DIY flute is a contemporary maker tradition. The plans below produce instruments acoustically equivalent to Irish-style tin whistles, simple-system flutes, and low whistles - the physical design is Western, the tube is modern.

What must transfer: Cylindrical or near-cylindrical bore; six finger holes; embouchure hole (transverse) or fipple/windway (whistle); correct hole placement for the chosen scale and key. The Flutomat family calculators handle this.

Key trade on cheap builds: Metal (copper, aluminum) is harder to voice and requires power tools; PVC is forgiving and hand-tool friendly. Tuning is iterative (enlarge holes by tiny amounts until pitch is correct against a chromatic tuner).

This field is plans-only - no meaningful commercial kit market exists. You source your own tube.

Group 1: Kits

None confirmed under $150 for a transverse flute or low whistle. The commercial whistle field sells finished instruments, not kits.

3. Pan Flute / Siku (PVC)

Origin: Pan pipes (panpipes) are found across the ancient world; the South American siku (Andean, Bolivia/Peru) is the most documented living tradition. The siku is a double-row panpipe played in a "hocket" style between two players. The Western "pan flute" solo form is derived from ancient Greek/Roman traditions. Both traditions use open-ended tubes of varying length, each producing one note.

What must transfer: Sealed tube bundles; each tube produces exactly one pitch; pitch set by tube length. The siku traditionally produces the Andean pentatonic scale; the builder selects the scale. No embouchure skill required beyond directing breath across the tube opening; the physics are forgiving.

What the cheap build trades away: The siku's hocket-playing tradition (two players sharing one instrument in interlocking parts) requires a partner. A solo PVC build works fine for melody practice but misses the communal playing form that is central to the tradition.

This field is primarily plans-driven, with minimal kit market.

Bottom line: Plans-only, very cheap, forgiving physics. The siku's cultural context is Andean Indigenous; the pan-pipe form is broader. Either way, this is a near-free afternoon build.

4. Ocarina

Origin: Vessel flutes using Helmholtz resonator acoustics have appeared independently across many cultures (Mesoamerica, China, Europe, Africa). The modern "sweet potato" ocarina is typically attributed to 19th-century Italian luthier Giovanni Donati; the 12-hole pendant ocarina form was standardized in the 20th century. The Aztec and pre-Columbian Mesoamerican forms are distinct traditions and are the ones flagged in the folk-strings catalog's Apache-fiddle-style note: they carry living cultural weight.

What must transfer: Vessel-flute physics (Helmholtz resonator, not open tube). Hole SIZE matters more than hole position (unlike flutes). Range is limited (typically one octave + a few notes). The six-hole and four-hole forms are simpler; the 12-hole Farina pendant form adds cross-fingering for chromatic notes.

This field has a real kit market and a strong 3D-print path.

5. Fife

Origin: Europe, specifically the Swiss and German military tradition of the 15th-16th century; spread via colonial-era British and American military bands. The American fife-and-drum tradition is well-documented in the Revolutionary War and Civil War eras. Not an Indigenous or non-Western instrument in its standard form; the six-hole cylindrical folk fife has Western European roots.

What must transfer: Six-hole cylindrical tube, open embouchure hole (transverse), no fipple. The fife is acoustically the simplest "real" wind instrument. Two registers (octave and a half range), no cross-fingering needed for a basic diatonic scale.

Kit market: Essentially none. Makers sell finished fifes. The instrument is simple enough to build from tube + published dimensions, but no commercial fife kit is confirmed.

Group 1: Kits

None confirmed. The fife is a finished-instrument market. No boxed build kit found.

Other Winds & Free Reed

Cross-references: Build Catalog - Native American Flute and Cheap Winds.md (QQQQQQQ) covers the NAF kit market, PVC transverse flute plans, siku, ocarina, and fife; those are NOT duplicated here. Wind and Free Reed Kits and Plans.md (CCCCCCC) is the original research brief this fire draws from and deepens. Non-Western Instrument Kits and Plans.md (GGGGGGG) provides the ney and shakuhachi baseline that this file cross-refs and expands.

1. Orientation

This catalog covers the rest of the wind and free-reed world that the NAF solo fire left on the table. The terrain is unusual: the free-reed highlight (concertina) is an expensive, expert build; the folk-wind highlights (ney, shakuhachi, kaval) are cheap materials but the hardest embouchures in any instrument family; and a cluster of folk flutes and whistles that look like afternoon projects turn out to be deeply different from each other in the time it takes to play them in tune.

The wind-specific hidden axis: voicing and tuning difficulty. Called out under every entry. With stringed instruments, the geometry is largely fixed and finishing is the main skill. With winds, the bore IS the instrument. Getting it to play in tune across its full range — cutting the fipple or window, undercutting tone holes, adjusting the splitting edge, developing the player embouchure for open-bore instruments — is fiddly, iterative, and the real time cost. A "playable" instrument (makes some sound) and an "in tune, pleasant" instrument can be many hours apart. Every time estimate below should be read as "to in-tune and comfortable," not just "to first sound."

Knowledge tags follow the integrity protocol: [ESTABLISHED] well-documented/high confidence; [PLAUSIBLE] reasonable but not directly verified; [UNCERTAIN] limited or contested; [UNKNOWN] outside reliable knowledge and not fabricated.

2. Free-Reed Instruments

2.1 Concertina — the free-reed highlight

Origin: England (Anglo/English), mid-19th century; Duet variants in Ireland, UK, and internationally. Free-reed instrument family; related to the accordion and harmonium but with individual reeds per button, both push and pull the same note on a fully chromatic system.

Close-enough bar: The Anglo concertina plays Irish traditional music and is the primary target of the kit/plans paths below. An English or Duet concertina is a different instrument; do not conflate. Both the Clover kit and the Tedrow essay produce Anglo instruments.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: High. The Clover kit assembles pre-made parts, which sidesteps most individual reed voicing. The from-scratch Tedrow path requires fitting accordion reeds into reed pans, gapping each reed, setting action, and hand-building bellows — all expert tasks. Bellows-making is the step Tedrow himself says took years to master.

The Tedrow from-scratch path is free in plans but costs hundreds in parts and many hundreds of hours. Concertina is included in this catalog as the free-reed highlight: it is the one acoustic free-reed instrument with a genuine kit AND a genuine plans path, which distinguishes it from everything else in this section.

2.2 Harmonica — rebuild and customize, not build

Origin: Germany (Hohner), mid-19th century; now worldwide. Diatonic and chromatic; free-reed instrument.

Close-enough bar: You do not build a harmonica from scratch as a hobbyist. Reed manufacture requires metallurgical precision beyond any home shop. What genuinely exists is a healthy rebuild, re-key, and customize ecosystem.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: Gapping (adjusting reed clearance) and tuning (filing reeds flat or adding solder to go sharp) are the real skills. Getting all 20 reeds of a diatonic in good shape is achievable in a few hours. Filing reeds to a different pitch is fiddly.

2.3 Melodica — buy and mod, no build path

Origin: Italy/Germany (Hohner Melodica, 1950s); now worldwide, popular in reggae, jazz, and classrooms.

Close-enough bar: Keyboard-operated free-reed instrument. Blow pipe or mouthpiece forces air over reeds. No hobby build path exists for the body (precision-molded plastic/metal, keyboard mechanism). The only DIY lane is reed-plate replacement for a failed reed, identical to harmonica practice.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: N/A for building. Individual reed replacement is beginner-accessible.

Bottom line

Buy a Hohner or Suzuki melodica (~$30-60 new), mod/tune individual reeds as needed using the harmonica reed-plate ecosystem (some reeds are shared). There is no melodica from-scratch or kit path; the instrument is a molded-body commodity.

2.4 Accordion — overwhelmingly rebuild, one niche kit

Origin: Germany/Austria, early 19th century; now worldwide. Piano or button keyboard; free-reed; bellows-driven.

Close-enough bar: The accordion body requires major industrial tooling. No hobby from-scratch build path exists. The rebuild/restore ecosystem is mature and the real DIY lane. One niche exception noted.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: Reed waxing/replacement, bellows repair (leathering), and tuning are the core rebuild skills. Each involves patience more than precision tooling.

2.5 Harmonium — no Western kit, real rebuild literature and parts pipeline

Origin: France/Germany (19th century); widely adopted and adapted across India and Pakistan; the Indian harmonium (Delhi and Calcutta styles) is now its own tradition.

Close-enough bar: Foot/hand pumped bellows force air through free reeds; keyboard-controlled valves select pitch. The instrument is much simpler internally than an accordion. A donor harmonium (used, cracked, failing reeds) is a realistic $40-100 purchase; the rebuild is the project.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: Individual reed replacement is accessible (pop out old reed, press in new one, check gap). Bellows re-leathering is harder — advanced, and the step most people outsource. Dry-climate cracking is the main failure mode on Delhi-style harmoniums.

Bottom line

No Western kit exists anywhere. The path is: buy a donor harmonium (craigslist, estate sales, $40-100), use Chuck White's free literature to diagnose, and source replacement reeds from Old Delhi Music (US) or import from Calcutta Musical Depot (India). The rebuild, minus bellows work, is genuinely accessible mid-level DIY. The bellows are the hard step; most rebuilders outsource or postpone them. This is a real path with a real community.

3. Ney (Persian / Turkish)

Origin: Persian and Turkish classical and folk traditions; one of the oldest instruments in continuous use. An end-blown cane or PVC flute, open at both ends, typically 60-70 cm; pitched by where the upper end rests at the corner of the lip. Plays 2.5+ octaves through overblowing and embouchure control.

Close-enough bar: Fingering (6 holes front, 1 back) and articulation (breath-controlled, single-note end-blown) must transfer. The ney is NOT a recorder or kaval — the sound is produced by the player's lower lip at the open end, not by a fipple or beveled edge. This embouchure is the hardest in the flute family: new players routinely take weeks to months before getting a stable tone.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: The HIGHEST in the catalog. The instrument itself is simple to make from PVC (an afternoon). Playing it in tune is the work of months, because the embouchure controls both pitch and tone: the player IS the voicing mechanism. Cane versions add a second axis — "one in a thousand good reeds" is the community consensus on finding a cane that plays well.

Group 1: Kits

None. No boxed ney kit exists.
