Cheapest real path: persianney.com + PVC pipe + $5. The kicker is that learning to produce a stable tone takes weeks to months. A PVC ney in D or C costs almost nothing; playing it in tune and with tone color takes serious embouchure work. Worth noting that the ney is one of the most musically rewarding instruments in the catalog, both as a sound and as a tradition. [ESTABLISHED] for plans existence and free-source status.

4. Kaval (Bulgarian / Turkish / Romanian / Macedonian)

Origin: Southeast European and Anatolian folk tradition; the primary shepherd's flute of the Balkans and Turkey. End-blown open flute (no fipple), 60-70 cm, 12 holes (8 finger + 4 tuning), plays 3 registers via overblowing and embouchure. Bulgarian and Turkish kavals are pitched differently (different hole spacing and bore); Romanian caval is longer and lower.

Close-enough bar: Articulation (end-blown, open-bore) and fingering (covered holes + embouchure register control) must transfer. The kaval is NOT a ney — the playing angle is different (kaval across the chin, held more like a transverse flute but blown at the end), and the bore diameter is larger (10-20 mm vs ney's narrower bore). Different fingering system for the registers.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: High. The instrument itself is easy to make from PVC — the Slama guide is beginner-accessible. Getting all three registers in tune requires iterative hole enlargement. The multi-register embouchure (kaba, orta, tiz registers) is an advanced playing skill requiring months of practice. "Kaval player in tune across all registers" is several years of work; "kaval that makes a sound and can play a melody in the first register" is one afternoon.

Group 1: Kits

None. Finished kavals on Etsy ($30-80) and from Bulgarian/Turkish makers ($50-200+); not kits.

Voicing tax is entirely in the player's embouchure, not in the instrument's construction. CPVC (high-temperature PVC) gives a slightly warmer tone due to its thicker wall; standard white PVC also works. [ESTABLISHED] for build feasibility.

5. Shakuhachi (Japanese)

Origin: Japan; Zen Buddhist and secular traditions; one of the most studied solo-flute traditions globally. End-blown bamboo (or PVC) flute, open at both ends, 1.8 shaku (~54.5 cm) for the standard key; played with the utaguchi (mouthpiece) at the upper-left lip corner. About 5 holes (4 front, 1 back).

Close-enough bar: End-blown, open-bore, breath-controlled. Pitch is controlled entirely by embouchure angle ("meri" and "kari" movements). Fingering overlaps with some Chinese end-blown flutes but is NOT the same as a recorder or whistle. Playing the shakuhachi in tune is an advanced embouchure skill.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: Second hardest in the catalog (ney is first). The PVC versions make an honest sound faster because the utaguchi cut is precise and repeatable. The bamboo path adds a second skill: carving the utaguchi from madake and tuning the bore. Full jinashi (natural bore) making is a lifetime craft in Japan. "PVC shakuhachi to stable tone" is days to weeks; "bamboo jinashi in tune" is months to years.

6. Recorder (Western / Renaissance)

Origin: Europe, medieval through Baroque; now worldwide. Fipple flute; internal windway; finger-hole covering controls pitch; Renaissance and Baroque fingering systems differ.

Close-enough bar: Fingering (seven holes + thumb hole) and articulation (fipple-blown, tongue-articulated) must transfer. A recorder is NOT a tin whistle or simple flute — the bore profile (cylindrical vs conical), windway geometry, and voicing differ significantly between the two.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: Fipple design is the entire difficulty for wooden instruments. Windway width/depth, labium (the lip/edge) angle, and undercutting the tone holes are the voicing variables. A cheap plastic recorder is pre-voiced at the factory; a wooden recorder from blanks puts all of that on the builder. Getting each note in tune and the instrument pleasant-sounding is a 20-60+ hour project.

State of the market (important correction): LMII (Luthiers Mercantile International) closed in 2024. No confirmed current off-the-shelf wooden recorder KIT has been found as of 2026-06-05. StewMac acquired some LMII inventory but a recorder-specific kit was not confirmed there. The field is plans + sources, not kits.

7. Tin Whistle / Penny Whistle

Origin: Ireland and Britain; now global. Simple conical-bore fipple flute with 6 holes; smallest and cheapest serious folk instrument in this catalog. Played in Irish, Scottish, English folk traditions and widely in Celtic-diaspora communities worldwide.

Close-enough bar: Fipple (recorder-family) articulation; 6 holes, conical bore; the D whistle is the standard starting point. NOT the same instrument as an Irish flute (which has 6 or 8 holes, open embouchure, and cylindrical bore).

Voicing/tuning difficulty: LOW for finished instruments (pre-voiced). HIGH if making your own from copper or PVC — the fipple design (windway, labium) is the hardest single step. Getting the tone holes in tune is the secondary step.

Group 1: Kits and finished instruments in scope

The honest answer for tin whistle: buy a finished one. Under $15, widely available, plays in tune out of the box. The DIY path is for curiosity/craft, not savings.

8. Irish Flute / Simple-System Wooden Flute

Origin: Ireland, Scotland, England; 19th century "old system" or "simple system" flute tradition. Open-embouchure cylindrical bore; 6 tone holes (traditional) or 8-10 holes on more complex copies. NOT the Boehm/metal concert flute (keyed mechanism, different bore profile — and no hobby path exists for that). The simple-system Irish flute is the one with a genuine from-plans tradition.

Close-enough bar: Open embouchure (blow across a hole, not into a fipple); 6 or 8 holes, cylindrical bore (unlike the recorder's conical bore). Articulation (tongue + breath) and fingering both transfer from other open-embouchure flutes. A good Irish flute in two octaves requires real embouchure development.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: High, with a specific bottleneck: the bore taper (Irish flutes have a very slight taper from head to foot) must be achieved with a long reamer, and undercutting the tone holes is how the builder tunes each note. Getting two octaves in tune is the real skill. Wooden blanks also need seasoning.

PVC avoids the lathe but is still a significant voicing project. A wooden Irish flute from blanks + reamers, done properly, is advanced-to-expert territory. Bottom line

Free plans exist; the PVC path is beginner-accessible; the wooden path is a full shop project. The finished simple-system Irish flute is one of the most playable and musical of the folk flutes, worth the effort if you have the tools. Doug Tipple's PVC guide is the real entry point under $150. Wooden from-blanks: under $150 in materials alone if you make your own reamers (possible via MIMF guidance using old files), but a significant time commitment.

9. Dizi (Chinese Transverse Bamboo Flute)

Origin: China; one of the central instruments in Chinese classical, folk, and opera music. Transverse (side-blown) bamboo flute, 6 tone holes + 1 membrane hole (mo kong); the membrane hole is covered with a thin bamboo tissue (dimo) that gives the dizi its distinctive buzzing, resonant tone.

Close-enough bar: Articulation (side-blown open embouchure) and fingering (6-hole coverage in pentatonic or chromatic variants) must transfer. The dimo (membrane hole) is the unique variable: tension and perforation of the membrane directly affect tone. A dizi without a proper dimo sounds like a simple flute; a dizi with good dimo installation is a distinct instrument.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: High. Bamboo sourcing and drying (months if from raw) is the material challenge. Hole placement affects pitch; Chinese dizi players commonly tune by sliding the head joint. The dimo membrane is its own skill: installation too tight or too loose changes the buzz quality and the pitch of each hole. Getting the dimo right takes practice.

10. Xiao (Chinese Vertical End-Blown Bamboo Flute)

Origin: China; an ancient instrument, played vertically (end-blown from above, like a recorder but open-bore); 8 holes in modern versions (5 front, 1 back, 2 extra at the foot). Darker, softer tone than the dizi; no dimo membrane hole. Closely related to the Japanese shakuhachi in playing technique.

Close-enough bar: End-blown open-bore; the blowing notch at the top of the xiao is a U-shaped cut, unlike the shakuhachi's more complex mouthpiece. Fingering system is different from both the dizi and the recorder. The xiao requires embouchure development similar to the shakuhachi — the instrument is more forgiving than the ney but harder than a fipple flute.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: High. Embouchure development is the main challenge. Bamboo sourcing (same as dizi; purple or black bamboo). The blowing notch geometry is less demanding than the shakuhachi utaguchi but still requires care. Getting two octaves in tune is the real work.

11. Willow Flute / Sälgflöjt (Scandinavian Overtone Flute)

Origin: Sweden and Norway (sälgflöjt / seljefløyte); also found in other European folk traditions. A tube flute with NO finger holes — pitch control is entirely through breath pressure and overblowing to access harmonics, plus an end hole covered by the index finger for fine adjustment. Traditionally made from willow bark slipped off a spring branch; modern versions use PVC or elder wood year-round.

Close-enough bar: This is an OVERTONE FLUTE. No holes are opened and closed to change notes; the player navigates the harmonic series (1st, 2nd, 3rd partials, etc.) through breath and finger-end technique. This is a fundamentally different technique from any other flute in this catalog. It CAN play complex melodies, but the musical vocabulary is different from chromatic or diatonic fingered flutes.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: Different from the others. The instrument produces no notes (it just buzzes) until the player learns to find the harmonics — that is the only "voicing" involved. There is no hole-based tuning; you are playing in tune by learning to reliably access each harmonic node. A few hours for first sounds; days for navigating 4-5 harmonics cleanly.

12. Quena (Andean Notch Flute)

Origin: Andes region (Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, Argentina, Chile); one of the oldest continuous flute traditions in the Americas. End-blown notch flute: the player blows across a U-shaped notch cut at the top of the tube. 6 holes (5 front, 1 back); typically in G or A.

Close-enough bar: End-blown, notch-cut embouchure (similar to ney family but with a cut notch instead of an open end); 6 holes; plays diatonic scale with chromatic options via half-holing. Articulation is breath + partial fingering. Similar embouchure family to ney and kaval but the notch makes first sounds more accessible than ney.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: Medium-High. The notch cut must be angled correctly (traditionally cut at about 45-degree angle at the top); once done, tone production is easier than ney but harder than fipple flutes. Hole placement determines tuning. "First sound" is hours; "in tune across two octaves" is weeks to months.

13. Bansuri (Indian Bamboo Flute)

Origin: India; one of the central instruments in Hindustani classical music (North India); also popular in Carnatic (South Indian) music and folk traditions across the subcontinent. Transverse (side-blown) bamboo flute; 6 holes; no membrane. The preferred material is Phyllostachys or a specific Indian wansi bamboo; the bore and wall thickness are critical.

Close-enough bar: Side-blown open embouchure (same family as the Irish flute and dizi, but without the dimo membrane). Fingering is 6-hole, often with half-holing for additional pitches. Indian classical playing requires extreme embouchure precision for meend (glides) and gamak (ornaments).

Voicing/tuning difficulty: Medium-High. Bamboo sourcing is the main challenge in the US: Indian wansi bamboo is not commercially grown here; substitutes include Phyllostachys bamboo (available in the US), Arundo donax, or bought bamboo tube from international sources. The bore dimensions are critical for tone; wall thickness of 5-9mm recommended. Getting all 6 holes in tune requires care.

14. Other World Folk Flutes (Brief)

Several more folk flutes have build paths but thin English-language documentation. Listed briefly:

Fujara (Slovak): Long overtone flute (~160 cm), fipple-blown with a side hole that creates resonance effects. Free plans exist in Slovak and some English; PVC version documented. Unusual but buildable. Search "Fujara PVC plans."

Hulusi (Yunnan, China): Gourd + single bamboo pipes + two drone pipes; free-reed type. Some English-language tutorials; the gourd and cane sourcing are the challenge. Search "Hulusi DIY build."

Algoza (Sindhi / Punjabi): Paired end-blown flutes played simultaneously; bamboo construction; very thin English build documentation; primarily apprenticeship craft.

Tilinca (Romanian): Open tube flute, no holes; overtone-only like the willow flute; Romanian luthier tradition. Near-zero English plans.

Transverse folk flutes across Eurasia (dilli kaval / Azerbaijani balaban / Iranian duduk / etc.): Most are finished-only imports from the country of origin; finished instruments available $20-80 from specialty retailers. No build kits confirmed.

Summary judgment: Almost entirely finished-only at or above budget. No confirmed build kit for any shawm, crumhorn, or folk horn under $150 was found in this research. The landscape:

Gemshorn path in brief: Hollow a cow/ox horn (or goat horn), drill the holes at the wide end, fit a fipple head. Some English documentation exists (MIMF threads, some YouTube); the craft is doable but thin on plans. Kelischek makes finished gemshorns and a brief construction note is on their site; no kit offered.

Homemade shawm from PVC + commercial reed: This is the most accessible path if you want the tone color of a reed instrument without the expense. PVC conduit + an oboe reed (or a bassoon reed for a lower instrument) + some carving to make a bell. The instrument you get is a crude medieval-shawm-adjacent instrument. Real documentation: MIMO project notes, occasional MIMF thread. Under $25 total. [PLAUSIBLE].

Didgeridoo

Didgeridoo (Yidaki / Didjeridu)

Origin: Aboriginal Australia, northern Australia; Yolŋu peoples of northeast Arnhem Land call it yidaki (the culturally specific regional name); "didgeridoo" and "didjeridu" are Western coinages, onomatopoeic, first recorded in the early 20th century. Continuous cultural tradition estimated at 40,000+ years. Classified acoustically as a brass aerophone (lip-buzz drone tube).

Cultural Note

The didgeridoo is a living sacred instrument at the heart of Aboriginal Australian ceremonial life. In northern Australia, Yolŋu and related peoples use it to accompany ceremony, dance, and song. It is not a folk curiosity but an active element of knowledge tradition held by people who are still here.

On who plays: These protocols are complex, regional, and not uniform. In northern Australia, where the instrument originates, many Yolŋu elders, including Djalu' Gurruwiwi and Burrŋupurrŋu, actively invite non-Aboriginal people to learn and play. In southeastern Australia, where the instrument is a recent arrival, some communities hold stricter rules; non-Aboriginal women playing is considered by certain SE Australian Aboriginal groups to violate cultural protocol. The strongest prohibitions are concentrated in the southeast, not at the instrument's place of origin. Full discussion at YidakiStory.com and the Aboriginal Art & Culture myths page.

On the builds in this catalog: The traditional material, a termite-hollowed eucalyptus branch, is tied to specific Australian ecosystems and is essentially unobtainable in the US. The PVC, agave, bamboo, and hardwood builds below are maker substitutes. They produce functionally similar wind instruments. They are not didgeridoos in the traditional sense and must not be presented or sold as Aboriginal-made.

Close-Enough Bar

The didgeridoo is not fingered. Technique is continuous lip-buzz (embouchure) plus circular breathing plus vocalizations into the bore. Any cylindrical or conical tube of the right length and bore will produce the drone. What the cheap builds trade away: tone depth and harmonic richness (PVC is brighter and thinner than eucalyptus; bamboo is brighter than wood; agave approaches hardwood tone); the irregular interior surface of the termite-hollowed original, which creates complex backpressure and timbre; visual and cultural resonance. None of these affect playability or technique. Playing mechanics transfer fully across all materials.

Group 1: Kits

No boxed assembly kit for a didgeridoo exists anywhere in the US market. Pre-assembled instruments are widely sold (Amazon, Terre USA, eBay; teak/bamboo/PVC blanks from ~$20) but those are finished instruments, not build kits. There is nothing to assemble.

The hardware-store snap-together PVC build below is the functional equivalent of a kit ($8–15, no tools, 15 minutes) and is the didgeridoo world's de facto entry-level build path. It is listed under Group 2.

Length-to-key reference table (straight cylindrical tube, l = 344 / (4 × f Hz)):

These are theoretical values for a cylindrical pipe. Actual pitch is slightly sharp; trim in small increments from the bell end to tune down.

Key Approx. Hz Length (cm) Length (in) Beginner notes
C (low, 2nd octave) 65 132 52 Standard beginner key; easy to drone
C# 69 124 49
D 73 118 46.5 Standard beginner key
D# 78 111 44
E 82 104 41 Standard beginner key; 10-ft pipe cut in thirds = 3 E-key didges
F 87 99 39
F# 93 93 36.5
G 98 88 34.5 Getting short; harder to drone
G# 104 83 33
A 110 78 31 Short, high; easier to play but less "didge-like"

Traditional Aboriginal instruments favor longer/lower keys (A to C in a lower octave, roughly 120–200+ cm); these are harder for beginners to drone on. Beginners: start at E, D, or C (104–132 cm / 41–52 in).

2B. Agave Stalk Builds

Giant blue agave (Agave americana) and related species are the US Southwest's native equivalent of the eucalyptus. The stalk (not the leaf; the tall flowering spike) turns woody after approximately one year drying in the desert sun and is the material of a thriving maker tradition centered in Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, and California. Agave didges are valued by players for explosive resonance, natural taper, and light weight.

Harvesting rules: Agave is not a protected cactus under Arizona Native Plant Law. Fallen/dead stalks on private property require landowner permission. Public land (BLM, Forest Service) requires written authorization for removal. Harvest only stalks that have already dropped their seeds. Fresh agave sap causes acute dermatitis; wear gloves.

Two construction methods: 1. Bore-through: preserve the intact stalk; bore out the soft pithy center with long auger/rasp/drill extensions; sand smooth; seal with epoxy. Preserves structural integrity, natural curvature, and resonant properties. Preferred by dedicated agave-didge makers. 2. Split-bore-reglue: split stalk lengthwise, hollow both halves, glue back together. Easier interior access but weakens the structure.

BOM: - Stalk: free (harvested) - Long auger bits and drill extensions (12"+ reach): ~$15–30 - Carbide rasps and files: ~$15–30 (if not owned) - Epoxy resin interior seal (required, not optional): ~$15–25 - Sandpaper: ~$5–10 - Exterior finish (epoxy coat or oil): ~$10–20 - Beeswax or carved wooden mouthpiece: ~$5–15 - Total materials: ~$50–100

2C. Bamboo Builds

Bamboo is structurally simpler than agave because the culm is already hollow; the main work is clearing the internal nodes. Result: a brighter, thinner tone than agave or hardwood, but richer and more complex than PVC. The Sachs bamboo modification technique (glue + hardwood sawdust applied to the interior) can push a cheap bamboo didge significantly closer to hardwood tone.

Large-diameter (2"+) bamboo is sold by Asian grocery stores, bamboo nurseries, and landscaping suppliers. Phyllostachys species (black bamboo, moso) work well. Budget ~$15–25 for a single culm shipped, or free if you have local access.

BOM: - Bamboo pole, 5–6 ft, ~2" internal diameter at mouthpiece: ~$15–25 (or free) - 3-ft threaded rod or rebar for node clearing: ~$5 - Beeswax: ~$5–10 - Propane torch (for darkening finish, optional): ~$15–20 - Spar varnish: ~$10–15 - Sandpaper: ~$5 - Total: ~$25–55

2D. Split-and-Hollow Hardwood (Sandwich Method)

The dominant modern approach for non-PVC didge building in Western maker communities. Split a branch lengthwise with a bandsaw, carve both halves to your bore profile, glue back together. This produces a genuinely wood instrument with corresponding tonal depth. The key variables are wood density and bore geometry.

Wood selection (from Wakademy's density table, [ESTABLISHED]): - Avoid all softwoods (pine, fir, spruce; density < 0.50): too light, weak bass - Light hardwoods (density 0.60–0.65): birch, elm, ash, walnut, chestnut; easy to work, decent tone - Recommended target (0.70–0.80): beech, fruit woods (apple, cherry, pear), maple, acacia, sycamore; best tone-to-workability ratio - Dense hardwoods (0.80–1.0): boxwood, holly, olive; excellent tone, hard to source in didge-appropriate diameters

Bore dimensions (Wakademy, [ESTABLISHED]): - Minimum external diameter at mouthpiece: 70mm - Minimum external diameter at bell: 110mm - Internal bore at mouthpiece: ~40mm - Internal bore at bell: ~90mm - Length: 140–160cm typical (adjust for desired key via formula above) - Profile: avoid 100% cylindrical or 100% conical; mixed profiles (e.g., 1/3 cylindrical + 2/3 conical) sound best

BOM: - Hardwood branch or log section (6 ft, 4–6" diameter): free if foraged/salvaged; $20–50 at lumber suppliers - Titebond II or slow-set epoxy: ~$5–15 - Rasps, gouges, carving bits: ~$20–50 if not owned - Sandpaper: ~$5–10 - Spar varnish or oil: ~$10–20 - Beeswax mouthpiece: ~$5–10 - Total: ~$30–80

Group 4: Close-Enough Cousins

The didgeridoo's specific combination (continuous lip-buzz drone, circular breathing, long open tube with no fingering) is essentially unique as a folk instrument. Other deep-drone aerophones exist in other traditions (Tibetan dungchen, Scandinavian lur, ancient natural trumpet) but they require different embouchure, are not played with circular breathing, have very different acoustic character, and have no accessible US build path under $150. There is no instrument in another tradition that can be built cheaply and said to "play like a didge." This is genuinely all there is.

Finishing

PVC/ABS: Spray paint, acrylics, or permanent marker on lightly sanded pipe surface (120-grit scuff). Heat gun allows artistic surface sculpting (dimples, bends, bell flare). Finish is purely cosmetic.

Bamboo: Leave natural with spar varnish, or use propane-torch charring for a dark finish: heat a 3–4 sq in patch until green-to-tan-to-brown, wipe with wet rag, repeat. Apply after node clearing, before beeswax mouthpiece. Shoe polish or varnish over the top. Varnish only when fully dry (mold risk on green bamboo).

Agave: Epoxy resin interior seal is required before playing, not optional. Without it the bore will crack and shed material. Exterior: one coat of epoxy (glassy, retains tone) or linseed/danish oil (more natural look). Cosmetic inlays: insect holes and desert-weathering marks in aged stalks can be filled with crushed turquoise, malachite, or other stones (standard Desert Mountain Didgeridoos technique).

Split hardwood: Before glue-up: sand interior to smooth bore, coat with thinned epoxy or spar varnish. After glue-up and shaping: danish oil, linseed oil, or 2–3 coats lacquer/varnish on the exterior.

Decoration note: Aboriginal didgeridoos are decorated with ochre-based pigments and dot-painting traditions that are part of a distinct artistic and ceremonial vocabulary. Non-Aboriginal makers typically use earth-tone acrylics, natural oil, or leave the material bare. Do not reproduce Aboriginal ceremonial designs.

Bottom Line

Cheapest real path: Hardware-store snap-together PVC. Five-foot length of 1.5" pipe + DWV Trap Adapter = $8–13, 15 minutes, no tools. Cut to 104 cm for key of E. Fully functional instrument.

Best natural-material US path: Agave stalk, if you are in the Southwest. Free material + ~$50–100 supplies + a weekend of active work (plus ~1 year drying time for a freshly harvested stalk, or immediate start with a found-dry stalk). Players consistently describe agave tone as approaching hardwood quality. The bore-through method (Desert Mountain Didgeridoos) is superior to split-reglue.

Best wood build: Split-and-hollow hardwood via the Wakademy method. Source a local ash, walnut, apple, or maple branch at 70mm+ diameter, 140–160cm. Split, bore, glue. Full weekend plus finish time. BOM under $80.

Key trade: PVC is instant, functional, and cheap. All natural materials require significantly more time, skill, and patience, but produce richer tone and an instrument that is genuinely yours. The tube is acoustically simple, which is why all of them work.

Confidence Audit

Evidence quality: Strong for PVC/ABS builds (multiple independent, active, reviewed sources with converging advice; decades of community practice). Strong for agave builds (dedicated maker literature; documented professional practice). Strong for bamboo builds (multiple step-by-step sources; Sachs modification documented across multiple rebuilds). Moderate for split hardwood (Wakademy is authoritative but French-language sources dominate the deepest technical detail; thin independent English build-log community). Strong for cultural protocols (YidakiStory, Wikipedia, Aboriginal Art & Culture site are each thorough).

Biggest confidence limiter: No live prices verified for bamboo poles, beeswax, or epoxy; BOM estimates based on hardware store pricing as of mid-2026, which will drift. PVC pipe costs cited in the Sachs PDF (~$1.49/5 ft in 2003) are substantially lower than current prices.

One thing to verify before acting: Current bamboo pole pricing and US availability before committing to a bamboo build; local bamboo nurseries may be cheaper than online. For the agave path: confirm local harvesting laws for your specific county/land management unit before collecting.

Frame & Hand Drums

Series: Sub-$150 Instrument Build Catalog. Worker RRRRRRR. Compiled June 2026. Prior survey superseded: Percussion and Idiophone Kits and Plans.md (Worker DDDDDDD, May 2026).

Orientation

Frame drums are arguably the oldest family of percussion instruments on earth, appearing in virtually every human musical tradition. What unites them structurally is simple: a membrane stretched over a shallow hoop or ring, with the frame depth much less than the head diameter. What differentiates them is everything else: the skin (rawhide, goatskin, fish skin, lizard skin, synthetic), the frame material (bent wood, carved wood, metal), the size (from the 6" kanjira to the 26"+ powwow drum), and the additions (metal rings for the daf and dayereh, gut snares for the bendir, jingles for the riq and tambourine, none for the tar or bodhran).

This catalog covers every documented build path under $150 in the US across all major frame drum and hand drum traditions. The family divides into:

  1. Native rawhide frame/hand drums (Indigenous North American) -- the most developed US kit market, multiple dedicated vendors
  2. Middle Eastern and North African frame drums -- daf, riq, bendir, tar, dayereh (Persian/Arab/Kurdish/North African)
  3. Irish bodhran -- dedicated kit market (UK-based, ships to US)
  4. Tambourine and variants (Mediterranean, European, South Indian kanjira)
  5. West African djembe (rehead path, not a kit) -- parts plus assembly from multiple US sources
  6. Loose heads and rims for builders (cross-tradition components)
  7. From-scratch BOM (any tradition's basic frame drum)
  8. Video build and rehead series (consolidated)

Anti-default field check: This is a worldwide family. The Native American drum kit vendor field and the Celtic bodhran market are prominent in English-language online retail, but they represent two out of perhaps twenty distinct frame drum traditions globally. This catalog makes a deliberate pass across Middle Eastern, North African, West African, South Asian, East Asian, Central Asian, and other traditions before declaring any category thin. Several traditions have very thin kit/build document trails in English; those gaps are named explicitly rather than padded.

No pitch tuning in this family. Frame drums produce timbre and resonance but not a specific pitched note. Skin tension during the drying process sets the voice; the build is correct when the skin is even and tight. This is the key reason the Native hand drum, the bodhran, the tar, and the bendir are all beginner-accessible builds: you do not have to tune a note.

Section 1: Native Rawhide Frame/Hand Drums (Indigenous North American)

Origin tag: Numerous Indigenous Nations across North America, including Plains, Great Lakes, Pacific Northwest, and many other regions. Single-headed rawhide frame drums vary considerably by nation and region; this catalog covers the general form sold through craft-kit vendors. Hand drums in this form are distinct from ceremonial powwow bass drums (the large community drum).

Close-enough bar: The kit builds a single-headed rawhide frame drum playable with a soft beater. Skin = rawhide (typically deer, elk, horse, cow, or bison). No pitch tuning; timbre is set by drying tension. No power tools; no glue; no cutting of wood (the frame is pre-bent). The build is: soak the hide, lace it wet over the frame, let it dry tight over several days.

Cultural note: The hand drum carries significant spiritual and ceremonial meaning across many Indigenous communities. The kits sold below are marketed for personal and craft use and produce personal drums in the general style of Indigenous North American frame drums; they are not powwow drums. The largest ceremonial drums are used in specific community and tribal contexts that are not accessible through craft kits. If you are not from a Native community and are drawn to these drums, approach with awareness: many makers treat the drum-making process itself as meaningful, and Cedar Mountain Drums (operated by a maker of Mingo heritage) frames its instructions in this spirit explicitly. You can make a drum; you are not obligated to adopt any ceremonial framing alongside it.

Group 1: Kits

All kits include: pre-cut rawhide head, pre-bent wood frame, rawhide lacing, beater makings, and instructions unless otherwise noted. Build time: 3-6 hours hands-on plus 1-2 days drying. No tools required beyond scissors and a soaking bucket.

Section 2: Middle Eastern and North African Frame Drums

This section covers five related instruments whose build paths share a structural core: a skin stretched over a shallow wooden ring. The differences are the additions (rings, snare strings, jingles, edge holes) and the specific skin type. All traditions are from the MENA region and adjacent areas. All have genuinely distinct playing techniques and musical contexts.

2A. Daf (also daff, duff)

Origin tag: Persian/Iranian/Kurdish; associated with Sufi devotional music, Kurdish folk music, and Persian classical tradition. A large (typically 16"-24"), shallow-framed circular drum with a goatskin or synthetic head and multiple interlocking metal rings or chains hanging on the inside face of the frame. Each stroke causes the rings to rattle and buzz against the head, producing the instrument's characteristic shimmer.

Close-enough bar: A large frame drum (16"+ diameter) with internal metal rings that buzz against the head. What must transfer: the ring buzz on each stroke, the large playing surface for full-hand strokes. A standard frame drum without rings is structurally a tar (Section 2D), not a daf.

Group 1: Build path (no pre-packaged US kit)

No dedicated daf kit exists in the US market. The documented path is a frame drum base plus a ring-attachment modification. Instructables hosts the clearest English-language guide:

Approach Materials Cost Source Confidence
Instructables "Frame Drum Daf Extension Kit" Frame drum base (any 16-22" goatskin drum) + metal jewelry chain with large double-links + 3D-printed or improvised mounting clamps Free plans; ~$10-25 for ring hardware; need a base drum instructables.com High (project confirmed real)

Ring construction detail: The Instructables guide specifies double-chain links (two interlocked rings per mounting point, then two more rings on the last link) using ~1.5mm silver or alloy wire wrapped around a 13.5mm dowel and closed with electronics solder. Commercial double-link jewelry chain with pleasant sound qualities also works. CAD files for 3D-printed clamps are included; improvised metal hook or tied-through-hole methods also documented in the thread.

For the base drum: Any 16"-22" goatskin-headed frame drum serves. A Mid-East or DOBANI production instrument in that size range runs approximately $25-65 [PLAUSIBLE; prices vary on Amazon/X8, verify before ordering]. Or build the base from loose components (see Section 6).

A full from-scratch daf (base + rings) in the US: roughly $50-90 total [PLAUSIBLE; depends on frame/skin source and ring hardware].

Group 3: Video tutorials

Persian-language video resources are richer than English-language for daf construction. Search "ساخت دف" on YouTube for Persian-source content showing the construction process. English-narrated full build videos were not confirmed this pass [UNCERTAIN].

Bottom line: No US kit. The Instructables ring-attachment modification is the documented cheap English-language route; total material cost beyond a base drum is $10-25. The base drum can be built from components (Section 6) or purchased as a finished inexpensive instrument. A functional daf is achievable for $50-90 total.

2B. Riq (also riqq, rik)

Origin tag: Egyptian/Arab; the riq is the classical tambourine of Arabic music, central to maqam and tarab ensemble playing. Small (8"-10" diameter), very shallow frame (~1.5-2" deep), goatskin or fish skin head (the thinner and more responsive the better), and exactly five pairs of brass cymbals mounted in paired slots in the frame. Played with highly refined finger technique: rolls, snaps, shake patterns. The riq is the percussion counterpart to the qanun and oud in classical Arab ensemble music.

Close-enough bar: The five pairs of matched brass cymbals are the defining characteristic and the hardest part to replicate cheaply. Small diameter and very thin responsive skin are the other functional requirements. A cheap modern tambourine with one row of jingles and a synthetic head is not an adequate substitute for serious playing; the overtone profile of the cymbals and the head response are both critical to the maqam context.

Groups 1-2: Build notes

There is no dedicated US riq-building kit. The build problem splits into two sub-problems: the frame/skin (solvable from Section 6 materials) and the cymbal sourcing (harder). Traditional brass riq cymbals are specialty items; 10 matched pieces with the correct dome geometry and ring frequency are not a hardware-store find. Options:

  • Buy an entry-level factory riq: Entry-level riqs from Darbuka Planet, Ethnic Musical, or Amazon run approximately $30-80 [PLAUSIBLE; confirm current pricing]; at this tier the cymbals are functional if not performance-grade.
  • Source cymbals separately: Small hand-hammered brass discs for tambourine jingle mounting are sold by ethnic music supply houses; expect ~$5-20 per set [PLAUSIBLE; hard to pin a current price without a confirmed source]. Mount in drilled or slotted holes in a shallow 8-9" frame drum rim.

English-language DIY riq build documentation is genuinely thin. The construction technique (cymbal mounting in slots, goatskin glued and tacked rather than laced) is described in reference sources but detailed tutorials are predominantly in Arabic-language video content. This is a field where the instructions exist but not in English.

Bottom line: The riq is technically a frame drum but the cymbal sourcing and mounting make it the hardest instrument in this section to build from scratch cheaply in the US. An entry-level factory instrument is realistically a better starting point than a DIY build for most makers.

2C. Bendir

Origin tag: North African / Maghreb (Morocco, Tunisia, Algeria, Libya); also used in Gnawa and Sufi ritual contexts. Medium-large (14"-16" diameter, shallow frame), goatskin head, played upright, with one or two gut or synthetic strings (snare strings) stretched across the inside of the head. The strings buzz against the underside of the skin on each stroke, creating the instrument's characteristic rattling resonance under the main drum voice. A thumb hole in the frame aids one-hand grip. Related to the tar (Section 2D) with snares added.

Close-enough bar: The snare strings must be present and properly tensioned against the underside of the head. Without them the result is a tar (or any plain frame drum); the bendir's character comes entirely from the string buzz. What must transfer: the snare resonance on both bass and treble strokes.

Group 1: Build/modification paths

Approach Materials Cost Source Confidence
Instructables "Frame Drum Bendir Extension Kit" Frame drum base + dacron cord or gut string + simple anchor hardware Free plans; ~$5-15 for cord + hardware instructables.com High
Cooperman Frame Drums "Bendir Strings" customization Cooperman adds 2 double strands of fine dacron cord, adjustable, to any model frame drum; send your drum to Cooperman $30 [ESTABLISHED] coopermanframedrums.com High

DIY string installation (free): Drill or punch two anchor points on the inner face of the frame, one on each side across the diameter. String dacron cord (0.5-1mm, similar to thin fishing line or light kite string) as two paired strands, crossing the drum face ~1-2cm above the head and running under light tension. The Instructables guide shows the specific geometry. Total material cost: ~$5.

Bottom line: Start with any 14-16" frame drum and add snare strings via the Instructables guide (free + ~$5 in cord) or pay Cooperman $30 to install them professionally. The DIY version is genuinely simple. Total bendir-conversion cost on top of a frame drum base: $5-30.

2D. Tar (Middle Eastern/Persian frame drum)

Origin tag: Iranian/Middle Eastern; the tar in this context is a large circular frame drum (distinct from the stringed tar of Iranian classical music). Used in Persian classical music (where it is the foundational frame drum), Turkish folk music, and across the broader MENA region. Shallow frame (2-3" deep), 16-22" diameter, goatskin or fish skin head stretched taut; no jingles, no snares, no rings. The playing technique uses specific finger positions and palm strokes. The frame is often very thin-walled; the skin very thin, giving a bright, responsive voice.

Close-enough bar: A large goatskin-headed frame drum with no additions IS functionally a tar. The structural build is the same as any plain frame drum; the tradition, tuning, and technique differentiate it.

Build path: The from-scratch frame drum BOM in Section 7 produces a functional tar. Any 16"-22" goatskin-headed frame drum sourced from the components in Section 6 or bought as a base DOBANI/Mid-East instrument serves.

Cooperman Frame Drums (Vermont) makes artisan-quality tars and bendirs as finished instruments, including several artist-model series (Glen Velez, Marla Leigh, David K., and others). These are above $150 but are the US reference-quality option if a serious instrument is the goal.

Bottom line: No separate kit or build process -- the tar IS the basic frame drum. Build it from the BOM in Section 7, or add a DOBANI frame drum as the base.

2E. Dayereh / Daire / Ghaval

Origin tag: Iranian, Central Asian (Uzbekistan, Tajikistan), Azerbaijani; the dayereh is a medium circular frame drum (25-40cm / ~10-16" diameter) with metal rings or chains attached to the inside of the frame, similar in structure to the daf but smaller. The Azerbaijani ghaval is a close relative with a similar ring-bearing structure. Used in folk and classical music; important in regional Sufi and devotional contexts.

Build path: Same as the daf ring-attachment modification (Section 2A) scaled to a smaller diameter. The Instructables daf guide applies directly; reduce the ring count proportionally.

English documentation gap: DIY dayereh build documentation in English is thin. The instrument is well described in reference sources but construction tutorials are predominantly in Persian, Uzbek, and Azerbaijani YouTube content. A direct search in those languages surfaces the relevant builds.

Cooperman Frame Drums produces both a dayereh (Rowan Storm model) and a ghaval (Classic and Velez models) as finished instruments, confirming the US maker awareness of these traditions.

Section 3: Irish Bodhran

Origin tag: Irish; the bodhran (pronounced "bow-rawn") is a single-headed circular frame drum, typically 14"-18" diameter, 3"-4" deep frame, goatskin or synthetic head, played with a tipper (a small two-headed wooden mallet) in Irish traditional music. Its documented history goes back to the Irish folk revival of the 1960s-70s; its claimed pre-revival origins are debated. It is now central to Irish trad sessions worldwide.

Close-enough bar: The bodhran is structurally a frame drum, but the tipper-based playing technique (two-headed stick technique, rapid alternating strokes) and the musical idiom (Irish trad session context) are specific to this instrument. A rawhide hand drum or a tar can make the same structural sound but is played with very different technique. What transfers: round frame + single membrane. What doesn't: the tipper technique and the session-music role.

Ultra-cheap variant (embroidery hoop): A 14" wooden embroidery hoop from any craft store (Hobby Lobby, Michaels: $3-8) can substitute for a proper bent-wood frame. Result is thinner and less durable but is a legitimate beginner build path; the Instructables guide documents this approach. Total cost on embroidery-hoop path: roughly $25-40.

Bottom line: The bodhran kit market is UK-dominated. Dragon Drums and McNeela are the vendors; prices need direct confirmation before ordering. For a US-sourced build, the scratch-build from Section 6 components at $60-85 is more practical and produces a sturdier drum. The embroidery hoop version at $25-40 works for a first attempt.

Section 4: Tambourine and Related Jingle-Frame Drums

Origin tag (tambourine): The tambourine (frame drum with jingle-bearing slots in the frame) appears across a very wide geographic distribution: Medieval and Renaissance Europe, Middle Eastern riq tradition (Section 2B), Italian tamburello (Puglia, Sicily), Greek defi, Brazilian pandeiro, South Indian kanjira. The structural principle is universal: pairs of metal discs mounted in slots or holes in the frame, jingling against each other and the head on each stroke.

Build path: No dedicated US tambourine-building kit was confirmed. The construction approach:

  1. Take a shallow frame drum rim (~2" depth, 8-18" diameter)
  2. Cut paired rectangular slots evenly spaced around the rim (~5 pairs for a riq-style, ~3-4 pairs for a tambourine)
  3. Insert paired metal discs (brass, steel, or zil bronze) with a small gap between them; secure with a pin or rivet through the slot

Jingle disc sets are sold by ethnic music suppliers and some drum supply houses; expect roughly $5-15 per set of jingles. The full tambourine build cost on top of a frame: ~$15-25 in jingle hardware.

Pandeiro (Brazilian): The pandeiro is a small (10") tambourine with a tunable head and a specific jingle (platinelas) geometry. No US kit was found; finished pandeiros from Cooperman Frame Drums and Latin percussion suppliers are available. Cooperman makes an artist-grade pandeiro [ESTABLISHED; price not confirmed this pass].

Kanjira (South Indian, Carnatic): A very small (6-8") tambourine with traditionally a monitor lizard skin head and a single pair of jingles; used in Carnatic classical music as a specialist percussion instrument. CITES regulations govern monitor lizard skins; modern instruments use synthetic heads. No US build kit or scratch-build tutorial was found this pass. Finished kanjiras from South Asian music importers: ~$20-50 [PLAUSIBLE]. Build documentation in English is effectively absent. [UNKNOWN for scratch builds in the US]

Section 5: Djembe (Rehead Path)

Origin tag: West African; the djembe is a goblet-shaped (not frame drum) single-headed drum with a goatskin head mounted using a rope-tension system. Originating in Mande-speaking West Africa (Mali, Guinea, Senegal, Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso), it spread globally via national ballet companies from the 1950s-80s and is now one of the world's most widely played hand percussion instruments.

Structural note: The djembe is NOT a frame drum -- it is a goblet drum with a carved wooden shell. It is included in this catalog because the brief names it explicitly and because the rehead path is one of the most documented DIY percussion builds anywhere. The body of the drum produces the resonance that makes the bass, tone, and slap technique possible; a frame drum is not a substitute.

Close-enough bar: The goblet shape positions the hands correctly for the three core tones (bass, open tone, slap); rope-tension system allows tuning. A rehead on an existing shell is the correct build path, not a kit.

This is not a kit build. The djembe rehead requires three separate components: a shell, a skin, and rope.

Group 1: Components for a Rehead

Component Spec US source Price Confidence
Goatskin head (standard, X8) Flat round, hair off, ~0.015" thick (~0.38mm); for 10"-14" drums X8 Drums 10": $16.80, 12": $17.80, 14": $18.90 [ESTABLISHED; out of stock at time of research -- verify availability] High (price); Med (availability)
Goatskin head (premium, X8) ~0.02" thick; for 16" drums X8 Drums 16": $24.08 [ESTABLISHED] High

Total rehead BOM on an existing shell: skin ($17-20) + rope ($15-20) = roughly $32-40 [PLAUSIBLE]. Full project on a used shell: shell ($20-60) + skin + rope = roughly $55-90 total. Well under $150 in either case.

Honest note on rope-pulling: Every experienced djembe builder makes the same point: pulling the vertical and diamond ropes to proper tension is genuinely hard on the hands and forearms. Without a tensioning bar or device, expect sore hands and slow progress. The ropes must be pulled very tight, and the head stretches and relaxes over 2-3 days requiring re-tightening. First-time reheads routinely take a full day of actual work spread across several days. This is not a reason not to attempt it; it is information about what the job actually is.

Skin thickness guidance: For beginners building on a smaller shell (10"), thinner skins (~0.015" / X8 standard grade) are the right choice. They are easier to tune and require less rope tension to achieve proper pitch. Thicker skins are appropriate for larger drums and more experienced builders.

Summary of the anti-default check: The frame drum catalog above covers 6 distinct traditions in depth (Indigenous North American, Persian/Iranian daf, Arab riq, North African bendir, Irish bodhran, West African djembe rehead) and notes the tar/dayereh/ghaval as closely related. The worldwide survey above identifies 9 additional traditions; most have absent or very thin English-language build documentation. The rich kit market is genuinely concentrated in the US (Native drum vendors) and UK/Ireland (bodhran). This is real, not a cataloging failure; most frame drum traditions outside these two streams are either learned from masters by ear or are served by inexpensive factory instruments rather than craft kits.

The ~1-in-10 dud rate: Natural skin rounds from any craft/supply source sometimes arrive with scarring, thin spots, holes near the edge, or uneven thickness that affects playability. Centralia states this explicitly in their product notes: "These are wild animals and will not be uniform in thickness or perfect in looks. There will be scarring, cut marks, and occasionally a hole near the edge of the round." This is industry-standard reality, not a vendor-specific problem. Practical guidance from experienced builders: order one size up from what you need, inspect before cutting to drum-head size, and treat natural variation as expected. Budget for a fallback order on drums you care about.

Rawhide and Goatskin Sourcing: Ethical and Practical Notes

Natural drum skins are a byproduct of the food and hide industries. The vendors in this catalog source rawhide from:

  • Centralia Fur & Hide: US-sourced; states that horse rawhide comes from natural deaths. Deer, elk, bison from licensed hunting or farming.
  • Wandering Bull: US-sourced; species not detailed on the main product pages.
  • goatskins.com: Goatskins processed for drum building; specifies black-salt processing (replaces older lime processing).
  • X8 Drums: Goatskins for djembe; sources from West Africa (Mali region cited on Hawkdancing-brand skins).

The drum-building craft supply market is not a luxury or specialty animal-products market; it connects directly to established livestock and hunting industries. Centralia's note that their horse rawhide comes from natural deaths is an explicit sourcing transparency statement worth noting; other vendors do not make equivalent statements on their current product pages, which is not unusual and does not imply different sourcing.

The practical note on natural skin variability (the ~1-in-10 dud rate, scarring, edge holes, uneven thickness) applies to all vendors selling natural-skin rounds. It is a property of natural materials, not a vendor quality problem.

Prices read June 2026. All prices are snapshots; verify before ordering. No em dashes used in this document.

Tuned Percussion & Lamellophone

Supersedes: non-drum sections of Percussion and Idiophone Kits and Plans.md (Worker DDDDDDD, 2026-05-29). Hand drums (djembe, frame drum, bodhran) are owned by Worker RRRRRRR and are NOT in this file.

The tuning axis: why percussion is different

Every instrument family has a hidden difficulty axis. In percussion and idiophones, that axis is tuning, and it separates builds that are genuinely accessible from ones that take weeks to years. Assembly skill (cutting, gluing, clamping) is nearly irrelevant here; the tuning step is the real gate. This catalog flags tuning difficulty explicitly on every entry because it is the single most predictive factor in whether a build produces a playable instrument.

Ranked from no tuning to the deepest:

  1. No pitch tuning: cajon, contact mic. You set timbre (snare buzz) but never a note.
  2. Cut-to-length tuning: pipe/conduit xylophone, PVC xylophone. Pitch is a function of tube length; cut to a chart, trim to tune. Forgiving.
  3. Slide-and-tap tine tuning: OEM kalimba kit. Slide tine in or out, tap with hammer, check tuner. One note at a time, gentle.
  4. Steel-tongue tuning: hank drum / tank drum. Grind or file tongues longer/shorter/thinner. Slow, irreversible if you overshoot. Thick tank steel compounds the difficulty.
  5. Forge-and-tune tine tuning: mbira dzavadzimu. You make the tine first (metallurgy), then tune. The metalwork precedes and constrains the tuning.
  6. Bar tuning: xylophone, marimba, balafon. Undercut the bar to lower pitch; remove material from the center arch (fundamental) and the nodal ends (overtones). A concert marimba bar is triple-tuned. This is a genuine craft skill.
  7. Hammer-tuned dome: handpan. Multi-month to multi-year skill, high failure rate. Not in scope as a beginner build.

This catalog is organized by instrument family, not by difficulty. Use the tuning flag on each entry to locate where the real work lives.

Anti-default note

Several instrument names in this scope sound Western by default. They are not. The kalimba is pan-African; the mbira dzavadzimu is Shona/Zimbabwean; the cajon is Peruvian Afro-descendant; the marimba has African origins (the balafon, gyil, amadinda, and mbila are its kin); the metallophone is gamelan-adjacent (Javanese, Balinese). The kit and plans market is largely US/European, but the instruments themselves are not, and where non-Western DIY traditions or build paths exist they are listed here alongside the Western ones.

1. Lamellophone family: kalimba, mbira, marimbula, and kin

Orientation

A lamellophone makes sound by plucking flexible metal (or in older forms, cane or bamboo) tines anchored at one end. The Shona mbira dzavadzimu is the instrument the Western kalimba derives from, via Hugh Tracey's mid-20th century commercial adaptation. The word "kalimba" is now a generic retail term covering dozens of OEM variations. The marimbula is the Caribbean (especially Cuban) bass lamellophone, derived from African instruments brought by enslaved people. The sanza, likembe, karimba, and njari are further variants across Central and West Africa. The Array mbira is a 1980s American invention that applies circle-of-fifths layout to a greatly extended tine array.

Close-enough bar: Any lamellophone requires the same physical technique: thumbs (and sometimes index fingers) pluck tines of varying lengths. The key variables that differ across the family are tine material (steel, spring steel, titanium, phosphor bronze), number of tines (8 to 200+), tuning system (diatonic, pentatonic, Shona modal, chromatic), and the presence/absence of a resonator cavity or gourd.

The tuning axis here: Kalimba kit = slide-and-tap (30 minutes to an hour). From-scratch tine-on-board = slightly harder (material selection matters). Mbira dzavadzimu from scratch = forge-and-tune (advanced metalwork preceding the tuning). Array mbira = not a DIY path. Marimbula = cut-and-install, moderate.

Origin: Pan-African lamellophone tradition; the modern "kalimba" kit form derives from Hugh Tracey's commercial Kalimba (1950s, South Africa) and feeds through the OEM factory market that now ships worldwide.

1b. Mbira dzavadzimu and the Shona lamellophone tradition

Origin: Zimbabwe / Shona people. The mbira dzavadzimu ("voice of the ancestors") has 22-28 tines in a specific Shona modal tuning, played inside a deze (calabash resonator) fitted with bottle-cap buzzers. The karimba (15 tines) and nyunga nyunga are related Shona forms. The tradition is oral and apprenticeship-based; most Western documentation is thin or secondary.

The build problem: Unlike the kalimba, an mbira is not assembled from precut parts. The tine is forged: the maker pounds spring-steel wire or strip stock on an anvil, wide and thin for low notes (more flexible = lower pitch), narrow and thick for high ones, then tunes by shortening or flattening. Bottle-cap buzzers are added for the characteristic rattle timbre. The body (gwariva) is typically a hardwood board with a bridge bar. Getting the Shona tonal system right requires knowing the target intervals by ear, not by a Western chromatic chart.

Titanium spokes produce a different, very clean tone (see Tom Whitwell build below). Bobby pins work for higher-pitched smaller instruments but have limited sustain. The material choice predetermines the sustain and tone quality before tuning begins.

1c. Marimbula and bass lamellophone

Origin: Cuba / Caribbean. The marimbula (also marímbula, rumba box, rhumba box) is a large-box lamellophone with 5-10 thick steel tongues tuned to bass notes. It arrived in the Caribbean through African enslaved musicians and became a bass substitute in Cuban son and other forms. Dennis Havlena's "bass kalimba" is a direct functional equivalent.

2. Cajon

Orientation

Origin: Peru, Afro-Peruvian tradition. The cajon is a box drum played by sitting on it and slapping the front plate (tapa). Internal snare wires or guitar strings produce the characteristic buzz. Brought to Spain by Paco de Lucia in the 1970s and now globally ubiquitous. The construction is fundamentally plywood joinery, which makes it one of the most accessible from-plans builds in percussion.

Close-enough bar: The technique (seated, front-plate slap) must carry. A cajon with no snare is just a box; the snare wire placement and tension are the key sound variable. There is no pitch tuning at all, which is exactly why the kit market is so beginner-friendly.

The tuning axis: None. Sound customization is snare wire type, front-plate thickness (3-5mm is typical), and how freely the plate is mounted. This is the instrument in this catalog with zero tuning difficulty.

3. Steel tongue drum / hank drum

Orientation

Origin: Modern Western, 2007. Dennis Havlena (Michigan, callsign W8MI) created the first tongue drum from a 20-lb propane tank in February 2007, inspired by the Swiss Hang and the Tambiro (a Zimbabwean instrument made from oil drums). He named it the "hank drum" (Hang + tank) and published the plans free. This sparked a global DIY movement. The instrument form is now commercially manufactured worldwide (under brands like Hluru, Lingting, HAPI, Meinl Sonic Energy) but the DIY path remains anchored to Havlena's plan.

Close-enough bar: All tongue drums share the same playing technique (mallets or fingers on steel tongues); the key variables are steel thickness (affects tone and tuning difficulty), tongue count and layout, and whether the instrument is a cut tank or a purpose-welded shell.

The tuning axis: Steel tongue tuning is the major difficulty axis for this family. You lower a tongue's pitch by grinding or filing it longer or thinner (more flexible = lower pitch). You cannot raise a pitch without adding mass (neodymium magnets work for small raises). Thick tank steel (typically 3/16") makes each tuning iteration slow and the feedback loop is long. Thin sheet stock tunes more responsively but requires welding skill to form the shell. This is the second-hardest tuning skill in this catalog after bar tuning.

Important: no true "assemble it" kits exist in this space. Unlike the cajon or kalimba, there is no box of precut tongue drum parts you assemble. Every tongue drum build is either buy-finished or build-from-raw-materials. Finished instruments start at $40-80 on Amazon.

Group 1: Kits (there are none)

No commercial assemble-it-yourself tongue drum kit has been found in this research pass. The market bifurcates cleanly into finished instruments (buy) and raw-material DIY builds (plans). This is genuinely the situation, not a research gap [ESTABLISHED by cross-search of Amazon, Etsy, major retailers].

Havlena plan detail: The tank is flipped; the base (thicker steel) is the top of the instrument. Radial tongues are cut into the base, 7-10 tongues typically. Havlena notes that proper tuning is achievable and not technically difficult ("if you can tune a guitar, you can tune the drum"), but it is time-consuming: realistic total build is 8-25 hours with tuning taking 8-15 of those. Group 3: Video tutorials

The Steel Tongue Drum Wikipedia article and Hluru's blog document the history and construction approach; most tutorial video content is on YouTube under "hank drum build" or "tongue drum DIY."

Bottom line: If you want a tongue drum under $150 and don't want to tune steel, buy one. The DIY path is chosen for the craft and customization, not for economy: a finished HAPI Mini at $60-80 costs about the same as the materials for a tank build, with a fraction of the time. The Havlena plan is still the canonical entry point, and the process is well-documented and achievable; the tuning is the honest cost.

4. Struck bars: xylophone, metallophone, marimba

Orientation

The worldwide family. Struck-bar idiophone traditions exist on every inhabited continent. The xylophone concept (wooden bars, struck with mallets) is documented in Southeast Asia (the Javanese gambang, Balinese gangsa), West Africa (the balafon, associated with the Manding people; the gyil of the Dagara people of northern Ghana and Burkina Faso), Central Africa (the amadinda and akadinda of the Baganda people of Uganda), southern Africa (the mbila / timbila of the Chopi people of Mozambique), and South/Central America (the marimba, whose origins trace to Africa). The Western concert xylophone and marimba are one branch of this worldwide family. The metallophone (metal bars instead of wood) is central to Javanese and Balinese gamelan tradition.

The build problem. The struck bar is the most skill-intensive DIY idiophone. A tube (metal or PVC) is simpler: cut to a length chart, support at the nodes (22.4% from each end), done. A wooden or metal bar requires undercutting: you remove material from the underside in an arch to lower the fundamental, and on serious instruments you also tune the second and third partial (the transverse overtones) to musically useful ratios. On a concert marimba the low-register bars are triple-tuned. This is a genuine craft.

The materials scope limit applies here strictly. Several of the best-known plan sets (makeamarimba.com P2 Mini-Marimba and above) have materials costs that exceed $150. Those entries are flagged and their scope noted; only the ones whose full materials BOM stays under $150 are presented as qualifying builds.

4a. Tube/pipe builds (metallophone and xylophone)

Origin: Tube instruments derive from the gamelan metallophone tradition (Java/Bali) and from Western physics-class pipe instruments; both use the same acoustic principle.

Physics note (applies to all tube and bar builds): The support points must be at the nodes of vibration, located 22.4% of the bar/tube length from each end. This is the magic number. Support anywhere else and you damp the fundamental. Longer = lower pitch; shorter = higher pitch. For a simple cut-to-length instrument, the EMT conduit or aluminum tube gives a clean pentatonic or diatonic set in under 2 hours. A chromatic set (13 pipes per octave) takes more time but uses the same physics [ESTABLISHED].

Tube vs. bar tone note: PVC sounds dull and plastic. EMT conduit (steel) sounds brighter with less sustain. Aluminum bar stock sounds most like a metallophone or glockenspiel. None of these approximate a marimba's warm wooden tone; for that you need wood bars and resonator tubes, which is the next tier.

4d. Non-Western struck bar traditions

Origin note: The instruments below are the direct ancestors of or cultural parallels to the marimba and xylophone. They are not Western instruments that happen to come from non-Western countries; they have distinct tonal systems, playing techniques, and construction traditions.

Instrument Origin / people Build situation Source / finished instrument reference
Balafon West Africa (Manding, Bwaba, Senufo, and others; Guinea, Burkina Faso, Mali) Hardwood bars (traditionally rosewood or similar dense local hardwood), gourd resonators with spider-web membrane buzzers for characteristic timbre, cotton-cord mounting. Construction documented in general terms online; Amazon "IE African Marimba Plans" covers the general approach. Gourd resonators can be substituted with PVC pipe. A simplified pentatonic balafon is buildable for ~$40-80 in materials if hardwood is sourced cheaply. Full gourd-resonated build requires sourcing gourds (calabashes). Bar tuning is the gate: same undercut-to-pitch method as Western marimba. IE African Marimba Plans (Amazon)
Gyil Ghana / Burkina Faso, Dagara people 14-bar instrument, liga hardwood bars, calabash gourds, goat skin and sinew fastenings; specific Dagara pentatonic tuning system. No Western DIY plan found; cultural instrument requiring traditional knowledge for authentic tuning. Finished instruments available from Africa Heartwood Project (non-profit, Ghanaian artisans) at ~$80-130. Africa Heartwood Project (Amazon)
Amadinda / Akadinda Uganda, Baganda people 12-log xylophone played by 3 players in interlocking rhythmic patterns; no gourd resonators (different sound character); Buganda pentatonic tuning. No formal Western DIY plans found. A single-player miniature amadinda (6-8 logs) could be built from wood rounds or dimensional lumber tuned by planing. allaroundthisworld.com reference
Gambang (gamelan) Java / Bali, Indonesia 17-21 wood keys suspended on cords over a boat-shaped resonator box; pelog or slendro tuning. No Western DIY plan set found; the construction approach (bar suspension on cord over resonator box) is documented in general terms and is buildable. Bar tuning to Javanese pelog intervals is specialized. General gamelan construction literature

5. Glass / found-tuned (brief mention)

Origin: Glass harp and water-glass instruments appear in European history from the 16th century; the bottle xylophone is a folk and science-education instrument worldwide.

These are listed briefly per the brief's instruction. Full treatment lives in the Weird and Experimental worker (HHHHHHH).

Instrument Technique Materials Cost Source
Bottle / water-glass xylophone Strike glass or plastic bottles filled to different water levels; more water = lower pitch Glass bottles or jars + water ~$0-5 (found/household) Phil Tulga guide; intemenos.com
Glass harp (crystallophone) Rub the moistened rim of a stemmed wine glass; friction produces a sustained tone Wine glasses with stems ~$0-20 (found) Robert Tiso how-to; Ontario Science Centre DIY

Tuning: Water level tuning is extremely forgiving but unstable (evaporation, temperature). These instruments are better thought of as science demonstrations than serious pitched instruments. Glass harp (rim-rubbing) can be genuinely musical and is the more interesting playing technique of the two.

6. Handpan (honest note only)

Origin: Switzerland, 2000. Felix Rohner and Sabina Schärer (PANArt) created the Hang from nitrided steel deep-drawn shells. The name "handpan" has become generic for the instrument type.

DIY situation (stated plainly): A real raw-shell and DIY market exists. Ayasa Instruments, Kita Pantam, Dave's Island Instruments, and Mudra all sell deep-drawn raw or nitrided shells so a builder does not have to form the steel. One published source cites complete DIY kits in the ~$300-500 range (specific prices not confirmed this pass [UNCERTAIN]). But the consensus from established makers is blunt: hammer-tuning a handpan requires training one's ear and hands over hundreds of hours of practice; almost everyone destroys their first several attempts; and a good-sounding instrument is not a beginner or first-year outcome. The raw shells alone price out above $150, and the skill cost is higher still.

This is not a beginner under-$150 kit space. The handpan is listed here because the brief asks for an honest note, not because it qualifies. Pro handpans cost $1,000-3,000 for a reason. If the appeal is "steel dome with a beautiful reverberant tone," a finished steel tongue drum at $40-80 gives you a related sound at a fraction of the commitment [ESTABLISHED, community consensus].

8. Sniper and back-country notes

OEM kalimba label proliferation: The 17-key mahogany DIY kit appears under Kmise, Donner, Moozica, Hluru, Eastrock, Finether, JOINPAYA, and others. At least some of these share a factory source; the recurring missing-glue and ill-fitting side-piece complaints appear across labels [PLAUSIBLE shared OEM source]. Price, not brand, is the real variable. Check actual Amazon listing reviews at time of purchase.

Kalimba Dream US shipping pause (June 2026): Kalimba Dream (Australia) has explicitly suspended US shipping due to removal of the de minimis exemption and new tariff structures, noting that postal services do not yet have a system to handle the charges. Their A$51.95 10-key DIY kit was previously a solid option. Verify status before relying on this source. [ESTABLISHED: stated on their site]

Havlena as a multi-instrument resource: Dennis Havlena's website (dennishavlena.com) is one of the load-bearing free-plans sites in this catalog, covering the hank drum, bass kalimba/marimbula, conduit xylophone, and more. His plans are plain HTML, sometimes hard to navigate, but the data is real and the builds are well-tested by a community of hundreds of builders.

EMT conduit price update: The classic Mother Earth News pipe xylophone article cited 1/2" × 10ft EMT conduit at $2-3. Current price (June 2026): ~$5.99 at True Value [ESTABLISHED: True Value listing]. The method is the same; the cost estimate is outdated in older sources.

makeamarimba.com materials scope limit: Jim McCarthy's plans are legitimate and widely used. But only the Simple Glockenspiel (~$20 materials) and Box Resonated Xylophone (~$33 materials) are within the under-$150 materials threshold. P2 Mini-Marimba and above require $250-1,700 in materials. These are not a loophole (cheap plan + expensive BOM): the catalog's $150 rule applies to the full materials cost, not the plan price.

Non-Western build-path scarcity: The Shona mbira has documented Western maker paths (GroupDIY, tinotenda, Instructables). The balafon has basic construction documentation and an Amazon plans product. The gyil and amadinda have almost no Western hobbyist build documentation; the best available path for gyil is to buy a finished instrument from Africa Heartwood Project and study it. This is genuinely sparse, not a search failure.

Alternate Mode CaJon DIY Kit scope clarification: This is an electronic trigger-conversion kit, not an acoustic cajon assembly kit. It converts any cajon into a MIDI percussion controller. Priced at ~$99 (2018); verify current price. Requires a separate FTB interface for power/MIDI communication, plus a drum brain or VST. Total system cost pushes well above $150 but the kit itself may qualify. Listed for completeness.

Electronic & Synth DIY

Sound-role is flagged per entry because "close-enough bar" on technique matters less here than knowing what a device actually does. Electronic instruments are tools for a sound type, not playing-technique instruments.

Price sources read or verified June 2026 unless otherwise noted. Key price changes from the prior survey: Korg NTS-1 mkII is now ~$199.99 (over budget; flagged and excluded from kits, retained as a note); Open Theremin V4.5 is now €189-239 (over budget; excluded). These were under budget in the May 2026 prior survey.

1. Atari Punk Console (APC) / Stepped Tone Generator

Sound role: Noise / stepped-tone / drone. Produces harsh, aggressive square-wave tones stepping across pitches set by two pots (one controls the oscillator frequency, one controls the step-rate). CV inputs on Synthrotek's version extend it toward sequencer-triggered noise. Not a melodic instrument; pure noise/drone/glitch character.

Origin: American circuit tradition (Forrest Mims III, "Engineer's Notebook II," ca. 1983; named by Kaustic Machines in 2002). Based on a 556 dual-timer IC. Now reproduced by many builders worldwide.

Close-enough bar: Any 556-based stepped-tone generator is the same circuit. Variants mostly differ in enclosure, CV capability, and whether a speaker is built in.

2. MFOS Noise Toaster

Sound role: Full mono synth voice. A self-contained battery-powered synth: VCO, white-noise generator, VCF (voltage-controlled low-pass filter), LFO, AR envelope generator, VCA, and a 1-watt amp/speaker built in. More instrument than noise box — you can play it expressively. Line out for recording.

Origin: American (Ray Wilson, Music From Outer Space, ca. 2010). Wilson died in 2016; synthCube carries on the PCB/kit production.

Close-enough bar: The Noise Toaster is a real battery-powered synth in a box. The voice chain (VCO → noise → VCF → envelope → VCA → amp) is analogous to any subtractive mono synth; the difference is no keyboard and no MIDI — it is knob-operated entirely.

3. MFOS Weird Sound Generator / Alien Screamer

Sound role: Noise / drone / experimental. Multiple oscillators interacting in chaotic ways — unpredictable and expressive. Not melodic; pure texture/noise/timbral play. The Alien Screamer is a simpler single-voice variant. Both are battery-powered tabletop noise instruments.

Origin: American (Ray Wilson / MFOS). Schematic-first designs; kits and PCBs via synthCube.

Close-enough bar: Noise/drone instruments in this class don't emulate a specific playing technique — you turn knobs. The "close-enough" question is whether you want controllable chaos (WSG) or pure random noise (Alien Screamer). Both are experimental.

4. Baby8 / Baby10 Sequencer

Sound role: 8-step (or 10-step) CV + gate sequencer. Drives other synths or drum voices — it does not make sound itself. Each step has its own CV pot setting the voltage (0-5V), plus an LED and a gate output. Classic pattern machine. The "instrument" here is the sequence it generates.

Origin: American CMOS circuit tradition (Baby10 originally from Captain's Analog; Baby8 is the 8-step commercial evolution). Based on the CD4017 decade counter IC. Global hobbyist community.

Close-enough bar: An 8-step sequencer is a 8-step sequencer. The Baby8/10 is analog (CV + gate), not MIDI. It drives CV-based synths (Eurorack, 0-5V gear, modified synths) directly.

5. Theremin (DIY, Under $150)

Sound role: Theremin pitch (monophonic, proximity-controlled pitch and optionally volume). The instrument produces a pure continuous tone whose pitch and volume are controlled by the distance of your hands from two antennas — no physical contact. The most pitch-sensitive DIY instrument in this catalog.

Origin: Russian (Leon Theremin, ca. 1920). Now a global hobbyist tradition with US-dominant kit market.

Close-enough bar: True heterodyning analog theremin (pitch + volume antennas, RF oscillators). Pitch-only versions (single antenna) are simpler builds but limited. Playability requires calibration; the antenna response must be set to a comfortable range. Digital theremins (Arduino-based) work but feel different from analog heterodyning — note the distinction.

Important price changes: The Open Theremin (formerly the best-documented kit in this price band at ~€74) is now the V4.5 Deluxe Bundle at €189-239 — over budget. The PAiA Theremax is ~$200 — over budget. See Group 4 for both as close-enough options at slightly over $150. Under-$150 kit options are now limited.

6. Gakken SX-150 Mark II

Sound role: Analog mono synth voice (stylus-controlled). A compact battery-powered analog mono synth with a ribbon/stylus "keyboard" — you drag a stylus along a resistive strip to control pitch, rather than pressing keys. 10 knobs for tweaking the voice (oscillator, filter, etc.). Has a built-in speaker and line out.

Origin: Japanese (Gakken/Chugan Corporation, 2008). Cult instrument; reviewed by Make: magazine. Now sold as an import.

Close-enough bar: The SX-150 is an instrument, not a kit to build — it arrives pre-assembled except for mounting. It teaches no soldering. Its closest cousins are the Stylophone and the Korg Monotron. The "build" here is trivial assembly.

7. Eurorack DIY Module Kits (Under $150)

Sound role: Varies by module. Eurorack modules are building blocks — VCO (oscillator/tone generator), VCF (filter), VCA (amplifier/gate), envelope generators, sequencers, utilities. An individual module does not make a complete instrument; it is a voice component. You need a case, power supply, and at least VCO + VCA to make a sound.

Origin: Eurorack format originated with Doepfer (German, 1996). The DIY kit market is global: US, UK, Germany, Australia, Japan, France.

Close-enough bar / sound-role per module type: - VCO = oscillator, generates pitch. Sound role: tone source. - VCF = filter, shapes timbre. Sound role: tone coloring. - VCA = amplifier, controls volume/dynamics. Sound role: gate/envelope control. - Envelope generator = AR/ADSR. Sound role: shapes VCA/VCF over time. - Sequencer = CV pattern generator. Sound role: drives pitch sequence. - Utility = mixers, multiples, attenuators. Sound role: signal routing.

Important caveat: A single module is not a complete instrument. To make melodic sound, you need at minimum a case + power + VCO + VCA. The mki x es.EDU path is the best self-contained "build a full synth module by module" plan in this budget.
