9. Circuit Bending

Sound role: Experimental / glitch / noise / transformed toys. Circuit bending is the art of short-circuiting audio electronics (toys, cheap keyboards, drum machines) to produce unintended sounds — glitchy loops, pitch instability, body-contact theremin effects, filter modulation. The instrument is the bent object; the practice produces entirely new sounds from existing circuits.

Origin: American (Reed Ghazala, 1960s — he coined the term and practice; published widely from the 1990s onward).

Close-enough bar: Circuit bending produces unique, one-of-a-kind instruments every time. No two bends are alike. The "sound role" is deliberately undefined — that unpredictability is the point.

The practice

Circuit bending requires no schematic knowledge and almost no electronics knowledge. The process: power a toy, use a low-voltage probe (or just bridging contacts with a wire) to find "bends" — points where connecting two contacts changes the sound interestingly. Then solder switches, pots, or body contacts to make those bends repeatable and performable.

Key reference: Reed Ghazala, Circuit-Bending: Build Your Own Alien Instruments (Wiley, 2005). The definitive book; covers history, tools, technique, and 18+ specific projects including Speak & Spell, Casio SK-1, and others. Available new and used ($15-30 used on Amazon/AbeBooks) [ESTABLISHED].

Ghazala's own site: anti-theory.com — project documentation and circuit-bending philosophy.

Circuit Bending Wiki: circuitbending.miraheze.org — community documentation of specific device bends.

Tooling (very cheap)

The tooling is the cheapest of any category in this catalog. You need: a multimeter (already assumed), a low-voltage probe or alligator clips ($5 set), wire, a soldering iron (already assumed), SPDT and SPST switches (~$0.50-1 each), potentiometers, and a drill for the enclosure. Total bending tool cost beyond what you already have: under $20.

Additionally, a DIY circuit bending kit exists (RetroFixes, ~$15-20 [PLAUSIBLE]) with resistors, capacitors, switches, and body contacts for quick experimentation: retrofixes.com

Target toys (where to find, what to buy)

Target Why benders like it Where to find Price
Casio SK-1 / SK-5 (sampling keyboard) The "holy grail" — massive bend potential: pitch bending, filter-like effects, loop manipulation, sampling glitches Thrift stores, eBay, Reverb $20-80+ on eBay (inflated by popularity) [PLAUSIBLE]
Speak & Spell / Speak & Math / Speak & Read (Texas Instruments, 1978-82) Classic bending targets; voice synthesis ICs respond dramatically to bends. Ghazala's 18 projects feature these. eBay, thrift stores $10-40 [PLAUSIBLE; varies wildly]
Cheap Casio keyboards (MT-series, PT-series) Abundant, inexpensive; many bend points. Less documented than SK-1 but easier to find. Thrift stores $2-15 [PLAUSIBLE]
Cheap kids' toys with voices (Furby, talking books, electronic games) Any battery-powered audio toy with a CMOS sound chip is a bending candidate. Thrift stores / dollar stores $1-10
Texas Instruments Learning toys (Vocoder series) Same IC family as Speak & Spell eBay / thrift $5-30 [PLAUSIBLE]

Finding targets: Thrift stores are the primary source. Goodwill, Salvation Army, local thrift shops. The rule of thumb: if it makes sound and costs under $10, it is worth probing. The SK-1 specifically has risen in price due to popularity; expect $30-80 now vs. "$5 at a thrift store" of a decade ago.

Safety: Never bend anything plugged into AC mains. Battery-powered devices only. The risk of circuit bending is frying the IC (the toy stops working); the risk of bending mains-powered gear is electrocution. Stick to battery devices.

Bottom line: The cheapest path to an experimental sound instrument in the entire catalog. Zero kit cost (you buy or find a toy); tooling cost under $20 additional. The book is the real investment and it pays for itself across dozens of projects.

10. Electronic Wind Controller (DIY / Open-Source)

Sound role: Wind MIDI controller / synth voice. Played like a wind instrument — breath pressure plus fingering determine note, velocity, and expression. Sends MIDI (or CV) to a synth or computer. Some designs include an onboard synth voice.

Origin: American (Lyricon, 1970s; Akai EWI lineage). Open-source DIY versions are global community projects, primarily documented on Hackaday.io and GitHub.

Close-enough bar: A DIY EWI must have: (1) a breath/pressure sensor for attack and dynamics, (2) touch or key sensors for fingering, (3) MIDI output. The fingering can match EWI (chromatic/saxophone-like) or be original. Pitch control from breath pressure alone (without fingering) is a different instrument (closer to theremin or pressure-pitch synth).

11. The Plans Tier: Schematic Ecosystems and Design Archives (the center)

This is the center of the synth-DIY hobby, not a footnote. The canonical designers are plan publishers first; the PCB and kit market exists to serve the plans, not the other way around. These are resources/ecosystems, not single products.

MFOS — Music From Outer Space (Ray Wilson, d. 2016)

What it is: The most beginner-accessible free-schematic archive in analog synth DIY. Dozens of designs from noise boxes to full synthesizers, all with complete schematics, BOMs, and build notes. synthCube carries on the PCB and kit production.

Path: Free schematic → source PCB (from synthCube or fabricate from MFOS Gerbers) → source BOM from Mouser/Tayda → solder. All designs fully documented.

Key designs: Weird Sound Generator, Alien Screamer, Noise Toaster, Sound Lab Mini-Synth (full mono subtractive synth), Euro Noise, Noise Cornucopia. Each entry has a project page with full documentation.

Links: musicfromouterspace.com (schematics) / synthcube.com (PCBs and kits) / "Make: Analog Synthesizers" (book companion)

Yusynth (Yves Usson)

What it is: A free archive of high-quality modular synthesizer designs, particularly filters and VCOs. Yusynth designs are revered in the Eurorack and 5U community for musicality and quality.

Path: Schematic-only → third parties sell PCBs (Soundtronics, occasionally Thonk); self-source BOM. Advanced builds requiring scope for calibration.

Key designs: Mini Moog VCF clone, Steiner-Parker VCF, ARP VCF clone, various VCOs. Each with schematic + BOM + notes.

Link: yusynth.net

Ken Stone / CGS (Catgirl Synth) + Serge legacy

What it is: Ken Stone's personal modular designs (CGS) plus a large set of Serge-inspired designs. Ken retired from PCB sales in 2016 and transferred both his designs and the Serge PCB production to Laurie Biddulph at Elby Designs (Australia; ships worldwide). The CGS site is archived; the designs remain.

Path: Schematics archived at catgirlsynth.com (partially) → PCBs and some kits from Elby Designs → source BOM. Advanced modular work.

Key designs: Dual oscillator, random voltage sources, Serge-style VCO/VCF/VCA, wave multiplier, gate sequencer.

Links: elby-designs.com (PCBs) / CGS archive (schematics)

Thomas Henry

What it is: Designs published in books rather than on a website. Famous for using ordinary parts in novel ways; his VCO-555 is widely called one of the best-sounding simple analog oscillators ever designed. PCBs from third parties (fonitronik, and archives at birthofasynth.com, sdiy.info).

Path: Buy book → extract schematic and BOM → find PCB from third party or design your own → build. Very advanced; requires scope.

Key designs: VCO-555, CGS VCLFO, designs in "Build a Better Music Synthesizer" (Tab Books, 1987) and "An Analog Synthesizer for the 21st Century" (Lulu, 2012).

Links: birthofasynth.com / fonitronik on various synth-DIY marketplaces / sdiy.info

Electronotes (Bernie Hutchins, 1970s-80s)

What it is: The foundational synth-DIY newsletter archive. Published by Bernie Hutchins from 1973 to 1995+, Electronotes documented analog synthesis technology in the era when Moog and ARP circuits were trade secrets. The archive is the intellectual foundation of the entire DIY community.

Path: Archive access (partially free, partially gated) → extract circuits → build from scratch. Historical + advanced.

Link: electronotes.netfirms.com

Jürgen Haible Design Archive

What it is: Legendary analog circuit designs by Jürgen Haible (d. 2011), preserved by the community after his death. Includes the Tau Phaser, Wasp filter recreation, and others. Not actively supported; schematics preserved.

Path: Schematic archives → community PCBs → build. Advanced.

Link: Various preservation mirrors; search "Jürgen Haible archive synth-DIY"

Look Mum No Computer (Sam Battle)

What it is: A UK maker and musician who documents his builds extensively on YouTube and his website. The Super Simple Oscillator (reverse-avalanche transistor circuit) is particularly notable as a genuinely free, minimal, interesting oscillator build with stripboard layout. The "1000 Oscillator" project documented many variants.

Path: Free schematic + stripboard layout on his site → build directly. Very beginner-accessible circuits.

Sound role: Oscillator / drone (the Super Simple Oscillator) + larger modular builds.

Links: lookmumnocomputer.com/projects / Super Simple Oscillator

Kassutronics

What it is: High-quality open Eurorack designs by Caspar Ockeloen-Korppi (Finland). Publishes schematics and PCB files on GitHub/blog; PCB+panel sets available cheap via his store and Thonk. Strong Eddy Bergman build documentation (see below).

Key designs: VCO 3340 (CEM3340/AS3340 chip-based oscillator), Precision ADSR, Wavefolder, Dual VCA, Slope.

Links: store.kassutronics.net / Thonk Kassutronics listings

Eddy Bergman (eddybergman.com)

What it is: An exceptionally well-documented step-by-step synth and module build site. Not a designer — a builder and documenter. Bergman has built dozens of DIY synths and modules (MFOS, Kassutronics, his own designs) and documented every one with photographs, wiring diagrams, BOM notes, and calibration steps. If a design is on Eddy's site, there is a high-quality build guide for it.

Link: eddybergman.com

diyelectromusic (Simon Botten)

What it is: A prolific UK builder documenting Arduino-based DIY synth and MIDI projects. Strong on Mozzi (Arduino audio library), MIDI controllers, and cheap Eurorack-format Arduino modules. PCB designs published. Builds posted January 2025 include a 6HP Eurorack Arduino Mozzi VCO module.

Links: diyelectromusic.com

HAGIWO

What it is: A Japanese maker (anonymous/pseudonymous) who publishes extremely cheap Arduino Nano-based Eurorack modules — LFO, VCO, delay, Euclidean sequencer, etc. — with free code and BOM on GitHub. The BOM is literally $6-8 in generic parts (Arduino Nano, AD9833 DDS chip, resistors). Community has adapted designs to PCBs; Modulove sells finished adaptations.

Link: github.com/ijnekenamay/HAGIWOs_Module

sdiy.info (Synth DIY wiki)

What it is: The community wiki for synth-DIY knowledge — IC datasheets, circuit theory, calibration techniques, troubleshooting, and links to every major design archive. Not a design source itself; the reference/index.

Link: sdiy.info

12. Supplemental: Piezo / Contact Mic (minimal build)

Sound role: Contact microphone / experimental. A contact mic picks up vibrations directly from surfaces — table tops, instrument bodies, water, glass, bone conduction, etc. Used heavily in experimental, noise, foley, and field recording contexts.

Origin: Global (piezo disc technology is universal; contact mic as instrument tool popularized by experimental community worldwide).

Notes on What Did Not Make the Budget

Korg NTS-1 mkII: Was ~$147 in the prior survey (May 2026). Now ~$199.99 — over budget. Noted here as a close miss; check Reverb/used market for sub-$150 copies.

Open Theremin V4.5 kit: Was ~€74 in earlier iterations. Now €189-239 as the "Deluxe Bundle." Over budget. Build from the open-source design instead (see theremin section above).

Moog Mavis: $349 — always over budget, but the best no-solder analog synth voice kit if you stretch.

PAiA Theremax: ~$200 shipped — the best all-in theremin kit (CV/gate outputs), $50 over budget. Worth the stretch for a playable theremin with control voltage outputs.

Music Thing Turing Machine MkII: £106.69 inc VAT (~$135 USD) — technically under budget but close, and GBP/USD fluctuation can tip it over. [PLAUSIBLE under $150 if bought directly from Thonk]

Mutable Instruments clones (Immutable Plaits): £125 (~$157) — close but over. The open-source Gerbers and firmware are free for self-build.

Tool Ladder (electronic-specific)

Tier 1 (required for any solder work): - Temperature-controlled iron (Hakko FX-888D, Pinecil, TS101) - Solder (63/37 or 60/40, rosin core) - Flush cutters - Digital multimeter

Tier 2 (once you build a VCO or theremin): - Chromatic tuner or frequency counter (for calibrating 1V/oct VCO or theremin oscillators) - Bench power supply (to bring up new builds safely, current-limited)

Tier 3 (from-schematic and troubleshooting): - Oscilloscope (even a cheap DSO138 or USB scope is a large upgrade over none) - Hot-air rework station (for SMD work; many Eurorack kits pre-solder SMD — read listings carefully)

The practical minimum: iron + multimeter. Adding a tuner covers the VCO. The scope is the real investment and the real capability unlock.

Bottom Line Across the Catalog

The electronic/synth DIY world covers a genuinely complete spectrum, and budget does not climb neatly with skill. The cheapest entry is piezo contact mics ($5) or circuit bending (thrift store toy + $20 tooling). The cleanest first solder kit is the Synthrotek APC Handheld ($30). The best "real synth in a box" build is the MFOS Noise Toaster (probably ~$110-150 with enclosure; verify). The best modular education path is the EDU VCO ($74). The best documentation in the entire field is North Coast Synthesis (but tariff caution for US buyers in 2026). The deepest free-schematic archive is MFOS. The cheapest per-module electronics is HAGIWO ($6-8 per module in parts, if you fab your own PCBs).

The plans tier is the center. Every kit in this catalog is a manufactured convenience layer over a free schematic. If you are comfortable ordering PCBs from JLCPCB ($5-15 for a board) and sourcing parts from Tayda Electronics or Mouser, you can build almost anything here for half the kit price or less.

Research notes: Prices verified by direct web fetch where possible (synthCube Noise Toaster page, AI Synthesis shop, North Coast SDIY kit page, Thonk listings) or via web search (Synthrotek APC, Zlob, EDU VCO, Gakken SX-150, Open Theremin, Rakit Baby8). Items tagged [UNCERTAIN] could not be confirmed from a live product page. Items tagged [PLAUSIBLE] are reasonable inference from available price data but not directly confirmed. Verify at checkout before acting on any specific price. Exchange rates (GBP/USD ~1.25, EUR/USD ~1.07) used for approximate conversions; verify current rates.

Keyboard & Mechanical

The organizing truth of this catalog: acoustic historical keyboards are almost entirely a $150 void. The harpsichord, clavichord, virginal, spinet, fortepiano, portative organ, hurdy-gurdy, and crank organ all fail the cost bar. The under-$150 reality lives in two places: DIY MIDI keyboard controllers (Arduino/Teensy builds, the only way to get a playable keyboard instrument for under $150) and punch-strip music boxes (the only cheap mechanical path). This is said once here and then backed up instrument by instrument below.

Cross-references: - Free-reed keyboard instruments (melodica, accordion, harmonium): Build Catalog - Other Winds and Free Reed.md (OOOOOOOO) - Stylophone-style builds, simple oscillator keyboards, circuit bending keyboard-shaped objects: Build Catalog - Electronic and Synth DIY.md (SSSSSSS) - Marble machine / kinetic sound automata: experimental fire (not yet written) - Full detail on historical keyboard kits and plans (clavichord, harpsichord, hurdy-gurdy tiers, crank organ): Historical and Mechanical Keyboard Kits and Plans.md (FFFFFFF)

1. Acoustic / Historical Keyboards: The $150 Wall

This section covers instruments in the order a builder would reach for them. The wall is real and it is described plainly. None of these qualify at under $150. Full kit/plan detail for all of them lives in the FFFFFFF survey.

1.1 Clavichord

Origin: Europe (Germany/Netherlands), 14th century onward. The simplest keyed string instrument: a brass tangent strikes the string directly. No jacks to voice, no quills. The most historically accessible keyboard to build.

Path state at $150: NO QUALIFYING PATH.

The clavichord is the cheapest historical keyboard to build, and it still starts at $2,329 for the smallest stage-1 kit (Zuckermann "King of Sweden," Stage 1, Stage 3 $3,665, finished $6,740). That is the floor. From plans: the Edinburgh Friends of St Cecilia's Hall sell a Hass clavichord drawing for ~£46 (~$58), and Marc Vogel GmbH sells fretted and unfretted clavichord plans at €49–109. But building from those drawings requires a spruce soundboard, tuning pins, bridge, strings, brass tangents, and a voiced case — materials alone are realistically $300–600+, before tools. A plan in the $50–100 range does not get you under $150 when the BOM is four times that.

Honest note: There is no clavichord build path under $150. Not from scratch, not from a partial kit, not from plans. The instrument that is "easiest to build" in this family still costs well over $150 to build. This is the honest floor.

See FFFFFFF for full kit/plan detail, tiers 1–3, and all current source links.

1.2 Harpsichord (all types: single, double, virginal, spinet)

Origin: Europe, 15th–18th century. Plucked-string keyboard; the core of the European early-music family.

Path state at $150: NO QUALIFYING PATH.

The cheapest kit entry for a harpsichord-family instrument is the Zuckermann Flemish Single at Stage 2 (case pre-assembled), ~$6,933. Virginals and spinets via The Paris Workshop run AUD $10,000+ through distributors. Museum plans (St Cecilia's Hall, Marc Vogel GmbH, Claviantica) are available in the $50–150 range for the paper itself, but building a harpsichord from plans requires a shaped bentside, a soundboard, bridges, wrestplank, jacks, plectra, strings, tuning pins, and full voicing capability — a BOM easily reaching $1,000–2,000 before labor. Even a cheap ottavino (the smallest spinet form) from the Renaissance Workshop Company runs ~$1,850 in third-party resale figures.

Honest note: No harpsichord-family instrument can be built for under $150. The gap between a plan purchase ($50–150) and a complete instrument ($1,000–$6,000+) is not addressable by sourcing cleverness. This is a fundamental cost of the family.

See FFFFFFF for full kit/plan tiers.

1.3 Fortepiano

Origin: Europe (Bartolomeo Cristofori, c. 1700). The historical precursor to the modern piano; hammer action, dampers, soft/loud capability.

Path state at $150: NO QUALIFYING PATH. The kit market has collapsed.

The kit path effectively does not exist in 2026: the Stein fortepiano kit that Zuckermann, Hubbard, and The Paris Workshop carried has dropped off all live catalogues. No new kit was confirmable as orderable in May/June 2026. Plans exist (Vogel GmbH: Stein 1775 €109, Walter 1795 €149, Cristofori 1726 €209), but building a fortepiano from plans is a multi-year, full-shop master build — the materials alone (Swiss pine soundboard, wire, Viennese action parts, hammer leather) run $500–1,500+, and professional fortepiano makers benchmark ~1,000 hours per instrument.

Honest note: No fortepiano build path exists under $150, or under $1,000 realistically. The kit market has collapsed. This is stated plainly and is not recoverable through sourcing.

See FFFFFFF for full detail on the historical kit path, plans sources, and finished instrument context.

1.4 Portative / Positive Organ

Origin: Medieval Europe. Small portable bellows-driven pipe organs.

Path state at $150: NO QUALIFYING PATH.

There is no portative or positive organ kit or tutorial-based build under $150, or anywhere near $150. Building even the simplest small organ requires metal or wooden pipes (cutting, voicing), a windchest, bellows or fan blower, a tracker action, and a case. The John Smith busker organ plans (for a crank-driven paper-roll pipe organ) are an adjacent tradition at £53 (~$67 USD), but building one from those plans costs £250–500+ (~$315–630+) in materials. The portative organ is an apprenticeship instrument: it is learned by working alongside an organ builder, not by buying a kit.

Honest note: No organ build path — portable or fixed — exists under $150. Not crank organ, not portative, not positive. The $150 wall is structural.

1.5 Hurdy-Gurdy

Origin: Medieval Europe; vielle à roue (France), Drehleier (Germany), zanfona (Spain/Portugal). Bowed by a rosined wheel, keys (tangents) stop the melody string.

Path state at $150: NO QUALIFYING COMMERCIAL KIT. One PLAUSIBLE from-files path exists, flagged.

The floor commercial kit is the Nerdy Gurdy (Netherlands) at €330–510 (~$360–560 USD), well above $150. However, the Nerdy Gurdy designer has released all build files (3D print files, cut files, and build documentation) free on GitHub and Thingiverse — a genuine open-source release. With all tools assumed (3D printer, laser cutter or hand tools), the build from files reduces to raw materials: hurdy-gurdy strings (~$30–50), hardware (bearings, tuning pegs, rosin, bridge: ~$25–40), and wood stock for any non-printed parts (~$10–20). A plausible from-files total is ~$65–110, inside $150.

Important caveats, both [UNCERTAIN]: 1. The Nerdy Gurdy's kit includes a pre-glued, pre-veneered wheel — the single hardest part. Building the wheel from scratch adds significant work and the wheel must be extremely true for the instrument to function. This is the real skill gate, not assembly. 2. String cost is the variable: specialty hurdy-gurdy strings from a supplier like Bow Brand or Aquila can run $40–60 for a full set. Guitar strings can substitute for some strings in a pinch, significantly lowering cost.

A from-files Nerdy Gurdy is probably under $150 in materials if you source carefully and substitute where possible. It is also probably the hardest cheap build in this entire catalog to make actually playable.

Origin of files: Nerdy Gurdy is a registered trademark; the open-source release is the designer's own choice. Free download at Thingiverse (search "Nerdy Gurdy") and GitHub.

Close-enough bar: A playable from-files Nerdy Gurdy is a real hurdy-gurdy: wheel-bowed, tangent-stopped melody string, drone strings, trompette buzzing bridge. The playing technique is identical. What the from-files path trades away relative to the kit: wheel precision (truing takes longer when done by hand), and the weeks of voicing (regulating the dog/buzzing bridge, cottoning strings) that is the real skill gate regardless of kit or files.

2. DIY MIDI Keyboard Controllers: The Real Under-$150 Path

This is where the catalog earns its keep. A MIDI keyboard controller converts key presses into MIDI data (Note On/Off, velocity) sent over USB or DIN-5 MIDI to a computer, DAW, hardware synth, or sound module. The controller itself makes no sound; it sends messages. The combination of a cheap Teensy or Arduino (with built-in or easily-added USB MIDI) plus a key matrix is the standard approach and lands well under $150 in all forms.

Origin: MIDI protocol standardized 1983, now a global standard. DIY MIDI controllers are a worldwide hobbyist tradition with deep online documentation and free firmware; the US (Teensy/PJRC, Arduino) is the dominant chip platform in English-language builds, but the project type is globally documented.

Close-enough bar: A MIDI controller is not itself an instrument — it sends data. "Playing a keyboard instrument" means pairing it with a sound source: a computer running software (free options: LMMS, Surge XT, the MIDI synth in any DAW), or a hardware synth. The DIY keyboard controller builds below produce a fully playable keyboard; the sound source is separate. This is the standard paradigm in all MIDI keyboard use, commercial products included.

What must transfer for "keyboard" function: 25+ keys laid out in chromatic order, generating MIDI Note On/Off, ideally with velocity (how hard a key is pressed). Optional: aftertouch, pitch bend, mod wheel, sustain pedal input, OLED display. All of these have been implemented in documented DIY builds.

2.1 Arduino / Teensy Button-Key MIDI Keyboard (Simplest, ~$10–35)

The bottom of the cost ladder. Uses tactile push buttons or cheap momentary switches as "keys," wired in a matrix to an Arduino Nano, Uno, or Teensy. Not piano-feel, but fully functional MIDI, easy to solder, and extremely cheap. Good for a first MIDI controller, a compact noodle pad, or a custom controller layout.

Group 1: Kits

No commercial kit specifically for this form factor has been confirmed. This build is from parts only.

2.2 Keybed + Teensy/Arduino MIDI Brain (Real Piano Feel, ~$50–100)

The step up from button switches: buy a replacement piano keybed (the actual piano-action mechanism with weighted or semi-weighted keys from a donor electronic keyboard or a surplus parts supplier) and wire it to a Teensy or Arduino as the MIDI brain. This gives real piano feel — same mechanism as in a $200 retail MIDI keyboard — for a fraction of the cost, because keybeds are salvageable from broken keyboards or purchasable surplus.

This is the path that delivers a real, gig-ready MIDI keyboard under $150.

Group 1: Kits

No commercial kit confirmed that combines keybed + MIDI brain in a buy-and-assemble format. This is a parts-and-tutorial build.

Velocity sensing note: Both salvaged and new budget keybeds have two contacts per key (two rows of diodes). Reading both contacts and measuring the time between them gives velocity — this is how every commercial keyboard does it. The firmware handles this; it is not significantly harder than a non-velocity build.

2.3 MIDI Launchpad / Grid Controller (Pads, Not Keys, ~$25–80)

A cousin, not a keyboard form: a grid of velocity-sensitive pads (4×4, 8×8) for triggering notes, clips, or samples. Not chromatic piano layout. Useful for beat production, scale-locked melody, and Ableton/DAW clip launching. Included here because it overlaps the MIDI controller build space and because many keyboard DIY guides also cover pad builds.

Close-enough bar: Pads are not piano keys — no octave layout, no white/black key distinction. What transfers: MIDI Note On/Off with velocity, sends to the same DAW/synth as a keyboard. What it trades away: linear chromatic range, piano technique compatibility. Launchpad-style is a different interface paradigm.

3. Mechanical / Music Box

This section covers the mechanical (non-electronic) path that does exist under $150: the punch-strip music box. Cylinder-and-comb music boxes have no realistic from-scratch path (confirmed in FFFFFFF); punch-strip does, and it is cheap and real.

What does not qualify under $150: - Crank organ (John Smith plans, £43/£53 USA, qualify as a plan purchase, but the materials build costs £250–500+ — BOM disqualifies) - Cylinder-and-comb music box (industrial metallurgy; no scratch-build path exists) - Barrel piano / player piano roll mechanism (well beyond $150 in materials)

3.1 Punch-Strip / Punch-Card Music Box (~$32–80)

Origin: Europe and Japan, 19th century; the punch-strip mechanism (a comb of metal tines plucked by pins on a programmable strip) was developed for portable music boxes and is now mass-produced in 15/20/30-note formats for the hobby market.

Path state: FULLY QUALIFIES AT $150. The cheapest real mechanical path in this catalog.

Close-enough bar: The punch-strip music box is the real thing: a metal comb with tuned tines, plucked by pins, producing the characteristic glassy music-box tone. The "build" here is the strip arrangement — you compose and punch a strip using the included punch tool, then crank the mechanism. The instrument is real; the skill is musical arrangement, not instrument fabrication. This is a craft/composition activity more than a lutherie build.

What it trades away vs. a cylinder movement: Fixed range (15–30 notes; no chromatic extensions); volume is small (no resonator box unless you build one); the mechanism is the whole instrument, not something you fabricate from scratch.

Build extension: You can build a custom wooden case/resonating box around any punch-strip movement, which turns this into a genuine woodworking + instrument build. A Sankyo or generic 18/20-note movement (~$12–20) + a small wooden box (~$5–15 in lumber) = a custom music box for ~$20–35 total. This is the real build path.

Bottom line: The cheapest real path: ~$32–40 for a generic 15-note kit. The best build experience: buy a 20-note movement (~$15 movement alone) and build a custom resonating wooden box around it (~$10–15 in lumber) for a total of ~$25–35. musicboxmaniacs.com is the community hub — strip software, shared arrangements, and a knowledgeable forum. This is a genuine craft project that produces a real musical instrument.

Confidence: Kikkerland at ~$40 is [ESTABLISHED] (confirmed in FFFFFFF survey); generic 15/20/30-note kits are [PLAUSIBLE] (extremely common on Amazon but specific prices fluctuate); musicboxmaniacs.com is [ESTABLISHED] (confirmed in FFFFFFF survey). Wooden case build costs are [PLAUSIBLE] based on standard lumber prices.

3.2 Sankyo / Generic 18-Note Movement + Custom Case (Build-Your-Own, ~$20–40)

Origin: Japan (Sankyo Seiki, est. 1946, dominant movement maker); also Reuge (Switzerland) and Thorens (Switzerland) at higher price points. 18-note movements are the standard "music box kit" format worldwide.

Path state: QUALIFIES. The minimum viable music box build.

This is the distillation of the punch-strip build above: buy a bare movement, build around it. An 18-note Sankyo movement is not a punch-strip device — it is a cylinder movement with fixed, pre-pinned tunes (you choose which tune when you order). You do not program it; you build around it. The result is a gift-quality music box with a specific song, in a case you made.

Note on the distinction: This is NOT the same as the punch-strip path. The Sankyo movement plays one pre-set tune (or is switchable between a small repertoire). You cannot program it with new tunes. The punch-strip kit (Section 3.1) is the one where you compose and punch your own music. Both paths qualify; they are different instruments.

The following keyboard-operated free-reed instruments are covered in Build Catalog - Other Winds and Free Reed.md (OOOOOOOO):

None of these have a sub-$150 build path except potentially via a heavily discounted donor/restoration project. See the winds/free-reed catalog for full detail.

6. Mechanical Automata and Kinetic Instruments (Cross-Reference Only)

Marble machines, rotary bell chimes, motor-driven mechanical instruments, and kinetic sound automata are not covered in this fire. They overlap primarily with the experimental / sound-art instrument family. A dedicated experimental fire will cover this when written.

The marble machine tradition (Wintergatan-style) and its DIY derivatives are widely documented on YouTube and Hackaday, but no confirmed under-$150 complete build path exists for a marble machine that functions reliably as an instrument.

Section A: Friction and Bowed-Weird

Musical Saw

Origin: Folk / vaudeville / circus tradition, US and Europe, late 19th–early 20th century. A hardware-store carpenter's saw, bent and bowed.

What it does / sounds like: Bowing the smooth back edge of a saw blade bent into an S-curve produces a pure, singing, theremin-adjacent tone with natural vibrato. The S-curve is held by the player's hand and knees; tightening the bend raises pitch, relaxing it lowers pitch. Range on a tenor saw is roughly two octaves (A-flat below middle C to F above high C). The sound slides seamlessly between notes — no frets, no discrete steps. Voice-like, haunting, eerie in a way few instruments match. The saw is trivially cheap. The technique is months of practice.

Close-enough bar (adapted): Any sufficiently flexible hand saw can produce this sound. A purpose-made singing saw has the right steel hardness and blade thickness for consistent response; a carpenter's saw works but may be less predictable. The technique transfer is 100% — you learn on what you have and the skill carries over.

Daxophone

Origin: Invented by German avant-garde guitarist and typeface designer Hans Reichel, 1980s. A friction idiophone whose sound is shaped in real time.

What it does / sounds like: A flexible hardwood "tongue" clamped over a wooden block that holds a contact microphone. You bow the tongue with a cello or bass bow; the pitch is shaped by pressing a second wooden piece (the "dax") at different points along the tongue's length. The result is uncannily voice-like and animal-like — wavering between phonemes, sliding through registers. Not a melodic instrument in the conventional sense; more a voice-simulator and texture machine. Reichel distributed his catalogue of proven tongue shapes as a typeface font file, since he was also a type designer — one of the stranger instrument-distribution methods on record.

What it does / sounds like (cheap version trades away): The ruler-daxophone (entry version) has less resonance and less control than the full hardwood instrument; the "voice" quality is present but rougher. The full instrument rewards obsessive fine-tuning of tongue wood selection and geometry.

Nail Violin (Nagelgeige)

Origin: Invented by German violinist Johann Wilde, 1740. A semicircular wooden board with graduated iron nails bowed to produce pitch. Also called Violino di ferro ("iron violin").

What it does / sounds like: Bowing the graduated nails produces thin, glassy, ethereal tones — somewhere between a glass harp and a very quiet bowed metal instrument. The chromatic scale runs across the arc of nails, largest (lowest) to smallest (highest). The sound is delicate and strange: each note sustains briefly, with a singing quality that fades to silence. Tuning is done by hammering nails in (raises pitch) or pulling out a little (lowers pitch).

What it does / sounds like (cheap version trades away): A plywood board with hardware nails works completely. The tonal quality of brass nails on a resonant wood body is better than steel nails on plywood, but the playing principle is identical.

Glass Harp

Origin: European parlor and concert tradition, 18th century. Benjamin Franklin later extended the principle into the armonica. The glass harp is the living playable version of the glass family for everyday builders.

What it does / sounds like: A wet finger rubbed around the rim of a wine glass produces a sustained, pure, singing tone. Pitch is lowered by adding water; raised by removing it. Multiple glasses in a row = a chromatic or diatonic scale. The sound is clear, ethereal, and ringing — a sustained bell with no decay. Used in classical, new-age, and experimental music; distinctive beyond its simplicity.

What it does / sounds like (cheap version trades away): Nothing. The household version is acoustically identical to a formal glass harp setup. The main upgrade is mounting the glasses to a board with silicone dots for stability, which is optional and cheap.

Cristal Baschet

Origin: Invented by Bernard and François Baschet, France, 1952. Glass rods coupled to tuned metal resonators; one of the most visually and sonically spectacular invented instruments of the 20th century.

What it does / sounds like: Glass rods stroked with a wet finger transfer vibration to tuned stainless steel bolts of graduated length; the bolts are fixed to an aluminium plate which couples them to large conical or sail-like metal resonators. The result is a sustained, singing, organ-like tone with strong overtone content — richer and more complex than the glass harp, with a slower decay and a more orchestral presence. Thomas Bloch is the instrument's most visible contemporary player. No cheap finished version exists anywhere in the market.

What it does / sounds like (cheap version trades away): A single-element build produces a few notes; it will not have the visual scale or full harmonic complexity of the concert instrument. The tone is real; the scope is reduced.

Glass Armonica (Orientation / Pro Ceiling)

Origin: Invented by Benjamin Franklin, 1761; revived in the modern era with quartz glass by Gerhard Finkenbeiner (Massachusetts). The Franklin revival is the form still in active performance use.

What it does / sounds like: Nested spinning glass bowls on a central spindle, motor-driven, played with wet fingers on the bowl rims. Because the bowls spin continuously, the sustained tone is more controlled and stable than the glass harp; the player controls pitch by touching different bowls (sized and color-coded by note) and timbre by finger pressure. Capable of full chromatic range; a serious concert instrument.

DIY path: None at reasonable cost. Glassblowing is required to create the nested bowl sets; quartz glass requires specialized facilities. The accessible DIY equivalent is the glass harp (above). This entry exists to show the full development arc of the glass friction family and to explain why there is no cheap build path.

Finished: G. Finkenbeiner Inc. (Massachusetts) — price not publicly posted [UNCERTAIN; thousands of dollars]. Glass Music International community for context and players.

Bottom line: Buy the sound with a glass harp for $0-40. The armonica proper is pro-built and out of range.

Waterphone

Origin: Invented and patented by Richard Waters, US, late 1960s–70s. The defining sound of horror and suspense film scoring for decades.

What it does / sounds like: A stainless steel resonator bowl partially filled with water, with tuned bronze/brass rods of varying lengths around the rim. Bowed rods produce eerie, sustained, wavering tones; tilting the instrument shifts pitch as water moves inside the resonator. The sound is an unmistakable sustained metallic moan or groan with glissando qualities — you know it from every horror trailer, horror game, and suspense cue since the 1970s. Played bowed (rods or rim), struck, or scraped.

What it does / sounds like (cheap version trades away): The commercial instrument is precisely tuned and has a large resonant mass. DIY versions can approximate the sound but rarely match the sustain or control of the original. The piezo/contact-mic shortcut produces a drier version of the sound.

Section B: Wind and Resonance-Weird

Aeolian Harp

Origin: Named for Aeolus, Greek god of wind; the principle is ancient. Popularized as a Romantic-era window harp in Europe (18th–19th century); still built by hobbyists worldwide.

What it does / sounds like: All strings are tuned to the same pitch, but wind excites them into different harmonics simultaneously. As wind speed varies, the chord shifts — a drone that breathes, swells, and recedes on its own. The player sets the instrument in a window or outdoors and listens; there is no performer interaction. The sound is meditative, continuously evolving, and impossible to replicate with any other instrument. Beautiful and strange in equal measure.

What it does / sounds like (cheap version trades away): Nothing essential. A pine box with nylon monofilament produces the same phenomenon as a handcrafted instrument with fine zither strings. The trade is tonal richness (fine strings have a sweeter overtone structure than fishing line) but the aeolian effect is identical.

PVC Pipe Organ / Nicolas Bras Tradition

Origin: Nicolas Bras, France, "Musiques de Nulle Part" (Music from Nowhere) project — 1,000+ instruments from PVC plumbing and scrap. The Blue Man Group is the commercial embodiment of the same idea.

What it does / sounds like: Tuned PVC pipes struck across the open ends (slap tubes) or blown across capped ends (pan-pipe style). Each pipe produces one pitch, scaled by length. Struck versions sound like a woody xylophone with a slightly plastic timbre; blown versions sound like a flute-organ hybrid. A set of five or more pipes arranged by pitch = a real playable instrument. The aesthetic is specifically industrial and found-material: hardware store as instrument shop.

What it does / sounds like (cheap version trades away): Nothing. PVC pipe organs are not a degraded version of something else; this is what it is.

Apprehension Engine

Origin: Designed by luthier Tony Duggan-Smith for film composer Mark Korven, Canada, c. 2015. An instrument built specifically and deliberately to score horror films.

What it does / sounds like: A collection of sound-producing elements mounted on pine planks: steel rulers and rods that are bowed (producing metallic shrieks, drones, and scraping resonances), an E-bowed guitar string running through a spring reverb tank (sustained metallic roar and shimmer), and optional additional elements (bowed rods, springs, etc.). Not a melodic instrument. A palette of carefully engineered dread: scraping, groaning, sustained metallic resonance, random harmonic content. Every element is oriented toward sound design rather than music in the conventional sense.

What it does / sounds like (cheap version trades away): A reduced build (no spring reverb, no E-bow) produces steel-ruler drones and scrapes without the full spectral range. The reverb tank and E-bow are what produce the most characteristic horror-score sounds; they are also the budget-sensitive components.

Singing Bowls and Friction Idiophones

Origin: Tibetan/Himalayan tradition (Nepal, Tibet, India); also standing bells in Japan (suzu, orin), Korea, and elsewhere. Multiple independent traditions.

What it does / sounds like: A metal bowl struck produces a clear, bell-like decay; rubbed continuously with a padded or wooden mallet produces a sustained, singing tone — the "singing" in the name. Calming, harmonic-rich resonance. Commonly used in meditation, sound healing, and experimental music.

Honest finding on DIY path: Traditional singing bowls are cast or hammer-forged from a bronze alloy (roughly 78% copper, 22% tin with other trace metals) and are not realistically DIY-able under $150 without foundry access. Bronze casting requires expensive equipment. A workshop-style "make your own bowl" experience (medieval hand tools + brass sheet) exists but requires significant metalsmithing skill and setup.

The accessible DIY path to this sound: Any metal bowl rubbed with a rosin-coated or wet wooden dowel produces a version of the singing effect. A steel mixing bowl from a thrift store ($1-5) + a wooden dowel ($1-3 from hardware store) + rosin (already noted in musical saw entry) = a real friction idiophone for under $10. The sound quality is rougher than a proper singing bowl but the principle is identical.

Buy path: New commercial singing bowls $20-60 (Amazon, many vendors). Hand-hammered Nepalese/Tibetan bowls $40-100. Buying is genuinely cheaper and produces better results than any realistic DIY path.

Section C: String-Weird and Invented

Tromba Marina (Trumpet Marine)

Origin: Medieval and Renaissance Europe, documented from the 15th through early 18th century. One of the stranger string instruments in the historical record: bowed, but producing natural harmonics and a buzzing bridge rattle that mimics a trumpet. Name origin debated; may relate to use on ships or to the trumpet-like tone.

What it does / sounds like: A single string — typically a cello D string — stretched over a very long (up to 6 feet) tapered triangular box. Played by bowing lightly above the touch points of the natural harmonic series (never pressing to the fingerboard). One foot of the bridge is free-floating and buzzes rhythmically against an ivory or glass plate set into the soundboard, producing a characteristic brassy rattle alongside the harmonic tone. The result sounds unmistakably trumpet-like — a bowed string instrument that sounds like a brass instrument. Eerie, droning, medieval.

What it does / sounds like (cheap version trades away): A simplified improvised body (maple beam, resonant box, styrofoam cooler) produces the same harmonic-plus-buzz effect as a formally constructed instrument. The tonal richness and projection are reduced; the playing principle and sonic character are intact.

Monochord / One-String Drone

Origin: Ancient Greece; Pythagoras used a monochord to demonstrate and measure musical intervals (~500 BCE). Persists across European, Indian, and other traditions as a tuning tool, meditation instrument, and theoretical demonstration device.

What it does / sounds like: A single string stretched over a resonant box. A moveable bridge divides the string, allowing the player to explore the harmonic series and just intervals. Played bowed (sustaining tones), plucked (short), or struck. Produces a single pure drone note and its harmonics. Meditative, resonant, simple. The monochord is where Western music theory was literally invented; playing one is a direct connection to that history.

What it does / sounds like (cheap version trades away): Nothing functional. Scrap lumber produces the same harmonic demonstrations as a fine-wood instrument. The trade is aesthetics.

Hurdy-Gurdy (Nerdy Gurdy Kit — Over Budget, Flagged)

Origin: Medieval European drone-melody instrument; crank-turned rosined wheel continuously bows the strings; a keyboard of wooden tangents frets the melody string.

What it does / sounds like: Continuous drone strings (bourdons) + melody string fretted by key-pressed tangents + optional buzzing bridge (trompette) activated by rhythmic crank speed changes. Dense, organ-like, distinctly medieval folk sound with a rich, complex timbre impossible to replicate with any conventional instrument.

Honest over-budget flag: The most accessible hurdy-gurdy kit is the Nerdy Gurdy (nerdygurdy.nl, Netherlands) — laser-cut wood, pre-made wheel, 3D-printed parts, all hardware. Cost: ~€330-510 ex-VAT + shipping + customs to US = realistically $400-600+ landed. Over budget. Listed here because it is the only realistic entry-level build kit for this instrument and the best path for anyone who wants to build one. No under-$150 path to a functional hurdy-gurdy exists; scratch builds from plans are major luthier-level projects.

Section D: Found-Object and Junk Tradition

Steel Tongue Drum / Hank Drum

Origin: Invented by Dennis Havlena, Michigan, February 2007. Inspired by the Swiss PANart Hang (invented 2001); the name is "Hang" + "tank." The original and most copied free instrument plan in this catalog.

What it does / sounds like: Tongues cut in a cross or star pattern into the top of an empty propane tank; each tongue produces a pitched bell-like tone when struck with fingers or mallets. Pentatonic or diatonic tuning is typical. Warm, sustained, meditative resonance — similar to a steelpan but with a rounder attack. The Havlena free plan launched an entire commercial instrument category; the commercial steel tongue drums sold today on Amazon and Walmart are direct descendants of his 2007 design.

What it does / sounds like (cheap version trades away): Nothing. The free DIY build is the original. The commercial versions are the industrial derivative.

Lithophone (Tuned Stone)

Origin: Ancient worldwide — the oldest known tuned instruments are lithophones. Modern DIY tradition documented by Bart Hopkin and in academic instrument-making literature. The iconic reference is the Great Stalacpipe Organ at Luray Caverns, Virginia: Leland Sprinkle spent three years (from 1954) selecting and sanding 37 stalactites across 3.5 acres of cave to produce a playable chromatic instrument — the world's largest. Not a build, but the spiritual center of the lithophone tradition.

What it does / sounds like: Stone bars suspended on cord or foam over a frame, struck with a mallet. Sounds like a xylophone with a stone character: harder, crisper attack; different and often longer decay than wood; a cool, dense resonance that varies significantly by rock type. Granite is harder and brighter; slate is more muted; limestone has a longer sustain.

What it does / sounds like (cheap version trades away): Nothing fundamental. Hardware-store slate tiles and granite floor tiles are the cheap version; they work as well as artisan-cut stone for playing. The trade is precision: commercial tiles are not of uniform thickness, so tuning each bar requires more grinding work.

Contact Mic / Piezo Enabling Technology

Origin: Piezoelectric effect discovered by Pierre and Jacques Curie, 1880. Applied extensively to DIY instrument-making since the 1980s, especially in Bart Hopkin's writing and the experimental-music community.

What it does: A piezo disc is a thin ceramic element that generates a voltage when mechanically deformed. Glued or taped to any vibrating solid surface, it picks up that surface's resonance and outputs an audio signal. This converts any found object into a playable instrument: a spring, a wooden board, a metal bowl, a tin can, a rock, a chain, a saw blade. The "instrument" is whatever you attach it to. This is the enabling technology for the daxophone, the waterphone, the Apprehension Engine, and most of the found-object tradition.

Cross-ref: The electronic/synth worker (SSSSSSS) covers the full piezo ecosystem including preamps, buffers, JFET circuits, and signal chain. This entry covers only the acoustic-weird application.

Beer Bottle and Kitchen-Percussion Tradition

Origin: Worldwide folk tradition; formalized in American jug-band music (early 20th century) and in experimental and sound-art music globally.

What it does / sounds like: Glass bottles blown across the open mouth produce a flute-like tone tuned precisely by water level. Struck with a mallet they produce a bell-like ring. A "bottle organ" or "bottle xylophone" is a ranked set of bottles tuned by water level and played like a keyboard percussion instrument. Kitchen objects — pots, pans, metal bowls, cans — produce their own pitched percussion. The collective sound is percussive-melodic; surprisingly musical when properly tuned.

What it does / sounds like (cheap version trades away): Nothing. This IS the cheap version.

Whirly / Corrugaphone / Bloogle Resonator

Origin: Exact origin unknown; popularized in experimental music and children's-science contexts; the instrument name is literally in the title of Bart Hopkin's most famous book (Gravikords, Whirlies & Pyrophones).

What it does / sounds like: A corrugated (ribbed) flexible plastic tube whirled overhead in a circle. The passing air excites the internal corrugations, producing resonant harmonics above the tube's fundamental frequency. As you spin faster, pitch rises through the harmonic series. Each step in speed produces a different harmonic: the effect is a breathy, flute-like instrument that plays natural harmonics by spinning speed alone. Strange, playful, genuinely musical.

Bullroarer

Origin: Among the oldest instruments documented on earth; found in Australian Aboriginal, Ancient Greek, Indigenous American, African, and many other traditions. Used for ritual, communication, and ceremony across thousands of years of documented use.

What it does / sounds like: A flat wooden slat on a cord swung overhead in a circle. The slat oscillates in the air stream, producing a deep, roaring, pulsating drone that varies in pitch and intensity with spin speed. More sound effect than pitched instrument; the sound carries remarkable distances (used for long-distance communication in Aboriginal tradition). The tone is primordial and immediately recognizable.

Kazoo / Mirliton

Origin: The kazoo was patented in the US in 1852; the mirliton (comb-and-paper) is older and found worldwide. Both are membranophones: they modify the player's voice rather than generating tone independently.

What it does / sounds like: Humming into the kazoo causes a thin membrane to vibrate sympathetically, adding a buzzy, nasal, singing timbre to the player's voice. It is not a separate sound source; it is a voice modifier. The "instrument" is the player's own voice with the membrane's character added. Surprisingly expressive in the right hands.

Section E: Kinetic and Mechanical

Marble Machine X (Aspirational Ceiling)

Origin: Designed by Martin Molin / Wintergatan, Sweden. The original Marble Machine video went viral in 2016; the improved Marble Machine X (MMX) has been in public development for years and became a multi-year public engineering saga.

What it does / sounds like: A self-playing music machine where programmable quantities of falling marbles strike vibraphone bars, bass strings, and a kick drum in sequence. The sound is a vibraphone-plus-rhythm machine with a mechanical, clockwork quality. The spectacle is the machine itself: thousands of marbles cycling through precision tracks and triggering instruments on cue.

Honest assessment: The CAD files are genuinely free. The virtual MMX programmer is on GitHub. These resources are real and open-source. The physical build is not a realistic under-$150 project or even a realistic under-$1,500 project. A full physical build requires CNC machining, 3D printing, precision metalwork, calibration tools, and potentially years of work — the original creator spent years on it and documented the engineering challenges publicly. This entry exists as the aspirational ceiling of the kinetic family and because the open-source CAD is worth knowing about.

Kikkerland Punch-Strip Music Box

Origin: Hand-crank music box tradition; the "compose-your-own" punch-strip variant has been produced by various makers since the early 20th century; Kikkerland's version is the current accessible standard.

What it does / sounds like: A 15-note hand-cranked metal comb mechanism. You punch holes in provided paper strips in any pattern; cranking the strip through the mechanism plays whatever melody you punched. Produces a tinkling, mechanical music-box tone. One reported quirk: tuned around A-flat rather than C, which affects playback of familiar tunes. Thoroughly charming; genuinely compose-your-own.

Cheapest builds (under $30 in new materials): - Glass harp — ~$0 with existing glasses - Bullroarer — ~$0-5 - Whirly/corrugaphone — ~$0-10 - Kazoo — ~$0 - Nail violin — ~$20-45 with scrap + existing bow - Hank drum — ~$0-27 - Aeolian harp — ~$20-40 - Monochord (Artec kit) — ~$12; scratch ~$10-45 - Beer bottle organ — ~$0-20 - Contact mic / piezo — ~$3-8 each - Musical saw (hardware store) — ~$25-60

Highest build complexity (technique or skill is the gating factor, not cost): - Musical saw — the sound is technically difficult regardless of saw cost - Daxophone — precise hardwood work; contact mic soldering - Cristal Baschet — glass-rod technique; metal tuning - Waterphone — brazing/soldering metal; low first-time success rate - Tromba marina — bow technique specific to harmonics; bridge fitting

Plans-only, no kit exists (expected in this family): - Aeolian harp, Apprehension Engine, daxophone, tromba marina, Cristal Baschet, nail violin, aeolian harp, PVC organ, hank drum, lithophone, bullroarer, whirly

Buy rather than build (honest findings): - Singing bowls — buy is cheaper and better than any realistic DIY alternative - Glass armonica — no DIY path; glass harp is the equivalent - Hurdy-gurdy — no under-$150 path; Nerdy Gurdy kit is $400-600+ US landed - Marble Machine X — CAD is free; physical build is a multi-year engineering project

The plans literature is load-bearing: Bart Hopkin's EMI journal (free, archive.org) and Dennis Havlena's website (free, dennishavlena.com) collectively cover more of this family than any other source. Read them before building anything.

Lever Harp

Orientation

This fire is the second tier of the harp series: the price band where the first real harp kits appear. The under-$150 tier (Build Catalog - Lyre and Harp.md) ended with two Kovac kits just below $150 (PVC Piper $144.60; HMS kit from $144.72) and the Sligo/Musicmakers free-plan + hardware routes that can barely land under $150 with aggressive wood sourcing. This band ($150-300) is where those paths comfortably land, and where the dedicated cardboard-frame folk harp kits (Waring, Backyard Music) live as proven one-stop assemblies.

What this band does NOT contain: a complete all-wood Celtic/lever harp kit. The Musicmakers Ballad Harp Kit (22-string wood kit) is $1,499. The buildaharp.com 26-string Celtic is ~£350 (~$440). All-wood lever harp kits start well above $300. This band gives you: cardboard-frame folk harps (Waring, Backyard Music), wood-hardware-and-strings kits where you supply lumber (Kovac Pine $173, Harpune $230), and the plans+hardware routes for wood harps where total all-in with lumber lands in band.

Musicmakers (harpkit.com, Stillwater MN) vs. Stoney End (Red Wing MN): Different companies. Musicmakers = harpkit.com, kit and plans maker. Stoney End = finished harp maker; kit status unconfirmed. Kept separate throughout. [ESTABLISHED]

The levers callout: Carried forward from the under-$150 file. No kit in this band includes levers. Per-lever costs: Loveland ~$17-18, Truitt ~$26 installed, Camac ~$34. Fully levering a 22-string harp adds ~$370-$770+ on top of any kit cost. Every harp in this band is lever-less or lever-ready (frame has mounting holes) with levers a separate, later project. PART ONE: HARP KITS (COMPLETE, BUY-AND-BUILD)

These kits ship complete: all frame parts, soundbox, strings, tuning hardware, and instructions included. No external wood sourcing required. You supply glue and a screwdriver.

1. Waring Harp Kit Family (Dennis Waring, ethnomusicologist)

Origin: Modern; designed by Dr. Dennis Waring (ethnomusicologist, educator, instrument maker). Based in Connecticut, ships internationally. The instrument design draws on Celtic/folk harp tradition; the soundbox material (corrugated cardboard) is Waring's signature innovation. All four models use the same construction logic: three-piece hardwood frame + die-cut corrugated soundbox.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: full basic Celtic/folk harp technique; standard zither pin tuning; nylon strings at standard spacing; G3 or C4 as lowest string. What the build trades away: the tonal warmth of a solid-wood resonator (cardboard resonates differently; endorsed players consistently describe the sound as better than expected but distinct from all-wood instruments). Levers not included in any model; frame is not confirmed lever-ready on these kits (unlike Backyard Music).

Note on assembly: The Waring kits are glue-and-screwdriver projects, not woodworking. Hardwood components (string rib, pillar, neck) arrive pre-shaped; the soundbox is die-cut and folds up. Assembly time: a few hours. Finishing time: optional (paint it yourself). Not a woodworking build.

Note on string count: Both single harps (Standard and Mini) have 19 strings. The double-strung harps have 19 strings per row = 38 strings total. No wire-strung option; all nylon.

The Mini at $185 is the floor of the band and the most portable (airline-carry-on size). The double-strung models at $245-295 are a specific technique choice (no crossed hands, echo effects), not just more strings; they require learning a different performance approach. Waring harps carry genuine endorsements from professionals including the president of Camac Harps France, harp therapists, and the editor of The Folk Harp Journal; the cardboard soundbox is consistently described as better than expected. 19-string range (2+ octaves) is narrower than the Backyard Music 22-string (3 octaves); factor that into repertoire decisions.

2. Backyard Music Fireside Folk Harp Kit Family (Willimantic, CT)

Origin: Modern; designed by Backyard Music (Connecticut). Corrugated cardboard soundbox + maple frame. 22 strings, 3 full octaves, G below middle C to G above treble staff. Standard 9/16" string spacing. Frame is lever-ready: has mounting holes for optional sharping levers (purchased separately at $15 each). Multiple kit variants from paint-your-own to pre-finished; also sells assembled.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: full 3-octave folk harp technique; standard colored strings (red Cs, blue Fs); standard 9/16" harp string spacing; lever-ready if you want to add key-changing capability later. What the build trades away: same cardboard-vs-wood resonance tradeoff as Waring. 22-string range is wider than Waring's 19.

Note on levers: Backyard Music sells its own levers at $15 each. A full 22-string levering = $330 in levers. Per Harp Column forum reports, the Backyard Music levers are functional but not the same quality as Loveland or Truitt. [PLAUSIBLE on lever quality assessment]

Note on variants: These four products build the same harp at different stages of completion. The Basic Kit ($189) is the traditional "you do everything" version. The Prepainted ($199) skips the cardboard painting step. The No-Mess ($225) arrives "ready for final assembly and stringing" with pre-finished soundbox. The assembled ($289) is a finished instrument, not a build.

3. Kovac Pine Harp Kit (John Kovac Harps, Georgetown KY)

Origin: Designed by John Kovac (US maker, Paraguayan harp tradition). The Pine Harp is the entry-level kit in Kovac's lineup: hardware, strings, plans, and DVD included; you supply pine lumber from a hardware store. Paraguayan-inspired: lightweight, compact, 26-string, no levers (Paraguayan harps traditionally change key by retuning). Kovac notes this kit "is more suited as a child's exploratory instrument" -- the main tradeoff vs. the Harpune is the absence of a proper soundbox and lighter string tension.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: Paraguayan-style folk harp technique, 26-string diatonic layout (C3-G6 range), 3.5 octaves, lighter string tension. What the build trades away: the resonance of a sound box (this design has no box unless you add one yourself -- Kovac notes you can add a box to the back, and the harp sounds significantly better if you do). Pine as a structural material is less resonant than hardwood tonewoods; Kovac recommends adding a soundbox if upgrading later. Not lever-ready as designed.

Note on wood: Pine = widely available, inexpensive ($20-40 at hardware store for the required lumber). No specialty lumber needed. Key warning from Kovac: choose pine with no holes or knots that might fall out later and weaken the structure. Alternatively, upgrade to better tonewoods (Kovac confirms this is possible).

4. Kovac Harpune Kit (John Kovac Harps, Georgetown KY)

Origin: Also designed by John Kovac; the Harpune is his flagship beginner/intermediate Paraguayan-style folk harp. Harpune = portmanteau of "harp" + "lacune" (gap, absence) -- a compact design with an open back but no traditional soundbox legs. The hardware is higher-quality than the Pine: chrome tuning machines with white knobs vs. the Pine's same machines. Includes a DVD. Kovac also describes optional "taquitos" (small dowels set behind strings to achieve semitones, a traditional Paraguayan technique) as an alternative to expensive sharping levers.

Close-enough bar: What transfers: full Paraguayan-style folk harp technique (diatonic, lever-less, 3.5 octaves, C to G); standard plucked-harp finger technique. What the build trades away: a traditional Paraguayan soundbox/resonator (the Harpune has an open back, not a full resonating box). The taquito semitone system achieves chromatic notes without levers, but taquitos must be physically moved to change key.

Note on wood: Same as Pine Kit -- you supply lumber. The Harpune is designed for "higher quality" wood than pine (Kovac notes recognized tonewoods produce better sound), though pine works. Materials from a hardware store: $20-40. True all-in: ~$250-270.

Note on taquitos: Traditional Paraguayan sharping technique using small dowels. Kovac includes a simple plan for these. Install a few weeks after the harp has settled in at pitch. Free to build from scrap dowel. This is the traditional non-lever path to chromatic notes on a Paraguayan harp.

PART TWO: PLANS + HARDWARE ROUTES

These paths require you to source wood locally and combine Musicmakers or Sligo hardware components; total all-in typically lands in the $155-270 range depending on model and wood sourcing.

5. Musicmakers Harp Plans Series (harpkit.com, Stillwater MN)

Origin: Musicmakers Instruments (Stillwater MN); the same company as the Ballad Harp Kit ($1,499) and Jolie Harp Kit ($1,725), but at the plans level you buy only the PDF + specialty hardware + strings, then source and cut all wood locally. Three models land in or near the $150-300 band for total all-in cost: Shepherd (22-string), Limerick (26-string), Studio (29-string floor harp).

About the plans: All plans are full-size PDF downloads; print at FedEx/Kinkos/Staples at large format. Musicmakers explicitly states they have successfully built all instruments themselves and the plans are known for quality and clarity. The same assembly instructions are included with the pre-cut kits sold at $1,499+.

Note on soundboards: Musicmakers sells a Small Soundboard Blank (19"x36") at $69 as a prepared tonewood soundboard. If you source local hardwood plywood (1/8" at Home Depot, ~$15-25 for a 4x8 sheet), you can cut your own soundboard and save the $69. Sound quality difference is real but the plywood approach is functional for a first build.

Note on the sale price: All plans are currently $14.50 (sale from $29.00). This has been observed active as of June 2026 but is a sale; verify before ordering.

PART THREE: HISTORICAL LYRES IN BAND

The brief calls out Michael J. King's Anglo-Saxon round lyres and Etsy makers in the $200-400 band. These are documented here; the lyre build kit market is thin at this price point (as of June 2026, the King kit Etsy listings are unavailable).

7. Michael J. King Lyre Plans + Kit Status

Origin: Michael J. King (UK luthier, making instruments full-time since 2002). Plans sold via payhip.com/lyreshop; finished instruments and kits historically sold through Etsy (shop: Thelyreshop). The broadest English-language lyre plans library in existence, covering 13+ plucked lyre types plus bowed lyres.

Kit status as of June 2026: [UNCERTAIN] Both known King kit Etsy listings (listing 544968660 "Anglo-Saxon Lyre Kit" and listing 507953876 "Anglo Saxon Lyre Michael J King Maple") are currently unavailable/sold out. King's 2017 blog post confirmed kits were available to order with 5-6 week lead times; as of June 2026, the kit listings are not live. King continues to sell plans (confirmed active via Payhip) and finished instruments at $600+. Kit availability should be verified directly at etsy.com/shop/Thelyreshop or via direct contact.

Known kit contents (from prior listing, as documented): Pre-routed/drilled maple body, quartersawn maple top (pre-routed and shaped), tailpiece, string set, pre-made bridge, USB with lyre DVD instructions, metal zither pins and key. Optional upgrade to wooden pegs in Sutton Hoo style.

Plans (confirmed active): Individual plans for specific Anglo-Saxon types (Sutton Hoo, Bergh Apton, Snape, Morning Thorpe, Prittlewell, Trossingen, Kravik, Oberflacht, others). Plans are £10-20 each (~$12-25). Plans + wood + hardware puts a scratch build at ~$60-100, firmly in-band. See Build Catalog - Lyre and Harp.md for the full plans-and-scratch-build documentation.

The plans+hardware routes are the workaround. - Non-Western harp build kits: None found in this band. Kovac kits (Paraguayan tradition) are the only non-North-American/European harp build tradition represented. African kundi/ngombi, Persian chang, Burmese saung-gauk: no English-language build kits in US market. [UNKNOWN for kit paths; [ESTABLISHED] that no kits were found]

Price shift to flag: - Roosebeck/Mid-East lyre-harps: the under-$150 file cited $90-220 based on earlier research; current pricing observed at $259-299 at the primary US dealer (Handcrafted World Instruments, fetched June 2026). This may reflect: (a) price increases, (b) the HWI listing including gig bags and extra string sets, or (c) both. The 8-string and 16-string models are sold out at HWI. Plain Amazon/eBay listings may still be at lower prices; not confirmed.

MATERIAL SOURCING NOTES

For cardboard-frame kit builds (Waring, Backyard Music): No additional materials needed beyond the kit. Only tools: Elmer's/PVA glue, screwdriver, optional paintbrush (for Backyard Music Basic kit).

For Kovac wood kit builds (Pine, Harpune): Pine 1x6 or 1x8 boards from Home Depot/Lowe's, $20-40 total. Kovac explicitly states it is easy to obtain. Key: select boards with no holes or knots. Optional soundbox: any flat plywood, scrap material.

For Musicmakers and Sligo plans builds: - Harp tuning pins: included in Musicmakers hardware packs. Alternately from elderly.com (~$0.55-0.75 each), Folkcraft, or Kovac (johnkovac.com). - Bridge pins and eyelets: included in Musicmakers hardware packs. - Nylon harp strings: Musicmakers model-specific sets ($39-145 depending on model); Kovac (included in kit); generic 22-34 string nylon sets on Amazon (~$50-60, quality varies). - Wire strings: Musicmakers model-specific sets ($50 for Limerick); provide a Celtic wire-strung character. - Soundboard: Musicmakers Small Soundboard Blank ($69) or 1/8" hardwood plywood sheet from Home Depot (~$15-25 for 4x8 sheet, cut to size). - Body wood: Local hardwood dealer or Woodcraft for walnut/cherry/maple; Home Depot dimensional lumber for economical builds. Kovac's Harpune instructions guide you to local big-box lumber.

For lyre scratch builds: See Build Catalog - Lyre and Harp.md for full sourcing notes (zither pins, strings, hardwood sources for lyre bodies).

ANTI-DEFAULT CHECK

Harp builds in this band by tradition/origin:

Non-Western: - Paraguayan folk harp (Latin America): John Kovac Pine Kit ($173), Harpune Kit ($230) -- both Paraguayan-inspired. [2 full entries] - Kovac's Paraguayan tradition carries taquito sharping technique (traditional South American, not European lever system)

Western / North American manufacture: - Celtic/folk harp (European tradition): Waring (Mini, Standard, Double Strung Mini, Double Strung), Backyard Music Fireside, Musicmakers Shepherd/Limerick/Studio, Sligo Waldorf -- [9+ entries]

Anti-default verdict: The harp BUILD KIT market in the $150-300 band is overwhelmingly US-manufactured and Celtic-tradition in design. This reflects the actual market, not a research default. The only non-Western harp tradition with kit infrastructure in US reach is the Paraguayan tradition (Kovac). Other non-Western harp forms -- African (kundi, ngombi), Persian (chang), Burmese (saung-gauk), Korean (gonghu) -- have no build kit or US-available plans infrastructure in this band. This is a genuine market gap, confirmed after explicit search. The Kovac Paraguayan kits are the anti-default anchor for this fire; without them, the band would be 100% Celtic.

Lyre entries in band: - Anglo-Saxon/Germanic (Western): Michael J. King plans + kit (uncertain) - A finished Anglo-Saxon lyre at $210 from an Etsy maker

REPORT-BACK

Mandolin

Context: why this band matters

The under-$150 survey found an honest ceiling: the traditional A-style acoustic mandolin kit that everyone points to (Saga AM-10) sits at $249.95. The $150-300 band is therefore where the actual mandolin kit market lives. It contains:

  • The Saga AM-10 / IVC MK0 OEM kit (A-style, pre-carved top), the dominant US kit reference
  • The Pango PMB-900S F-style DIY kit, the only in-stock F-style build kit at this budget
  • B-stock all-solid F-style single units from Washburn via Guitar Kit Shop
  • A realistic plans-and-materials path for both A-style and F-style scratch builds

Origin tag

Italy, late 17th century, Neapolitan bowl-back style; A-style (oval hole) and F-style (scroll, f-holes) American descendants dominant in bluegrass and old-time. Tuned GDAE, 8 strings in 4 paired courses, plectrum-played.

Close-enough bar

The canonical mandolin has an arched carved top and back; that arch is the structural and sonic signature. A flat-top or box-body build transfers the fingering and plectrum technique fully but trades away the carved-top resonance. At $150-300, the primary question is whether you are buying a pre-carved body kit (A-style) or an unfinished F-style body (scroll already cut but no carving done for you on that body shape). Label builds plainly.

What the AM-10 is: The top and back arrive pre-carved but left thicker than finished spec so you can do final graduation work. The rosewood fingerboard is pre-fretted. The peghead is left oversized so you shape your own profile. This is a genuine luthier kit that requires neck fitting, final graduation, finishing, and setup -- not a snap-together model. Assembly time: 40-100+ hours depending on how much refinement work you do. Mandolin Cafe build threads confirm it produces a functional instrument; tone is "kit-level" until you put real finishing work into the graduations.

F-style is the prize in this band. The scroll body is the definitive bluegrass mandolin silhouette (Gibson F5 lineage). No F-style kit exists under $150 for a retail buyer. This band has one reliably in-stock option.

Group 2: Plans + Written Tutorials

At $150-300 total project cost (plan + materials), a from-scratch A-style mandolin is a realistic undertaking. An F-style from scratch is achievable in the lower-quality wood tier but demands more skill and sits tighter in the band.

A-Style from Scratch: BOM Analysis

Economy A-style BOM (plain maple, budget hardware):

Component Low High
Spruce top blank $15 $30
Maple back $15 $35
Maple sides $10 $22

Binding, finish, glue, misc $15 $28
Total materials $109 $232

Add a $20-35 plan set: total project cost $130-267. The lower range easily fits the band; the upper range is tight but achievable. Landing under $200 requires discipline: cheapest credible tonewoods, economy tuners, wipe-on finish. Landing under $250 is comfortable with mid-grade sourcing. [PLAUSIBLE -- ranges confirmed by cross-checking supplier prices; not a verified build, just cost modeling]

F-Style from Scratch: BOM Analysis

The F-style body adds complexity (scroll, f-holes) but the primary cost driver vs. A-style is whether you use plain or figured/flamed maple. Plain maple F-style can stay within the A-style cost range. Curly/flamed maple adds $20-60 to the back.

Variable Economy (plain maple) Mid-grade (mild figure) Premium (flamed maple)
Wood cost delta vs. A-style ~$0-10 ~$15-35 ~$40-80
Total materials $115-250 $130-270 $160-310
+ Plan $30-35 $30-35 $30-35
Total project $145-285 $160-305 $190-345

Economy F-style clearly fits the band. Mid-grade is tight at the ceiling. Premium flamed maple likely exceeds $300. The F-style from scratch can land in the band with plain or mildly figured maple and economy hardware. [PLAUSIBLE at economy tier; UNCERTAIN at mid/premium tier]

Mandolin Bottom Line ($150-300 band)

The definitive A-style kit: Saga AM-10 at ~$210 (Amazon) to $250 (Saga direct). Pre-carved top, all hardware, step-by-step manual. The only widely available traditional A-style acoustic mandolin kit in the US at any price. Has 48 Amazon reviews averaging 3.7/5 (common for a kit that requires real luthiery skill to finish well).

The only in-stock F-style kit: Pango PMB-900S at $225 from Guitar Kit Shop. Ships from China. Solid spruce top; back/sides material uncertain (likely laminate). F-style scroll body with f-holes; unfinished. No US community build threads found as of this research. [PLAUSIBLE as a kit; UNCERTAIN on build outcome]

Best all-solid F-style in band (if you can get it): Washburn B-Stock units (PWB-597/598/599) at $299 -- all solid wood, but single-unit B-stock with unreliable ongoing supply. These are project mandolins from returned Washburn instruments, not production kits.

Scratch build: A-style from plans + economy tonewoods: $150-260 total. Achievable in this band. F-style from plans + plain maple: $145-290 total. Also achievable. Use Siminoff's F5 drawings ($29.95) + construction manual (~$50) for the most supported path. The plans-and-scratch route has more community documentation (Mandolin Cafe, Siminoff resources) than any kit.

Key trade: The AM-10 gives you a pre-carved top -- the single hardest operation in mandolin lutherie -- for ~$210. That's the primary value proposition of this band. If you want an F-style body, the Pango PMB-900S is the current gateway; no traditional US-stocked F-style kit exists under $300.

Anti-Default Pass

Non-Western mandolin kit market at $150-300: No kits for the liuqin (Chinese plucked chordophone), bouzouki, charango, saz, or related traditions were found in this US price band. The only non-Western manufacturer actively supplying this market is Pango Music (China), which is the dominant F-style kit source in this band -- so the non-Western sourcing point cuts in an interesting direction: the Chinese manufacturer IS the kit supply here, not an underrepresented category. The Western kit supply (Saga) is itself sourced from the same Chinese OEM ecosystem. This market is structurally dependent on Chinese manufacturing at this price point. [ESTABLISHED]
