Banjo

Solo fire, $150-300 band. Researched fresh 2026-06-05. Companion to Build Catalog - Mandolin and Banjo.md (under-$150 coverage). Supersedes that file's banjo section for the $150-300 tier. Prices captured 2026-06-05; treat as ranges and verify on the day. All sources US-reachable unless noted.

BANJO ($150-300 BAND)

Origin tag: American, with direct West African roots. The banjo descends from gourd-body, skin-head lutes brought to the Americas by enslaved West Africans: the Jola akonting (Senegal/Gambia/Guinea-Bissau), the Mande ngoni, the Wolof xalam, and related instruments. Early American forms were gourd-body tackhead instruments. The 19th-century minstrel banjo (fretless, 5-string, 12" rim, tacked goatskin) is the direct predecessor of the modern open-back. The resonator bluegrass banjo is a 20th-century development. All of this is covered in depth in Build Catalog - Mandolin and Banjo.md; that file handles the under-$150 market, including the gourd-banjo and akonting builds.

Close-enough bar: A conventional modern 5-string banjo has a short 5th-string drone anchored partway up the neck, a floating bridge on a tensioned membrane head (Remo or equivalent synthetic, or skin), played with finger picks (three-finger bluegrass) or bare fingers (clawhammer/frailing/old-time). The 4-string (tenor, plectrum, Irish tenor) uses a plectrum and different tuning (CGDA tenor, GDAE Irish, DGBE Chicago). The minstrel banjo is fretless, tackhead (skin tacked directly to rim, no hooks), and played stroke-style or clawhammer -- it is the ancestor form, not a simplified substitute. A box-top instrument is not in this catalog tier; that was covered in the under-$150 file.

Honest-Ceiling Statement

The $150-300 banjo kit market is thin and has contracted significantly since 2020. The dominant brands that defined this price band have either exited or discontinued their kits:

  • Saga RK-2/OK-2: Gone from Saga's kit catalog (sagamusic.com shows no banjo kits as of June 2026). Resale on eBay/Reverb at variable prices, treat as unreliable supply. [ESTABLISHED: they existed; ESTABLISHED: they are gone from Saga]
  • Gold Tone MC-KIT(RES) and MC-KIT(O): Discontinued at Gold Tone, list price was ~$739 -- over band and no longer available new.
  • Musicmakers Tenor Banjo Kit: Discontinued 2024 at $449 -- over band and gone.
  • Backyard Music (kits under $150): Production paused, OOS as of June 2026 -- covered in sub-$150 file.

After a complete search of the current US market, there are two active small-to-independent-maker kit lines and one large Canadian kit vendor with in-stock product in this band. The Solo BNJK-50 is the only conventional round-pot 5-string resonator kit confirmed in stock. Carver Banjos fills the historical/minstrel lane with a US-made tackhead kit. Below those, the parts route and scratch-build paths round out the tier.

Note on Carver Banjos: This is a small US-based maker specifically focused on historical banjo construction. The Modern Minstrel at $199 is the cheapest complete, playable-on-delivery kit in this band. What it IS: a 19th-century-style minstrel instrument -- fretless, tackhead (no tension hooks), played clawhammer/frailing/stroke-style, very different sound and playing feel from a modern 5-string. What it is NOT: a substitute for a conventional 5-string banjo. Label it clearly. If you want a modern fretted round-pot 5-string, this is not that; it is the ancestor form. Note on Solo BNJK-50 (confirmed from direct product page, June 2026): The BNJK-50 is the most documented in-stock conventional banjo kit in this band. Specs confirmed: sapele body + resonator, poplar laminate fretboard (not rosewood), 22 frets pre-installed, 26.25" scale, 2-way truss rod. Reviews (6 total, 4.5/5) consistently mention two fit issues: (1) neck-to-pot angle may require a shim, and (2) one high fret may choke out across all strings -- both standard DIY kit adjustments. Post-adjustment reports describe good tone and playability. Solo covers US tariffs as of June 2026 (stated explicitly on product page). Assembly guide PDF available from their site at no charge. Solo also has a YouTube channel with builds and demos. The BNJK-50 is the one solid current conventional kit in this band. Say so plainly.

Note on Solo BNJK-40 (4-string) and BNJK-60 (6-string): The BNJK-40 is a tenor banjo -- 4 strings, suited for CGDA (standard tenor), GDAE (Irish tenor), or DGBE (Chicago). It is the instrument of jazz banjo, Dixieland, and Irish folk. Not a substitute for 5-string clawhammer or bluegrass. The BNJK-60 is a banjo-guitar: 6 strings, EADGBE tuning, played like a guitar but with the banjo's membrane-head tone. All three Solo models share the same sapele/chrome/resonator construction and the same price tier ($220-240).

Note on Saga RK-2/OK-2: The brief identified these as "surviving as dealer/resale $150-360, note availability." After checking Saga's website (sagamusic.com, their instrument kits page returns no banjo results) and searching resale markets: the RK-2 and OK-2 were once the standard budget kit recommendation across every banjo forum. They are now resale-only. Reverb and eBay show scattered individual listings, prices variable. Before acting on any resale listing: verify the kit is complete (all hardware, bracket hooks, tension hoop), check the rim for warping (common in stored kits), and inspect the head. Resale of old kits is not the same as buying a current production item. [ESTABLISHED: discontinued; PLAUSIBLE: occasional listings exist in the band on secondary markets]

Budget Parts Route (Possible In-Band, No Tone Ring)

A conventional pot assembly + neck + hardware parts build CAN land in the $150-300 band, but only by using the cheapest components available, which means no tone ring. The tone ring is a large portion of what makes a conventional banjo sound like a banjo -- removing it produces a noticeably thinner, flatter sound. This path is documented here for completeness, not as a recommendation over the BNJK-50 kit.

Estimated total BOM: ~$200-295. Achievable in-band with careful sourcing, but no tone ring, no assembled neck (you are building it from a blank), and the hardware quality will be entry-level across the board. The Solo BNJK-50 at $239.99 beats this for most builders: it includes a pre-shaped sapele neck with frets installed, resonator, all hardware matched, and a finished-design pot. The parts route makes sense only if you want specific custom dimensions or materials, or if you already own some components. Market Structure Note

The $150-300 banjo kit market has a clear structural story as of June 2026:

What existed (2010-2023): Saga RK-2/OK-2 at ~$150-180 were the standard entry. Gold Tone MC-KIT at ~$700 was the premium DIY. Musicmakers had a tenor kit at $449. Backyard Music had sub-$150 open-back kits. This was a four-vendor market with options at multiple price points.

What exists now: One large vendor (Solo Music Gear) with three in-stock sapele kits ($220-240). One small US specialty maker (Carver Banjos) with historical-style kits starting at $199. Saga is out. Gold Tone kits are out. Musicmakers is out. Backyard Music is paused OOS.

What this means for a builder: The Solo BNJK-50 is effectively the one modern-style 5-string kit in stock in the US at this price point. If you want a conventional resonator 5-string with a fretted neck, that is your option. If you want to go historical, Carver's Modern Minstrel at $199 is better-made and more interesting than anything else in the band. If you want to scratch-build, the plans route is rich (Folkcraft, Witulski, StewMac instructions) with BOM landing in-band for conventional open-back without a tone ring.

Bottom Line

Cheapest in-band kit (conventional): Solo BNJK-40 4-string at $219.99. In-stock, fretted, resonator, conventional hardware. If you want 5-string, BNJK-50 at $239.99.

Cheapest in-band kit (historical / minstrel): Carver Banjos Modern Minstrel at $199. In-stock, fretless, tackhead goatskin, 10" rim, 19th-century ancestor form. A genuinely different instrument, not a simplified 5-string.

Best value for a modern-style 5-string: Solo BNJK-50 at $239.99. The only confirmed conventional resonator 5-string kit in stock. Pre-fretted, 2-way truss rod, resonator, all hardware. Requires a neck shim at setup (common DIY adjustment; every review mentions it, no one thinks it's a dealbreaker).

Parts route: Possible in-band (~$200-295) but produces a tone-ring-free instrument and more build complexity than the Solo kit. Makes sense if you want custom dimensions or wood, or already own some parts. Free StewMac build instructions cover the process completely.

Plans + scratch: Folkcraft $20 plans + economy hardware = BOM ~$110-180 in-band. Witulski's free series is the best free scratch-build guide. A conventional open-back without a tone ring is the achievable in-band target; adding a tone ring pushes the BOM above $300.

Key trade: Below $300 you can build a fretted 5-string kit (Solo BNJK-50, full conventional design, needs a shim and some fret dressing) or a more historically interesting fretless minstrel tackhead (Carver, completely different instrument). No middle option currently exists -- the Saga kits and Gold Tone kits that once occupied that middle lane are gone.

5-string conventional kit market status (honest ceiling): As of June 2026, Solo BNJK-50 appears to be the only round-pot fretted 5-string kit in stock at any price below $400 from a US-reachable source. This is not a temporary gap -- the Saga line is discontinued, the Gold Tone line is discontinued, Backyard Music is paused, and no other manufacturer has filled the void. If Solo Music Gear raises prices or goes OOS, there is no fallback kit at this tier that is currently available. Say so plainly before acting.

Anti-Default Check

The banjo is American in origin and the $150-300 kit market is entirely US and Canadian (Solo Music Gear is Ontario-based, Carver Banjos is US-based). No equivalent kit market exists in other countries or regions for this instrument at this budget. The West African ancestral instruments (akonting, ngoni, xalam) and the gourd-banjo tradition are documented in the companion file (Build Catalog - Mandolin and Banjo.md) as the under-$150 cross-cultural build route. In the $150-300 band, the Carver Minstrel kits explicitly gesture toward the historical minstrel tradition (early 19th-century American, bridging the gourd-lute ancestry and the modern instrument). No Chinese, European, or other regional kit market for banjo in this band was found after deliberate non-Western search pass. Scarcity is genuine, not a search failure. [ESTABLISHED on absence: confirmed after full search pass]

Same-OEM / Relabel Watch

  • The Solo BNJK-50, BNJK-40, and BNJK-60 share the same sapele/poplar construction and appear to be from the same Chinese-OEM supply chain under the Solo label. They are distinct products (different string counts and configurations) but the same manufacturing source. This is normal; do not count them as three independent vendors.
  • Carver Banjos kits are designed and built by the maker. Not relabeled imports.
  • No other relabel situations found in this band.

Acoustic Violin

Band OVERRIDE: $150-300 (standard sub-$150 band does not apply to this file)

Scope and cross-references

This file covers carve-and-setup kits, white instrument completion paths, and plans+tonewood builds for standard 4/4 Western violin (violin/fiddle). Band override: $150-300 total project cost in the US.

Do not duplicate content from: - Build Catalog - Bowed Strings.md (WWWWWWWW): sub-$150 bowed strings; electric violin kits; VW-1 and StewMac kit noted there as over-band references; non-Western bowed strings (erhu, rebec, sarangi, morin khuur, etc.) covered there.

What this file does NOT cover (no kits or achievable build paths in band): - Viola: no carve-and-setup kits available; white body theoretically possible but total project exceeds $300. See scope table below. - Cello, double bass: no kits at any consumer price point. Documented in Bowed Strings file; no change.

De minimis note: US de minimis exemption suspended for China/HK (May 2025) and all countries (August 2025). All imports from overseas now face duty. Practically: StewMac kit and OWT wood are US-domestic; VW-1 is a US-distributed Saga product (Taiwan origin, duty absorbed into retail price); Strad posters ship from the UK.

Anti-default note: Deliberate non-Western pass run. For this instrument and band, paths are US-distribution-based or US-stocked (StewMac, Saga/Anton Breton, Old World Tonewood). No violin-family carve-and-setup kits from non-Western sources were found US-available and in band. The erhu, rebab, and other non-Western bowed instruments are covered in the Bowed Strings file.

Violin / Fiddle

4/4 standard violin; folk fiddle variants use identical construction

Origin tag: Western Europe (Cremona, Italy; luthier tradition established 16th-17th century); spread globally. The modern violin form was standardized by the 19th century; folk fiddle playing traditions exist worldwide using the same instrument.

Close-enough bar: A real acoustic violin build transfers: arched carved spruce top with bass bar; arched carved maple back; bent maple ribs on a mould; spruce or maple neck with ebony board; fitted soundpost; fitted bridge. The acoustic resonance is load-bearing in ways no electric build is. Plate graduation (thickness tapering across the surface) and arching height directly shape tone. The cheap version trades: speed of factory graduation (plates may be too thick or uneven), bridge fit quality, soundpost placement accuracy. Those three factors alone determine whether a completed violin sounds like a musical instrument or a screech box. A builder willing to do a proper bridge fit and have soundpost placement verified by a luthier can recover much of what cheap materials cost. A builder who leaves them as-shipped cannot.

Group 1: Kits

Kit = buy, assemble, and set up. Plate carving and major shaping already done.

StewMac kit build notes (FiddleHangout community): The included bridge blank has too small a radius for comfortable playing; strongly recommended to source a pre-fitted or pre-radiused German bridge instead (~$8-20). The purfling material is paper-core and swells on glue contact; work fast. Plates may be thicker than optimal and can benefit from careful light re-graduation. Soundpost placement is the highest single-impact adjustment; if uncertain, have a luthier check placement before stringing up. Use hot hide glue (preferred) or red-label Titebond (reversible aliphatic resin, acceptable) for all joinery. Blue-label Titebond II (PVA) is not appropriate for violin construction.

VW-1 path notes: The VW-1 body is genuine solid carved wood, not laminate. A competent setup person can produce a playable violin from this. It requires more baseline knowledge than the StewMac kit (no instructions; buyer does full setup from nothing) but the initial outlay is lower and the plates are already assembled. This is closer to a "white instrument completion" than a kit in the conventional sense.

The Strad lutherie posters (violin working drawings) Full-scale working drawings of historical instruments (Stradivari, Guarneri, Amati, and others) published by The Strad magazine; used as construction references by professional and advanced makers worldwide. Single flat-rolled: £22.95 each [ESTABLISHED]; single folded: £14.95 each [ESTABLISHED]; 2+ folded bundle: £9.99 each [ESTABLISHED]. "Returned or flawed" stock (edge damage only) also available at £9.99. Ships from UK; no de minimis exemption; US tariff on printed matter (HTS 4911) is typically low but verify current rates. Poster is reference only; same BOM as Strobel path above. Tells you WHAT the dimensions are, not HOW to work. Pair with Strobel for procedure. Community standard for serious builds. The lutherie poster category contains 90+ prints; violin-specific posters are under the Violin and Lutherie sections. thestradshop.com
Old World Tonewood pre-carved wood sets European spruce top + maple back, 80-85% carved (arching roughed in, f-holes roughed); Bosnia/Austria origin, 25+ years old; stocked in the US by OWT. NOT a kit: no hardware, no neck, no fittings. Buyer completes carving, does all joinery, finishes, and sets up. VLN-PCKIT-2899 and VLN-PCKIT-3399: $225 each (1 in stock each as of research date) [ESTABLISHED, verified at oldworldtonewood.com]; VLN-PCKIT-1099: $205 OUT OF STOCK Add shaped neck blank (~$30-$60), hardware (~$80-$120), strings/bow extra. Total project: ~$300-$400+ [PLAUSIBLE]. The wood alone is in band; full completion is over band. Best path for a builder who wants genuine European-origin luthier-grade wood at a reasonable entry price and is willing to do serious finish carving. The pre-carved state means the most tedious roughing work is done; what remains is graduation refinement, joinery, and setup. One in stock each: verify before planning a build. oldworldtonewood.com

GAL plans note: The Guild of American Luthiers catalog (84 plans as of 2026) contains no standard violin or fiddle plans. Their bowed instrument plans are: Hardanger fiddle (#11), Low-Cost Bass Viol (#29), English Treble Gamba (#40), Savart-style Upright Bass (#50), Double Bass (#64). For a printed full-scale plan, The Strad poster is the standard source for violin.

Source What they stock Price range Link

Group 3: Video tutorials and community resources

Resource Notes Link
YouTube: "violin making from scratch" series Multiple independent makers have documented full builds on YouTube from raw billets to playable instrument. Quality varies; prioritize makers who show actual graduation thickness measurements, plate thickness maps, and soundpost fitting, not just glue-up sequences. Search "making a violin" + "full build" for the better series. YouTube search
StewMac fiddle kit instructions (official) StewMac's free online instructions for the #5342 kit; includes recommended tool list; useful even if not building from the kit for general process overview stewmac.com/fiddle-kit-instructions
FiddleHangout forums Community forum; "Anybody construct a StewMac fiddle kit?" thread (archived) documents a real kit build with specific pitfalls. General lutherie discussion active. fiddlehangout.com
Maestronet: Making and Maintenance forum Most serious English-language online community for violin makers and restorers. Advanced discussions on graduation, varnish, bridge fitting, soundpost placement. Not a beginner walkthrough; invaluable for specific technical questions once you are mid-build. maestronet.com

Group 4: Close-enough cousins

Instrument Why it counts / why only a cousin Cost band Link
Hardanger fiddle Same fundamental body construction as violin (carved spruce top, carved maple back, bent ribs); adds sympathetic strings under the fingerboard and a distinctive carved peg box. Bowing and fingering technique identical. A violin builder who adds sympathetic peg holes and an underboard can build one. No kit available anywhere; build path uses GAL Plan #11 + violin BOM. Plan: ~$32-$37 [PLAUSIBLE]; full project ~$200-$300+; sympathetic strings + additional peg materials add ~$20-$40 over a violin build GAL Plan #11
Baroque violin setup Same body construction as modern violin; different setup (gut strings, no chin rest, lower lighter bridge, no end button on tailpiece, baroque bow). Any violin build can be set up baroque. Listed here only to flag: the StewMac kit or a from-plans build can be completed in baroque setup for essentially the same budget. Not a different build path, a different setup choice. Same as violin paths above —

Bottom line

The StewMac Fiddle Kit #5342 (~$241-$266) is the only complete carve-and-setup violin kit available in the US at any price under $300. There is no competitor. The market here is genuinely thin: one real kit, one white body completion path (VW-1, total ~$200-$240), and a from-plans path that enters the bottom of band with economy wood.

The cheapest path to a playable acoustic violin in band is the VW-1 body ($139.95) plus hardware and setup: total ~$200-$240. It requires more setup knowledge than the StewMac kit but costs less upfront.

The from-plans path (Strobel $29.50 + economy tonewood + hardware) can reach playable for $150-$295 depending on wood grade. This is a 40-80+ hour build for a skilled maker; a first build is more. The acoustic violin is unforgiving: graduation thickness and soundpost placement are acoustically load-bearing in ways that most other instrument builds are not. A luthier checkup on the soundpost before final string-up is worth the cost.

Hard scope: other bowed strings in the $150-300 band

Cello No kit paths. White cello bodies from European suppliers: EUR 400-600+; far over band. Documented in Bowed Strings file; unchanged
Double bass No kit paths at any consumer price point. Documented in Bowed Strings file; unchanged
Non-Western bowed strings (erhu, rebec, morin khuur, etc.) Covered in Build Catalog - Bowed Strings.md; most erhu kits are sub-$150. Out of scope for this file

Build Catalog: Electric Guitar and Bass -- Mid-Tier ($150-300)

Band: $150-300. Overrides Sub-$150 master spec band for this file. Read alongside: Build Catalog - Guitar and Bass Under 150.md

Tariff Context (June 2026)

Critical for any non-US source. Conditions are in flux; verify before ordering.

What happened: - De minimis exemption: suspended Aug 29, 2025, for all countries. No more duty-free packages. - IEEPA tariffs: struck down SCOTUS 6-3 on Feb 20, 2026 (Learning Resources v. Trump). Not in effect. - Section 122 (Trade Act 1974): 15% global tariff, enacted Feb 20, 2026 to offset IEEPA void. Expires ~July 19, 2026. Active as of this writing. - Section 301 on China: intact. ~7.5% for HTS 9207.10 (musical instruments/guitar kits). - MFN base rate (HTS 9207.10): ~5%.

Effective rates by origin (June 2026): - US domestic: 0%. BYOGuitar and StewMac kits have no import friction. - Canada (Solo Music Gear): ~20% (5% MFN + 15% S122) unless USMCA origin rules met, which is uncertain for assembled wood/hardware kits. [UNCERTAIN] - Australia (Pit Bull Guitars): ~20% (5% MFN + 15% S122, no S301). - China (Harley Benton/Thomann): ~27.5% (5% MFN + 7.5% S301 + 15% S122).

S122 sunset: Section 122 is scheduled to expire around July 19, 2026. If it lapses without replacement, Australian and Canadian rates drop to ~5% MFN and Chinese drops to ~12.5%. This changes the Pit Bull and HB math significantly. Verify the tariff situation before ordering any non-US kit.

Landed cost formula used in this catalog: - Pit Bull (AU): (list price USD incl. GST / 1.10) + $51 EMS shipping + 20% tariff on CIF value. - Harley Benton (via Thomann DE, China origin): list price USD + ~$40-50 shipping + 27.5% tariff on CIF. - Solo (CA): list price USD as shown + ~20% tariff on CIF [UNCERTAIN on USMCA].

$51 shipping for Pit Bull and $40-50 for Thomann are estimates from research; actual shipping varies by weight and option. All landed costs below are approximate; verify at checkout.

Anti-Default Check: Electric Guitar Kits ($150-300) Are Western/Chinese-Dominated

The global search was run. The commercial kit market in the $150-300 assembled-kit band is genuinely dominated by US, Australian, Canadian, and Chinese-origin vendors. Here is why:

  • Japan (Hosco): Sells quality guitar parts and kit components, but not assembled kits shipped direct to US buyers in this band. [ESTABLISHED]
  • Korea: Major manufacturers (Cort, etc.) sell complete instruments, not DIY kits to consumers.
  • India: Luthiery supply market exists but no kit vendors identified at this tier.
  • Latin America/Africa/Middle East/SE Asia: No commercial electric guitar kit vendors identified at this price point. [PLAUSIBLE that individual luthiers exist; no catalog-able sources found]
  • AliExpress/Taobao: Chinese-sourced kits exist in the $50-200 range but most land under $150 for US buyers even after duty, and lack the curated QC of named brands. One exception below.

Harley Benton (Thomann/China) is the non-Western-origin entry in this catalog. The field is what it is.

byoguitar.com | Ships from New Hampshire | US domestic | No duty

The imported kits (most of the line) are manufactured to BYO's specs. All prices below confirmed June 5, 2026 from their catalog page. [ESTABLISHED]

Close-enough bar: Standard Western electric guitar forms. Bolt-on neck on most kits; set neck on LP-style (STD, LPC). Hardware and pickups are budget/functional; most builders swap pickups and pots.

1F. Harley Benton / Thomann (China-origin, German distributor)

US storefront: thomannmusic.com | Ships from Germany (China-origin goods) | ~27.5% US tariff (MFN + S301 + S122) | Prices below confirmed June 5, 2026 from thomannmusic.com US storefront [ESTABLISHED]

Harley Benton is Thomann's house brand, made in China. The kits are entry-level quality but notable for: (a) very low list prices, (b) 1,000+ reviews on most models giving real QC data, (c) Thomann's 3-year warranty and 30-day return. The China origin means ~27.5% total tariff, but list prices are low enough that landed costs fall in-band.

Origin tag: China-manufactured. Rengas wood bodies (a tropical hardwood, similar to light mahogany), maple necks, laurel fingerboards. Bolt-on only on guitar kits. Bodies pre-sealed (pore filler applied) -- reviewers note this complicates staining but enables direct painting.

Close-enough bar: Standard Western electric guitar forms. Pre-wired electronics (no soldering required per Thomann). Bolt-on neck throughout.

Part 4: Parts Builds

For builders who want to assemble a guitar from components rather than a kit, the key US domestic suppliers in this band are:

StewMac: Swamp-ash body blanks $126-$152 [UNCERTAIN, verify at stewmac.com]; bolt-on maple necks available separately. Total body + neck + hardware could land $200-300 in this band. StewMac also sells pre-slotted nuts, fret wire, and all finishing supplies. Their parts quality is notably higher than kit hardware.

BYOGuitar: Sells bodies, necks, and hardware separately. Bodies + Necks section: byoguitar.com/Guitar_Kits/Bodies-Necks-and-Wood.aspx

Warmoth: Premium US-made bodies and necks, most in the $150-300+ range per piece. Over-band for a complete build but worth knowing for selective upgrades. warmoth.com

LMII (Luthiers Mercantile): Closed 2024. Do not quote as an active source.

Confidence Audit

Evidence quality: Strong for BYOGuitar (full catalog page scraped), Solo (individual product pages with Open Graph metadata), Harley Benton (Thomann US storefront page). Moderate for Pit Bull (list prices from WebSearch snippets; site timeout issues during session). Weak for StewMac (JS-rendered pages; prices from secondary sources only). 1. Ukulele (Solid-Wood and Koa Tier, $150-300)

Origin tag: Hawaiian. The ukulele's modern identity is Hawaiian, derived from the machete da braga brought by Madeiran Portuguese immigrants to Hawai'i ca. 1879; the instrument's name, tuning, and cultural role were shaped on the islands. Manufacturing spread globally through the 20th century but the prestige wood association (koa) and the highest-end sourcing remain Hawaiian.

Close-enough bar: The distinction between the laminate-kit tier (under-$150 catalog) and the solid-wood tier is real. All-solid-wood plates resonate differently from laminate: better high-register sustain, more complex overtone decay, and material aging (solid wood opens up tonally over years; laminate does not). An all-koa ukulele plays and sounds substantially differently from a Grizzly basswood/veneer kit. The skip is not audiophile mysticism; it is a documented acoustic difference that becomes audible above beginner playing level.

Group 1: Kits

The commercial all-solid ukulele kit market in the $150-300 band is essentially empty as of June 2026.

Group 2: Plans + Tonewood Sets (the real all-solid path)

Kamuela Hardwoods, Kamuela, Hawai'i (Big Island) — the anchor source:

Kamuela Hardwoods sells individual koa ukulele building sets retail via their Shopify storefront. Sets are sustainably harvested Hawaiian koa from the Big Island. These are NOT complete kits — they are tonewood body sets only (top + back + sides + binding pieces). The buyer still needs to supply neck, fretboard, tuning machines, nut/saddle, bridge, strings, hardware, and finish. But the wood component IS in the $150-300 band.

Note: Winkler Woods (also Hawaiian koa, Oahu) offers koa ukulele sets wholesale only — $1,500 minimum order. Not accessible for individual builders.

What a 6-piece set includes vs. what it does NOT: A Kamuela set includes: bookmatched top plates, bookmatched back plates (or one-piece for concert), and side strips. It does NOT include: neck blank, fretboard, tuning machines, nut, saddle, bridge, strings, glue, or finish. The buyer bends sides (steam bending or kerf-bending), cuts and fits the top/back, and does all assembly. This is a luthier's build requiring a mold and basic bending setup. Not a beginner project.

A builder with no scrounging tolerance hits $320-353.

Non-koa all-solid path (lower cost): For an all-solid build without Hawaiian provenance: solid mahogany, sapele, or walnut ukulele tonewood sets (top + back + sides) are available from StewMac's tonewood section and eBay lutherie sellers for ~$40-80. With the same hardware range, total project is $131-258. This is the cheapest all-solid-wood ukulele build route and the lower end lands well within band.

2. Mountain Dulcimer (Upper Tier, $150-300)

The under-$150 catalog covers Backyard Music ($69), Jaromin ($90), and Folkcraft Cardboard ($105). This section starts where those end.

Origin tag: Appalachian American. The mountain dulcimer (also: Appalachian dulcimer) is a fretted box zither indigenous to Appalachian folk tradition, likely developed in the early 19th century from European precedents (épinette des Vosges, Scheitholt). Three-string and four-string variants common; hourglass and teardrop body shapes.

Close-enough bar: The cardboard and plywood kits in the under-$150 tier produce real, playable instruments but with a resonance ceiling. A solid-wood body in cherry, walnut, or ash transmits differently: better bass response, longer sustain, richer harmonic complexity. The tonal difference is not dramatic on a fundamental modal-tuning dulcimer played with a noter, but it becomes more apparent with more complex fingering or when amplified. The cardboard tier is sufficient for learning; the solid-wood tier is for the player who intends to keep the instrument.

3. Bowed Strings Remainder ($150-300)

This section covers what the under-$150 bowed strings catalog documented as over budget, minus the acoustic violin (fully covered in Build Catalog - Acoustic Violin 150-300.md). Do not duplicate violin content.

Four subsections: viola (scarcity documentation); EUB at $150-300 (the real build tier); better electric violin and viola; electric cello at this tier.

3A. Viola (Scarcity)

Origin tag: Western Europe; viola is the alto voice of the string family, tuned a fifth below violin. Body construction is identical to violin (carved spruce top, carved maple back, bent maple ribs) but at larger dimensions (39-43cm back length vs. 35-36cm for 4/4 violin). No standardized size.

Kit status: No carve-and-setup viola kits exist at any price. There are no commercial viola kits, period, not even at $1,000+. This is genuine scarcity, not a search failure.

White viola bodies: US-distributed white viola bodies (assembled but unvarnished, no neck or fittings) exist in principle from European suppliers via US distributors including International Violin Co. (Baltimore, MD) and Vitali Import. Pricing is [UNCERTAIN]: the Acoustic Violin 150-300.md file (GGGGGGGG) estimated ~$180-250 for a white viola body; the International Violin website is JS-rendered and live pricing could not be confirmed. Saga/Anton Breton (the maker of the VW-1 violin white body) does not appear to offer a viola equivalent, but this has not been directly confirmed — verify at swstrings.com or intlviolin.com before planning a build.

Total project: Even if a white viola body lands in band at $180-250, completion requires: neck fitting (skilled work; viola necks are not straight swaps), ebony fingerboard, bridge, pegs, tailpiece, chinrest, strings, bow, varnish, and setup. Total project to playable: $300-450+ [PLAUSIBLE based on violin project analog + viola-specific premium]. The $300 ceiling is exceeded in any realistic complete build. This subsection documents scarcity.

From-plans viola (advanced reference): Henry Strobel's Viola Making, Step by Step ($25, henrystrobel.com) is the standard English-language text. Materials parallel violin: tonewood set for viola (spruce top, maple back/sides) from International Violin or ILS at ~$60-120 economy, with hardware ~$80-120 and strings/bow extra. Total project ~$280-420. Some builds could land in band with economy material choices and careful setup. But this is a first-build risk for most people — viola graduation and arching tolerances are no easier than violin.

3B. Electric Violin and Viola ($150-300)

The under-$150 catalog covered: 3D-print OpenFab Modular Fiddle at ~$95-140 (violin config, basic hardware); wood-body electric violin plan routes under $150. The $150-300 band adds real pickup quality to those base builds.

Origin tag (electric violin): The electric violin emerged in the 1930s as a studio instrument; the modern solid-body electric violin was developed independently by multiple makers through the 1990s-2000s. The OpenFab Modular Fiddle (Portland, OR) is the anchor DIY resource.

3C. Electric Upright Bass (EUB) at $150-300

The real opportunity in this section. The EUB at $150-300 is not a separate instrument tier from the under-$150 build — it is the same Libellula build at a meaningfully better string and pickup specification.

Origin tag: The electric upright bass emerged from the double bass lineage in the mid-20th century. The Ampeg Baby Bass (1962) was the first mass-market EUB. The modern DIY EUB tradition centers on Liutaio Mottola's Libellula design (Boston, MA), a free-plans instrument that has been built by the international double bass DIY community for over a decade.

Why this band matters: Upright bass tone is more string-dependent than almost any other instrument. The budget strings used in the under-$150 Libellula build (~$20-40/set) produce a playable but thin, somewhat lifeless tone. Real upright bass strings — even mid-tier D'Addario Helicore Hybrid 3/4 (the standard recommendation for arco+pizzicato EUB work) — run $90-130/set. Upgrading strings is what the $150-300 band buys. The body, neck, and hardware costs are the same.

Anchor resource: - Mottola's Libellula plans: free at liutaiomottola.com. 3/4 scale; solid minimal body (no acoustic resonating chamber); endpin; pickup routing. Clear drawings; US community proven. This is the only well-documented free EUB plan in English. - Instructables EUB: free; more visual, less detailed. Covers an independent builder's approach.

Helicore Hybrid is the go-to recommendation for EUB players who do both arco and pizzicato. Fishman BP-100 is a recognized, reliable bridge transducer. Pushes over band at all configurations. Included here because the $142 pickup cost is the single component that takes an otherwise in-band build over. Serious performance instrument.

The sweet spot: Libellula (free plans) + D'Addario Helicore Hybrid 3/4 strings ($95-120) + Fishman BP-100 or similar quality transducer ($70-90) + body/neck/hardware ($100-160) = $265-370. The lower end of hardware costs can bring this to $265-300 — solidly in band for a real-strings, real-transducer EUB.

Batch kit note: The Pulga/Moscha EUB batch kit project (a TalkBass community effort to produce a parts kit specifically for the Libellula or compatible design) is not released as of June 2026. Watch TalkBass.com EUB builder threads for status.

3D. Electric Cello (brief)

Carolyn Matthews' electric cello build (documented in Build Catalog - Bowed Strings.md) sits at the tight $150 edge of the under-$150 catalog. The $150-300 band does not open dramatically new paths for electric cello. The same body-from-plans + bridge transducer approach applies: a step-up bridge transducer ($50-90) over the basic piezo brings total to roughly $200-280. A K&K StringCello dual-sensor ($249 at K&K Sound, plus body/hardware) would land a cello build at $350-450 — over band. The in-band electric cello path is the Matthews/community build plus a Fishman or Shadow transducer in the $50-90 range.

Bottom line (bowed strings remainder)

Viola acoustic: no kit exists at any price; total project exceeds $300 even with a white body in band. The EUB (Libellula free plans + Helicore Hybrid strings + Fishman BP-100) is the genuine $150-300 build opportunity in this family: a real-strings, real-transducer electric upright for ~$265-300. Electric violin and viola builds in this band add meaningful pickup quality (K&K Violinissimo ~$197 or Fishman V-200 ~$190) to the OpenFab or wood-body base, landing at $292-317 at the quality-pickup end or $150-180 at the basic-piezo end.

Jouhikko / tagelharpa (Scandinavian bowed lyre) Borderline. Some European craftspeople sell unfinished jouhikko kits or semi-finished bodies at ~€90-180 (~$100-200). But international shipping + current tariffs make final US-landed price [UNCERTAIN]. No US-stocked source confirmed. Community: search "jouhikko kit" or "tagelharpa build"
Erhu / huqin (Chinese) No. Premium student erhu kits at $150-300 are not meaningfully different from buying a finished instrument at the same price. The DIY erhu path is sub-$100 and covered in Build Catalog - Bowed Strings.md. No separate upper-tier kit market found. --
Rebec (medieval) No. Scratch build under $100 with domestic wood; no kit at any price. Same as base-tier finding. --

Honest finding: The kantele is the only instrument across the 47 in the worldwide pilot with a documented commercial kit that specifically lands in the $150-300 band. Everything else either has no kit at all (balalaika, charango, cuatro, jouhikko, rebec) or has builds that remain well under $150 regardless of wood quality. This is genuine scarcity; "this is all that exists" after a real sweep is the correct answer.

Anti-default pass (worldwide check)

Deliberate non-Western run, required by master spec.

  • Ukulele section: Hawaiian instrument by origin (Portuguese immigrant influence; instrument identity is Hawaiian). The tonewood sourcing section connects to the instrument's homeland (Big Island koa). The mango and Cuban mahogany set options at Kamuela add non-koa Hawaiian wood paths.
  • Mountain dulcimer: Appalachian American folk instrument with European predecessor roots. No non-Western analog in this band was found — documented scarcity, not omission.
  • Bowed strings: EUB and electric violin/viola are Western families. Non-Western bowed instruments (erhu, rebab, morin khuur, sarangi, masenqo, marovany adjacent bowed variants) are covered in Build Catalog - Bowed Strings.md, and their build costs are well under $150 in almost all cases. No meaningful $150-300 tier was found for those instruments because they do not become significantly more expensive to build in this band. Documented.
  • Folk strings sweep: Ran balalaika (Russian), charango (Andean), cuatro (Venezuelan), jouhikko (Scandinavian), rebec (medieval/MENA-origin), erhu (Chinese). None have meaningful upper-tier kits in this band. The kantele (Finnish) is the one confirmed hit.

Anti-default result: The coverage distribution here is thin because the market is thin, not because Western instruments were defaulted to. The two main opportunities in this file — koa ukulele (Hawaiian) and EUB strings upgrade — are both non-European by instrument identity or by dominant material sourcing. The folk strings sweep ran all non-Western entries and found nothing to add beyond the base-tier catalog findings.

Concertina & Free Reed

Worker JJJJJJJJ: Concertina and Free Reed. Starting work.

Scope statement: This file covers: the concertina (Anglo/English/Duet) fully; melodeon and diatonic accordion rebuild paths; harmonium rebuild at the upper tier; the PAiA Theremax and theremin-adjacent kits that cleared the $150 floor; and bandoneon. The PVC/cheap wind instruments, basic harmonica re-keying, and melodica are covered in XXXXXXX and not repeated here.

1. Orientation

The $150-300 band is where the free-reed world gets philosophically strange. Almost every instrument in this family has its first real kit far above $300 (the Clover concertina kit is $1,400), and yet the parts-only paths are genuinely interesting starting at $115-200. What this band actually buys you:

  • Harmonium rebuild (confirmed in-band): Donor instrument + full replacement reed sets from a US source, total $178-240, lands cleanly in $150-300. This is the most concrete story in this file.
  • PAiA Theremax (historically in-band): A genuine heterodyne theremin kit at ~$189-200 shipped. Caveat: PAiA's website went offline in April 2026 following the founder's death; availability is uncertain as of this writing.
  • Concertina from-plans (BOM may land at low end of band): The Tedrow photo-essay path has parts costs in the $200-400+ range depending on sourcing; the lowest-cost first attempt may barely enter this band. No kit exists under $1,400.
  • Melodeon, bandoneon: No in-band kit or parts path found after a real search. Confirmed thin.

Free-reed voicing note (applies to all entries): Reed voicing - adjusting gap, gapping, and fitting - is the defining skill of free-reed DIY. Unlike a string instrument where geometry is largely fixed at assembly, a free reed's behavior depends on the gap between tongue and frame, valve weight, chamber dimensions, and bellows pressure. Getting 30+ reeds all speaking cleanly and in tune is the primary time cost of any concertina or accordion build. The harmonium is somewhat more forgiving because individual reeds are replaceable and pre-tuned; the from-scratch concertina is not.

Knowledge tags: [ESTABLISHED] well-documented/high confidence; [PLAUSIBLE] reasonable but not directly verified; [UNCERTAIN] limited or contested; [UNKNOWN] outside reliable knowledge.

2. Concertina (the headline)

Origin: England, mid-19th century. The Anglo concertina (the primary DIY target) is a bisonoric free-reed instrument: each button produces a different note on push versus pull, arranged in the Wheatstone C/G layout for Irish traditional music. The English concertina (unisonoric, chromatic, single-note per button regardless of bellows direction) and the Duet systems (Hayden, Crane, MacCann) are different instruments. Kit and plans paths below produce Anglo instruments unless noted.

Close-enough bar: The Anglo concertina plays different notes push vs. pull, creating a fundamentally different technique from the English concertina or melodeon. Build logs for the Clover kit produce an Anglo; Tedrow's essay is also Anglo. An English concertina from these plans/parts does not exist as a documented cheap build path.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: High to very high. Individual reeds must be gapped, valved, and fine-tuned after assembly. The bellows are the hardest single component -- traditional cut-card bellows with linen/leather hinges at each fold took Tedrow years to master. Pre-buying a kit (Clover) sidesteps most voicing because the reeds arrive pre-tuned; the Tedrow from-scratch path does not.

3. Melodeon / Diatonic Accordion

Origin: Western Europe (France, Germany, Italy); button accordion with one or two rows of buttons, each row producing a single diatonic scale. The standard Irish/folk melodeon (B/C or G/C layout) is the primary target of the DIY community.

Close-enough bar: The melodeon is bisonoric like the Anglo concertina but plays diatonic scales rather than the full chromatic layout. Technique is different enough that a melodeon and a concertina are not interchangeable.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: Same family of issues as the concertina: bellows, reed waxing, gapping. A rebuild of a donor melodeon is achievable; building one from scratch requires all the same components as an accordion, which is specialist industrial territory.

Group 1: Kits

No melodeon/diatonic accordion kit in the $150-300 range was confirmed in this research. The melodeon.net forum has active discussion ("Does anyone make a kit?" thread with no definitive answer); the community consensus is that no ready-made melodeon kit exists from any current supplier. The Accordion Centre Birmingham self-assembly kit noted in XXXXXXX was not confirmed for current price or US availability and may no longer be offered. [UNKNOWN for current kit availability]

No kit exists. The lane is: buy a dead melodeon ($30-80), use Accordion Revival to diagnose, order replacement reed plates or wax from Liberty Bellows (~$30-50), re-leather bellows if needed. The full rebuild lands solidly in $150-300 depending on the donor and scope. YouTube content for from-scratch single-row construction exists but is thin and not backed by a kit or plans community.

4. Harmonium (Indian / Western) Rebuild

Origin: France/Germany (19th century Western harmonium); India/Pakistan (Delhi and Calcutta style Indian harmoniums, now their own independent tradition). The Indian harmonium is the more relevant DIY target in this band: widely available as a used instrument, simpler internal layout than an accordion, and backed by a real US parts pipeline.

Close-enough bar: The harmonium is a free-reed, bellows-driven keyboard instrument. The Indian (Delhi-style) harmonium is hand-pumped; the Western parlor harmonium is foot-pumped. Technique (melody on right hand, drone/accompaniment on left) is different from concertina or accordion; this is a keyboard-layout free reed.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: Individual reed replacement is accessible: pop out failed reed from its slot, press in replacement, check gap. Bellows re-leathering is harder -- this is the step most rebuilders outsource or postpone. Dry-climate cracking (especially of the wooden case) is the main failure mode on Delhi-style instruments.

5. PAiA Theremax and Theremin-Adjacent Kits

Note: The PAiA Theremax is listed here -- adjacent to the free-reed section -- per the brief's instruction to include mid-tier electronic wind/theremin kits that exceeded the sub-$150 floor. The theremax is a theremin, not a free-reed instrument; it produces continuous-pitch tone controlled by hand proximity to antennas, not by breath or reed. Cross-reference the JJJJJJJJ electronic fire if a synth-only path is wanted.

5.1 PAiA Theremax (9505K / 9505KC)

Origin: PAiA Electronics, Oklahoma City; founded 1959 by John Simonton; operated for decades by Scott Lee. The Theremax (model 9505) is a classic heterodyne theremin kit using two radio-frequency oscillators; one fixed, one variable (controlled by the pitch antenna). The beat frequency between them is the audible output. Both pitch and volume antennas are included in the full 9505KC kit (kit + lectern case).

Close-enough bar: The theremin is played by moving hands near antennas without physical contact. It is an electronic instrument, not acoustic. Techniques are unrelated to any wind or reed instrument. Included here because: (a) the brief explicitly scopes it to this fire, and (b) it is the mid-tier theremin kit that cleared the $150 floor and fits the $150-300 band.

Voicing/tuning difficulty (electronic): Soldering skill required (through-hole components, manageable). Tuning the oscillators to the correct zero-beat frequency requires patience and a good ear; the PAiA tuning guide covers this. Once built and tuned, the instrument is stable. Getting expressive tone from a theremin is a separate, years-long playing skill; the build itself is a one-time project.

STATUS NOTE (important as of 2026-06-05): PAiA founder Scott Lee passed away on April 21, 2026. His son Nathan Lee is working to restore PAiA operations, but as of this writing the website is reporting a temporary outage and current orders/fulfillment are uncertain. The price below is the last-documented figure before this transition.

The Theremaniacs kit (~$150 borderline, pitch-only, no volume antenna, no soldering required) is a simpler option at the floor of this band -- genuinely functional but limited vs. the Theremax.

6. Bandoneon (and Other European Free-Reed Cousins)

Origin: Germany, mid-19th century; central to Argentine and Uruguayan tango; also used in some German folk and sacred music. The bandoneon is a bisonoric button accordion with a complex asymmetric button layout (different from both the Anglo concertina and the melodeon).

DIY status: No kit exists. No documented from-scratch plans path exists in any language at any price. The bandoneon is handmade by a small number of specialist workshops (primarily in Germany and Argentina); internal parts are not standardized and are not sold separately by any known commercial source. The community consensus: this is repair/restoration territory only, not build territory.

Budget reality: A used non-playing bandoneon (estate sale, eBay) can be $200-600+; even a basket-case instrument for parts costs more than $300 typically. Restoration requires specialist knowledge of the specific instrument's button layout (which varies by maker and era). [ESTABLISHED for no-kit status]

Verdict: No in-band path. Noted and closed.

Other European free-reed cousins not covered above:

The garmon (Russian/Caucasian diatonic button accordion) and sheng (Chinese free-reed mouth organ) both have active traditional manufacture but no Western-accessible kit. The sheng, worth a separate note: individual replacement sheng reeds are available from Chinese suppliers on AliExpress and Taobao (~$1-5 USD per reed for standard sheng reeds), and repair/tuning of a used sheng is a real accessible project -- but a sheng is not a bellows instrument and the build tradition is not in the concertina/accordion family in the same way. If Mark wants to pursue sheng repair, that belongs in the non-Western free-reed fire.

Instruments covered by origin tradition:

  • England / Ireland: Anglo concertina

The harmonium entry explicitly names both Delhi and Calcutta traditions, distinguishes their reed types, and points to both US-source (Old Delhi Music, Illinois) and Indian-source (Calcutta Musical Depot) supply chains. The concertina entry covers Anglo, English, and Duet variants. Western default not smuggled in silently.

Handpan & Steel Tongue

Worker IIIIIIII: Handpan and Steel Tongue. Starting work.

Build Catalog: Handpan and Steel Tongue Drum — $150–300 Tier

Band: $150–300 (BAND OVERRIDE — supersedes under-$150 tier for both instruments) Cross-reference: Under-$150 tier handpan honest note and steel tongue drum / hank drum entries are in Build Catalog - Tuned Percussion and Lamellophone.md (Worker YYYYYYY, 2026-06-05). Do not repeat that ground. This file picks up where it left off.

What this probe is and is not

The under-$150 catalog flagged handpan as "honest note only" and steel tongue drum as a DIY path requiring 8–25 hours of tuning work. This $150–300 probe asks: does the higher band change the picture? The answer is mixed and honest:

  • Handpan: The band barely touches the raw shell market and does not touch the skill problem. A shell set exists at $299.99. Tuning a handpan to a playable instrument still requires hundreds of hours of hammering and a high first-attempt failure rate. The band buys you a starting canvas, not a path to success. This is a probe, not a recommendation.
  • Steel tongue drum: This is the real $150–300 story. HAPI Drum's lineup of fully finished, US-made, professionally tuned instruments spans $169–$296. A DIY tank-drum build remains far cheaper; the $150–300 band is almost entirely finished-instrument territory for this family. Both paths are laid out below.

The honest verdict is at the bottom of this file.

1. Handpan: raw shell market

Orientation

A handpan requires two deep-drawn steel shells (top playing surface + bottom) that are hammered-tuned to specific note areas (the "ding" center tone and surrounding "tone fields"), then glued together and post-tuned again after the glue cures. The raw shell market exists specifically so builders do not have to form the dome themselves (which requires a hydraulic press or significant hammer-sinking skill). The shells are the cheapest input; the tuning is the wall.

Origin tag: Switzerland (PANArt Hang, 2000); the instrument form is now global. Shell suppliers: Netherlands (Ayasa), Germany (Baur&Brown), Brazil (Mudra), USA (Dave's Island Instruments / Dii). The instrument draws on the steel pan tradition of Trinidad and Tobago and is influenced by the Tambiro (Zimbabwe, oil-drum origin).

The skill wall, stated plainly (ESTABLISHED from multiple established maker sources): - "A high quality handpan is not built without hundreds of hours of hammering no matter how much you read or how many professional builders you talk with." — Saraz Handpans (Asheville, NC), one of the oldest US handpan makers still in production. - "Almost everyone destroys their first attempt along with many more after that." — Saraz. - "Tuning a handpan is an art that takes months to learn." — MAG Instruments. - "It takes nothing less than persistent obsession to succeed as a quality handpan builder." — Saraz. - Community consensus on handpan.org and Facebook groups (Exchange of Knowledge Handpan, Sale and Development Tools Handpan): expect to ruin your first several shells before getting a playable result.

None of this is discouragement as a rhetorical move. It is the accurate state of the craft, from the people who do it professionally. The brief asked for brutal honesty; this is it.

Group 2: Handpan from scratch — gas cylinder / steel tradition

This is the origin-story path: form the dome yourself from flat steel or a modified tank, then tune. It is the most demanding path in the catalog.

Why gas cylinders don't straightforwardly work for handpan: A propane tank produces the right general shape (a dome with a curved surface) for a steel tongue drum / hank drum, but the geometry is wrong for a handpan. A handpan requires a precisely proportioned deep-drawn shell with a flat rim, specific curvature in the playing surface, and consistent wall thickness. A propane tank is a cylinder with a domed top, not a hemispherical bowl, and the proportions don't map correctly to handpan note-field geometry. The DIY handpan-from-steel-blank tradition uses flat sheet steel with hydraulic press forming (or hammer-sinking over a form) — not a propane tank.

The from-scratch steel tradition (documented):

Approach Materials Cost estimate Notes Difficulty
Hammer-sinking from flat sheet steel 1.0–1.2mm low-carbon DC04 steel sheet blank, hardwood or steel sinking form, sledgehammer, ball-peen hammers, grinder, tuner Sheet steel ~$30–80 depending on size; forming tools either on-hand or add $50–150 No hydraulic press required for hammer-sinking, but this is the slowest forming method; produces uneven thickness without significant skill. The PANArt founders used pneumatic tools and precision forms; backyard hammer-sinking is feasible only with hundreds of hours of practice just to form the shell. Expert forming + expert tuning = the two hardest skills stacked
Hydraulic press forming from sheet steel Same sheet steel; requires access to a hydraulic press (shop or rental) + purpose-built dies/forms Sheet steel ~$30–80; press access varies ($0 if you have one, $50–200/day rental, or makerspace membership) Produces better and more consistent dome geometry than hammer-sinking. The deep-draw forming step is what shell sellers (Ayasa, Dii, etc.) do industrially. DIY press forming without precision dies produces lumpy results. Expert; the forming step is a craft in itself before tuning begins

Nitriding note: DC04 steel handpans are typically gas-nitrided after forming to harden the surface and set the tuning stability. This requires access to a nitriding oven or a professional heat-treatment shop. Without nitriding, DC04 steel is softer and the tuning is less stable. Some builders skip nitriding and use stainless steel instead (Ayasa AISI 430, Baur&Brown stainless options), which eliminates the nitriding step at the cost of different tonal character. Stainless shells also cost more. The Dii shell at $299.99 is plain low-carbon steel, unnitrided — the buyer must decide on finishing.

Dave's Island Instruments online course: Dii sells a "How to Build a Handpan" course at dii.thinkific.com [PLAUSIBLE it exists; price not confirmed — check before relying on]. This is the most direct US-based entry point into structured handpan-building education if going the raw-shell route. [UNCERTAIN course price and current availability]

Bottom line: handpan in this band

The Dii shell set at $299.99 is the most accessible confirmed in-band US entry point into handpan building. But the shell buys you a canvas, not a path. The remaining cost is tooling, finishing, and hundreds of hours of tuning practice — none of which is in-band. The Baur&Brown approach (~$143 for two shells before shipping) is cheaper on shells but adds international shipping uncertainty.

The real budget for a first handpan attempt: shells $150–300 + basic hammers $50–100 + tuning ring $30–60 + finishing materials/nitriding ~$0–200 depending on approach + unlimited hours. A realistic minimum all-in budget for a first serious attempt is $400–700, not counting the fact that most first attempts produce an unplayable instrument.

This band is the floor of the conversation, not a viable budget for the build. If the handpan sound is the goal, see the verdict at the bottom of this file.

2. Steel tongue drum — upper tier ($150–300)

Orientation

The steel tongue drum (hank drum, tank drum) is the accessible cousin. It shares the "steel dome with resonant struck tongues" aesthetic and produces a related sound, but the tuning is far simpler (file/grind tongues to length vs. hammer-tune the whole dome), the failure rate on a build is much lower, and finished instruments land squarely in the $150–300 band from quality US makers.

Origin: Modern Western, 2007. Dennis Havlena (Michigan) cut the first tongue drum from a 20-lb propane tank. The instrument now exists as both a DIY tradition (the Havlena plan) and a commercial product line. The commercial line matures in the $150–300 band.

Close-enough bar vs. handpan: A steel tongue drum and a handpan are both played with hands or mallets on a steel dome and produce a sustained, reverberant pitched tone. They are not the same instrument. The handpan uses interlocking note fields that resonate sympathetically, producing a complex harmonic cloud; tongue drums use discrete cut tongues with simpler resonance. A tongue drum in the $150–300 range is a real instrument with a beautiful sound. It is not a handpan substitute; it is a different instrument that shares some aesthetic territory.

Group 2: DIY steel tongue drum — upper-tier builds in $150–300

Why DIY in this band if finished instruments exist? The Havlena tank-drum is already documented in the under-$150 catalog (basic 20-lb propane tank, ~$20–40 in materials, 8–25 hours including tuning). In the $150–300 band, the DIY path adds: a larger body (100-lb LP tank, a 50-gallon propane or nitrogen tank, an acetylene tank — all produce deeper, richer bass notes); thinner sheet steel welded into a custom shell (better tuning response); or more sophisticated tongue geometry. None of these are kit paths; there are no pre-cut, pre-tuned steel tongue drum kits on the market [ESTABLISHED — multiple searches returned no such product].

4. Honest verdict

The steel tongue drum is the real $150–300 story. The HAPI Drum lineup ($169–$296) represents the best-positioned instruments in this band: US-made, professionally tuned, real musical objects, widely available. No DIY kit path exists; the market choice is buy finished or build from raw materials using the Havlena plan or a sheet-steel approach. The Havlena build costs $20–40 and is under-$150, so in this band you're mostly buying finished unless you're deliberately choosing a larger or more ambitious DIY build.

The handpan is genuine but barely in-band and still pro-leaning. The Dii shell set at $299.99 is the one confirmed US in-band purchase. But buying the shells is not building the instrument. The shell is to the handpan what buying a blank guitar body and neck is to building a guitar, except the tuning skill required is on the order of magnitude harder. A guitar builder might tune to pitch in a weekend. A handpan builder should expect months to years before producing a playable instrument, with high probability of destroying their first shell. The community consensus from established builders (Saraz, MAG, handpan.org) is consistent and unambiguous on this.

Positioning for the compendium: - Steel tongue drum: achievable in this band. Buy finished (HAPI) or build larger (Havlena variant). The skill gate is low; the result is musically real. - Handpan raw shell: floor of conversation is in-band ($150–300 for shells), but the build is not in-band. A realistic handpan build attempt starts at $400–700+ all-in and requires hundreds of hours. This is a pro-skill project. - Steel tongue drum as handpan substitute: honest is that they're different instruments. The HAPI Omni is the closest commercial tongue drum to handpan aesthetic territory. They share a sound family; they do not sound the same.

5. Sniper and back-country notes

Dave's Island Instruments as the US handpan hub: Dii (Lakewood, CA) is the only confirmed US-based source for in-band handpan shells found in this search. They also offer rentals, private lessons, group classes, and the online building course. If you're going to try the handpan path in the US, this is the starting point.

Kita Pantam suspended: As of June 2026, kitapantam.com returns "Account Suspended." This was a previously cited shell source and is currently not available. Anyone with a saved link should verify before acting.

Mudra minimum order wall: Mudra's Mira Shells are technically priced in-band per shell (€65–70) but their minimum order of 11 shells (a box) makes them an industrial supplier, not a solo-builder resource. This minimum is explicitly stated on their site. Do not list Mudra as an option for a single-instrument build.

Ayasa is still the quality benchmark: Ayasa Instruments (Netherlands) is widely regarded as the highest-quality shell source in the community. Their pricing requires contact (no live price list). The Baur&Brown DC04 upper shell at €65 provides a useful proxy for Ayasa DC04 pricing [PLAUSIBLE; not confirmed directly]. Ayasa also offers nitrided shells and their proprietary Ember Steel, both of which would push above the band.

HAPI Tuneable drums: HAPI's tuneable line starts at $296 and allows the player to retune the drum to different pentatonic scales. This is a genuinely useful feature for someone who wants flexibility without committing to one scale. Worth investigating current models at hapidrum.co/hapi-tuneable-drums.aspx if scale flexibility matters.

Shell sourcing outside the major vendors: The handpan.org forum has active discussions about shell sourcing, including smaller and regional suppliers not captured in this search. Before committing to a build, browsing the "Developments, Creations, and Influences" section of handpan.org is the most efficient way to find current-state community knowledge on shells, materials, and tooling.

The DII online course: Dave's Island Instruments also offers a "How to Build a Handpan" course at dii.thinkific.com. Price not confirmed during this search pass [UNCERTAIN]. If going the raw-shell route, a structured course from a US maker who actually sells the shells is the most sensible learning path available in the US market.

7. Anti-default verification

Steel tongue drum: Invented in Michigan in 2007 (Western, modern). The commercial finished instrument market is predominantly US-made (HAPI) and OEM Asian (Hluru, Meinl OEM). The instrument form draws on the West African/Caribbean steel pan tradition through Havlena's stated inspiration from the Tambiro (Zimbabwean oil-drum instrument).

Handpan: Swiss origin (PANArt, 2000). The global shell-making market is Netherlands (Ayasa), Germany (Baur&Brown), Brazil (Mudra), USA (Dii), Iran (Kita — currently suspended). The instrument draws on Trinidad and Tobago steel pan acoustics and on the Zimbabwean Tambiro.

Non-Western adjacent: The steel pan tradition (Trinidad and Tobago) is the direct acoustic ancestor of both instruments in the modern sense. Any builder pursuing the handpan path seriously should study steel pan construction literature alongside handpan-specific sources; the acoustic physics overlap significantly. Secrets of the Steel Pan by Anthony Achong (1,200+ pages) is recommended by Saraz as required reading.

HALF ONE: WINDS ($150-300)

Orientation

The $150-300 wind horizon is genuinely thin for true assembly kits. The NAF kit market almost entirely lives under $150 (see QQQQQQQ); the wooden Irish flute is primarily a tool investment (reamer), not a kit; the shakuhachi making kit from NaturalMateriaStudio is real and confirmed in-band; and the PAiA Theremax — the historically canonical mid-tier wind electronics kit — is unavailable as of June 2026 because the company's website is offline following the death of founder Scott Lee on April 21, 2026.

The wind half has three genuine in-band stories: the shakuhachi tool + bamboo path, the Irish flute from-blank-and-reamer path, and a note on EWI/electronic wind DIY whose parts costs largely underrun the band floor. A separate honest note covers what happens to the NAF kit market at this price level (spoiler: you transition from build kits to finished artisan instruments).

1. Native American Flute (NAF) — Upper-Tier Honest Assessment

Origin: Indigenous North America (multiple nations, traditions). See Native American Flute and Cheap Winds for full cultural framing, IACA-1990 labeling law, and the two main kit vendors.

Close-enough bar: Same requirements as the under-$150 tier: two-chamber bore, external block mechanism, cedar construction, pentatonic-minor fingering. Nothing changes structurally in this price band; the question is what exists.

What the $150-300 range actually contains for NAF:

The Stellar Teaching Package ($41.25/unit, minimum 10) is an institutional bulk purchase, not a personal kit. If you are building multiple NAFs (for group instruction, family, or iteration), the Stellar multi-kit path lands in the band. This is not a single-instrument build; note it as such.

Etsy custom cedar kits: Individual makers on Etsy sell handmade unfinished or partially finished NAF-style cedar kits at $80-$200+, with pricing that can land in-band. Quality and authenticity vary sharply. These are maker-to-maker sales, not standardized kit products. Search: Etsy NAF flute kits. Group 2: Plans and tutorials

Same as QQQQQQQ: the Flutopedia suite, NAFlutomat, Goss Native Flute Handbook, Shands PDF. All free. Materials for a scratch-built cedar NAF total $20-60. No incremental plans path exists that reaches $150-300 for a single flute. The upper-tier scratch-build path (e.g., sourcing premium old-growth western red cedar from a specialty dealer) might reach $80-100 in materials; it does not typically reach $150 even at the premium end.

Bottom line

The NAF kit market has a hard ceiling around $120 for individual kit items (Blue Bear drone G/F#). If you are spending $150-300 on a NAF, you are buying a finished or near-finished instrument from an artisan maker, not assembling a kit. This is the honest verdict. The band is below the commercial kit market's top; it is above the point where build kits generate a distinct option space. The QQQQQQQ catalog's Pre-Bored Drone ($85) is the highest-value construction project in the NAF family short of going full scratch-build, and it is well under $150.

2. Wooden Flute from Blank + Reamer (Irish / Simple-System Path)

Origin: The Irish simple-system wooden flute is a late-18th / early-19th century European classical instrument adopted into Irish traditional music. The dominant construction model is conical-bore, typically in African blackwood, cocus wood, boxwood, or other dense hardwoods. It is an instrument with worldwide adoption through the Irish diaspora and the global Celtic music revival.

Close-enough bar: The key physical requirements: conical bore (the bore tapers from embouchure to foot, wider at top), cylindrical embouchure hole, six finger holes, and optionally one or more keys for accidentals. The simple-system flute plays a diatonic scale using covered/uncovered holes, overblows for the second octave. Articulation: transverse, embouchure-controlled, no fipple. The technique is distinctly different from the NAF (open embouchure, not a fipple instrument). The playing technique is harder than the NAF to start but lower-friction for experienced flute players.

The reamer reality. Building a wooden Irish flute from a blank is primarily a REAMER investment, not a kit purchase. The conical bore must be bored precisely and tapered correctly. This requires either: - A dedicated wood boring machine + a conical reamer (the traditional path) - A pillar drill + graduated drill bits + careful hand finishing (the accessible shop path) - A pre-bored commercial blank (eliminates the reamer requirement)

The reamer alone is the major cost variable. Quality conical reamers purpose-made for flute making are specialty tools costing $100-$300+ new; secondhand taper-pin reamers sourced from retired machinists on eBay can be had for less but require verification of taper geometry.

Voicing/tuning difficulty: Moderate-high for the bore (the taper must be right before tone-hole placement begins); high for embouchure development (an open transverse flute takes practice to voice well). Tone-hole undercutting for intonation is a real skill. This is not a one-weekend project.

Group 2: Plans + written tutorials (BOM $150-300 for first build)

BOM estimate for a first build: - Wood blank (African blackwood, 1" round stock, 60cm): $50-120 depending on source and grade - Conical reamer (used from eBay or industrial source, correct taper): $80-200+ - Tone-hole drilling jig or careful hand-drill work: minimal if you own a drill press - Ferrules, rings, mouth-plate (optional): $10-40 - Files, sandpaper, oil: $5-15

Total first-build BOM: $150-300, with the reamer as the dominant cost. Subsequent builds cost $50-120 (just the blank).

3. Wooden Recorder from Blank

Origin: Europe, broadly; the recorder (flauto dolce) has medieval and Renaissance roots across Western Europe; it was revived as an educational instrument in the 20th century through Carl Orff's influence. The sopranino, soprano, alto, tenor, and bass forms are the standard Western family. The instrument is built worldwide commercially.

Close-enough bar: Fipple (windway + splitting-edge) instrument; six tone holes plus thumb hole; internal cylindrical bore (soprano/alto) or slight taper. Playing technique is distinct from the transverse flute: no embouchure shaping needed, so easier to produce tone; intonation is controlled by breath pressure and subtle embouchure adjustment.

Post-LMII supply situation. Luthiers Mercantile International (LMII) was the main US supplier for recorder-making blanks and specialty reamers. LMII closed in late 2024 after 50+ years; their inventory was transferred in part to StewMac, but StewMac does not carry recorder-specific supplies (their focus is stringed instruments). This has removed the main US kit-supply source for the recorder-from-blank path. [ESTABLISHED — LMII closure confirmed by multiple forum discussions including ClassicalGuitarDelcamp.com and JazzGuitar.be, late 2024.]

What remains:

The reamer is still the rate-limiting expense and the MIMF community is the best live resource for current sourcing. For a first recorder build, consider starting with maple (cheap blank) and a soprano size (smaller/cheaper reamer). The fipple voicing is the real craft challenge, not the bore geometry.

4. Shakuhachi Mid-Tier: Tool Kit + Bamboo

Origin: Japan. The shakuhachi is an end-blown bamboo flute of 1.8 shaku length (54.5cm) in the root key, played with a downward angle at the open top end; the embouchure is one of the most technically demanding in the flute family. It derives from the Chinese xiao (end-blown bamboo flute) introduced to Japan in the Nara period (7th-8th century CE). The traditional Japanese shakuhachi has strong Zen Buddhist associations through the Fuke sect; a related instrument remains in use in China (dongxiao/xiao), Korea (tungso / danso), and Vietnam (tiêu). The instrument form is worldwide.

Close-enough bar: End-blown bamboo tube, no fipple; the player's lower lip placement at the notched top edge produces sound via embouchure. Five holes (four front, one back). Plays 2+ octaves via overblowing and embouchure. The embouchure is weeks-to-months to develop; this is the hardest single axis in the catalog. The bamboo itself is the second axis: "one in a thousand good reeds" in the ney tradition applies here too. Good madake bamboo that plays well after making is rare.

The mid-tier problem. The Mejiro Co. (Japan) offered a comprehensive shakuhachi making kit at approximately $900 USD, now sold out and not replaced at that price. No shakuhachi making kit in the $150-300 band is currently confirmed from a single commercial source. What IS in-band is:

5. Electronic Wind: PAiA Theremax and EWI/MIDI Wind DIY

Origin: Electronic wind instruments as a category date to the 1970s; the EWI (Electronic Wind Instrument) was commercialized by Akai in the 1980s. PAiA Electronics (Oklahoma City, USA) pioneered DIY electronic music kits from 1967 onward. The REMI (Recorder Electronic Musical Instrument) is a 2010s maker community project from Australia. MiniWI is a Nordic open-source project.

Close-enough bar for the electronic wind: The playing technique must require a breath control sensor (or breath pressure transducer) and finger-based tone-hole control (capacitive touch pads or physical tone holes), producing MIDI output or audio directly. A breath-controller-only keyboard device is not an EWI. The technique involves actual breath-based articulation, which makes it wind-adjacent.

PAiA Theremax: status as of June 2026

The PAiA Theremax is — or was — a DIY theremin/wind-controller kit historically priced at approximately $180-200 USD shipped, firmly in-band. It was produced by PAiA Electronics, the longest-running US DIY electronic music kit company. PAiA.com is currently offline. PAiA founder Scott Lee died on April 21, 2026; his son Nathan Lee has stated he is working to restore operations, but the site and order processing are suspended as of this writing (June 2026).

Note: The Theremax is technically a theremin (optical/proximity control), not a wind instrument. It was included in the brief as a "wind-adjacent" example of mid-tier electronics kits. A theremin with a breath control attachment would be a closer analog; the Theremax does not require breath to play.

Flag for Mark: If PAiA restores operations and the Theremax kit re-appears, it is a legitimate in-band kit at its historical price. Monitor paia.com. [ESTABLISHED kit exists at historical price; UNAVAILABLE to order as of 2026-06-05]

HALF TWO: PERCUSSION ($150-300)

Orientation

The $150-300 percussion half has clearer in-band options than the winds half. Cedar Mountain Drums occupies the core of the frame-drum story, confirmed at $155-$250. The djembe shell-kit path from Djembe Drums & Skins lands just in-band at the large size. The cajon build-kit market tops out well below $150 (the Meinl MYO-CAJ at $59.99 is the reference floor; no premium cajon BUILD kit in $150-300 has been found). The marimba side has the makeamarimba.com P2 Mini-Marimba whose total build (plan + materials) runs $240-$340. The McNeela bodhran kit is under $150 and does not belong in this tier. The steel tongue drum and handpan are reserved for Worker IIIIIIII and not duplicated here. The kalimba DIY kit market maxes out around $60-80 for individual kits, well below the band floor.

Cross-check: the under-$150 catalogs (RRRRRRR and YYYYYYY) documented the Centralia Fur & Hide kits fully; this catalog notes only the sizes and species that breach $150 and land in-band.

1. Cedar Mountain Drums — Native Rawhide Frame/Hand Drum Kits

Origin: Indigenous North American; multiple nations. Cedar Mountain Drums, operated by Patrick Pinson (of Mingo heritage), has sold traditional-style drum kits since 1989 from Portland, Oregon. The kit form produces a single-headed rawhide frame drum in the North American hand-drum tradition. See RRRRRRR for full cultural context and the lower-tier frame drum field.

Close-enough bar: Same as the RRRRRRR Native rawhide entry — stretched rawhide over bent wood frame, laced wet and dried tight. No pitch; timbre set by drying tension. Beater plays the drum seated or standing. The Cedar Mountain distinction from Wandering Bull and Centralia is species quality, rim material, and the maker's cultural grounding.

Why Cedar Mountain is in this catalog and not RRRRRRR: All Cedar Mountain kits are $155-$250 for standard kits and $200-$300 for hoop & frame drum kits — the entire product line exceeds $150. RRRRRRR flagged them as over-budget and listed them for context. This catalog covers them fully.

Group 1: Kits

Hoop & Frame Drum Kits: $155-$250. Includes pre-cut rawhide head (species choice below), rim (deodar cedar, willow oak, or yellow cedar), hand-cut rawhide lacing, beater makings, and complete instructions. Sizes range from 12" through 20" (multiple rim options: 13", 14", 16", 17", 18", 20"). [ESTABLISHED — confirmed from search results 2026-06-05]

Hoop & Frame Drums (Made-to-Order finished instruments): $155-$245. Not a kit; included for orientation on what the finished equivalent costs relative to the kit.

Species option Price modifier

Note on rawhide species: All four species are offered. Buffalo hide produces a deeper, heavier timbre. Deer is the most commonly chosen for tone and workability.

US source: cedarmountaindrums.com/product/hoop-drum-kits/

Build process: Soak the rawhide; lace it wet across the frame following Patrick's instructions; let dry 1-2 days. 3-6 hours hands-on. No tools required beyond scissors and a soaking bucket. Patrick Pinson has documented the process in videos at cedarmountaindrums.com/about-drumming/drum-making-with-patrick-pinson/ — these are tradition-informed and worth watching before starting.

Bottom line

Cedar Mountain is the only kit vendor in the frame-drum field run by a maker of Native heritage, and the entire product line is within the $150-300 band. If artisan quality and tradition-grounded context matter in this build, Cedar Mountain is the choice. The instrument itself is the same construction approach as the Wandering Bull and Centralia kits; what changes is the maker's background and the rim material quality (deodar cedar is a step up from standard steam-bent maple).
