3. Bodhran — Honest Assessment for the $150-300 Band

Origin: Ireland. The bodhran is a shallow single-headed frame drum, typically 14"-18" in diameter, with a skin (traditionally goat) stretched over a circular wooden frame. It is the primary percussion instrument in Irish traditional music. The making process parallels Native rawhide frame drums: soak, stretch, dry.

The $150-300 problem. The only confirmed commercial bodhran BUILD kit from a major vendor is the McNeela Music DIY Bodhran Kit at $75 USD — confirmed from the product page metadata (meta-product:price:amount: 75, currency: USD) as of 2026-06-05. [ESTABLISHED] This is significantly under $150. McNeela's kit includes webbing, elastic band, and written instructions. It does not appear to include a full pre-bent frame + goatskin head combination; it is a finishing/assembly kit for a basic drum.

No bodhran BUILD kit priced $150-300 was found in this research pass from any major supplier (McNeela, Custy's, Roundstone, Etsy). The bodhran kit market, like the NAF market, lives below the band floor.

Component-path bodhran in $150-300: A quality bodhran can be built from components at this price level: - Turned or steam-bent ash/beech frame (14"-18"): $40-80 (Etsy makers, specialist suppliers) - Goatskin head, already mounted, from a luthier supplier: $30-60 - Tipper (beater): $10-30 - Total: ~$80-170 for a full-size build depending on frame and skin source

But this is component sourcing, not a kit purchase. The bodhran making community is thinner on documentation than the NAF or frame-drum communities. Resources: the Chiff & Fipple forum covers bodhran making sporadically; the MIMF has threads.

Roundstone Drum Company (Connemara, Ireland) makes premium bodhrans by hand; finished instruments run $150-500. These are not kits. Listed for orientation on what a well-made bodhran costs at this price level. [PLAUSIBLE; existence confirmed; US shipping details UNCERTAIN]

Honest verdict: If you want to build a bodhran in the $150-300 band, the path is component sourcing (frame + goatskin + tipper) rather than a commercial kit. The McNeela kit at $75 is the only confirmed commercial option and it is under budget. This tier is genuinely thin for bodhran BUILD kits.

4. Djembe — Shell + Rehead Build Path

Origin: West Africa. The djembe is a rope-tuned goblet drum played with the hands, associated primarily with the Mandé people of West Africa (Guinea, Mali, Burkina Faso, Ivory Coast, and neighboring countries). It has spread globally through African music instruction and world-music communities. The construction is: a carved hardwood shell (traditionally lenké, djalla, iroko, or mahogany), a goatskin head stretched over the shell with steel rings, and vertically running rope under extreme tension that holds the head in place and sets the pitch.

Close-enough bar: The djembe technique (bass/tone/slap with both hands on a single head) must carry. A djembe shell with head but poor rope tension is not a djembe; the tension system is essential to the sound. A build from a raw shell requires: fitting the crown ring + base ring correctly, threading the rope, and tensioning (traditional rope-pull technique or a rope-puller tool).

This is not a beginner build (even with all skills assumed): the bearing edge must be correctly shaped before heading, and achieving proper rope tension requires significant physical effort (rope pulling is often a multi-person or multi-tool task). The build is achievable; it is time-intensive.

Group 1: Shell + Kit Build Path

The main US vendor in this space is Djembe Drums & Skins (Sevierville, TN; formerly goatskins.com, now djembedrumsandskins.com).

Ghana Full Kit at large size (~$175) is the in-band option. The Ivory Coast shell alone ($220-280) is in-band for the shell, but you'd still need to add rope ($15-30) and goatskin ($20-40) to complete the build, pushing over $300 for a complete Ivory Coast build.

What you still need to do: Rope-tensioning. The shell comes with rope included in the "Full Kit" option, but tension is the skill: - Traditional method: tie the vertical ropes, then work the diamond-pattern horizontals by hand (hours of pulling) - Tool path: rope-puller tool from Djembe Direct (~$20-30) makes this achievable solo - Rope puller: djembedirect.com/double-djembe-drum-rope-puller/

Bottom line

The Ghana full kit (large, ~$175) is the most achievable in-band djembe build. The Ivory Coast shells are premium but most complete builds exceed $300 in total. The rope-tensioning step is the real labor investment; budget 3-6 hours and a rope-puller tool. The result is a genuine West African rope-tuned djembe.

5. Struck Bars: makeamarimba.com Project 2 (P2) Two-Octave Mini-Marimba

Origin: Marimba — African origins via multiple transmission paths; the modern concert marimba is a Western/Mexican hybrid of African and Indigenous American struck-bar traditions. The P2 Mini-Marimba is a contemporary US/Australian design intended as a stepping-stone between classroom xylophones and concert instruments.

Close-enough bar: The playing technique (mallets, bilateral, struck bars) is the same as any marimba or xylophone. The P2 uses individual PVC pipe resonators (one per note) tuned to the correct length for each bar — the hallmark of a proper marimba vs. a box-resonated classroom xylophone. Two chromatic octaves.

The tuning axis (from YYYYYYY): Bar tuning = undercut the bar underside to lower pitch (more material removed from center = lower fundamental; material from ends = lower overtones). The P2's 45-minute included video covers bar tuning for the harmonics. This is a genuine craft skill, not an assembly task.

The P2 is the best documented tuned-percussion build in the $150-300 zone (or just over it). The plan is cheap; the materials are the investment. The result is a two-octave marimba that stands up for adult playing and is meaningfully superior to box-resonated classroom instruments. The bar-tuning step (covered in the video) is the real craft skill and the thing to study before starting.

6. Cajon — Honest Upper-Tier Assessment

Origin: Peru, Afro-Peruvian tradition. See YYYYYYY for full origin and technique details.

The $150-300 build-kit problem. The Meinl MYO-CAJ kit at $59.99 (confirmed at Sweetwater, June 2026) is the most capable commercial cajon BUILD kit available anywhere. The Schlagwerk MyCajon kits (German, includes adhesive, ~90-minute build) are in the same range. Both are fully under $150.

No premium cajon BUILD kit in $150-300 has been confirmed. What exists at this price level is: - Finished performance cajons with built-in pickups, pedal hardware, or internal snare adjustment systems (these are buy-not-build) - A from-plans premium cajon with better materials than the standard kit: figured maple or ovangkol tapa, premium snare wires, a bass port or speaker port

From-plans premium cajon BOM estimate (upper tier): - 1/2" Baltic birch (body panels): $20-40 - Premium figured or exotic tapa (3-4mm): $20-60 (ovangkol, wenge, zebrawood plank) - Professional snare wire set: $15-30 - Hardware (bolts, L-brackets, sandpaper, finish): $10-20 - Optional: pickup + jack for amplification: $10-30 - Total: $75-180 depending on wood choice

This from-plans premium build can land in the $100-180 range with quality tapa — the lower end of the band. No kit vendor provides this at $150-300; it is a material-upgrade from the from-plans path documented in YYYYYYY.

Honest verdict: The cajon BUILD category is genuinely thin in the $150-300 band. The kit market is fully served by under-$150 options. If you want to spend $150-300 on a cajon BUILD, the path is: use the from-plans designs in YYYYYYY, but upgrade the tapa to a premium figured wood and add a pickup. No boxed kit exists for this.

7. Kalimba and Metallophone — Honest Upper-Tier Assessment

Kalimba DIY kit market ceiling: The OEM 17-key kalimba DIY kit market ($22-45 for kits from Kmise, Donner, and other labels) and the bolt-and-board approach ($10-15) covered in YYYYYYY have no equivalent BUILD kits in the $150-300 range. The closest thing to "better kalimba for $150-300" is a handmade finished kalimba from an artisan maker (Etsy, Africa Heartwood Project, etc.), which is a buy-not-build purchase.

Metallophone/glockenspiel bar sets: The classroom metallophone market (Studio 49, Sonor Global Beat) lands in the $80-130 range for finished diatonic instruments — under $150. No build kit for a metallophone in $150-300 was found; the aluminum-bar-stock approach from YYYYYYY costs $20-50 in materials.

Honest verdict: Both categories are genuinely thin as BUILD options in this band. The kit markets are well under $150; the $150-300 tier for both is the finished-instrument market, not the build-kit market.

Orientation: what this probe is for

The under-$150 fire (CCCCCCCC) established clearly that no acoustic historical keyboard has a build path under $150. This fire probes the next band: does anything change at $150–300?

The honest answer is: almost nothing. The clavichord is the one instrument with a theoretical toehold in this band, and even that toehold is partial. This file documents that partial path fully and then closes the file on harpsichords, virginals, spinets, and organs with a confirmed floor and a pointer to the right source.

A well-documented "this tier doesn't really exist for historical acoustic keyboards, here's why and here's where the floor actually is" is a successful deliverable for this probe. That is what this file delivers.

1. Clavichord: The Honest Probe

Origin: Europe (Germany, Netherlands, England), 14th century onward. The simplest keyed string instrument: a lever key lifts a brass tangent that strikes a string pair, which also frets the string length — both sounding the note and determining pitch simultaneously. No jacks, no quills, no escapement. The simplest keyboard action in Western history.

Why it's the target of this probe: The clavichord is the cheapest historical keyboard to build because it has the fewest parts, the simplest action mechanism, and the smallest materials requirement. It is the only instrument in this family where a $150–300 total is even theoretically discussable.

Close-enough bar: A clavichord IS a clavichord — there is no cheap substitute that transfers the technique. The tangent-strike action and the resulting ability to apply vibrato (Bebung) by varying key pressure are unique to the clavichord. A MIDI keyboard is NOT a clavichord. A DIY string instrument is NOT a clavichord. This is an all-or-nothing instrument: either you build the actual thing or there is nothing in this band. This is flagged plainly here because the under-$150 MIDI path in CCCCCCCC is the real cheap keyboard path — it just does not produce a historical keyboard.

1.1 The Kit Market: VOID in this band

No clavichord kit is available for $150–300, or anywhere close.

The floor of the commercial kit market: - Zuckermann "King of Sweden" fretted clavichord (smallest kit): Stage 1 = $2,329, Stage 3 = $3,665, finished = $6,740. [ESTABLISHED] — verified live June 2026 at zhi.net. - Carl Fudge / Charles Wolff "Small Clavichord" (Stonington, CT; clavichords.com): prices not published on the website, contact required. Historically priced around $1,300–1,500 based on community reports; likely higher now. [UNCERTAIN] on current price; [ESTABLISHED] that the firm is operating and offers three kit models (Small, Schiedmayer, Hubert). Contact: info@clavichords.com. - The Paris Workshop via distributors: cheapest clavichord kit is £3,995 (EMS) / AUD $7,100 (Carey Beebe). [ESTABLISHED]

The kit floor is approximately $1,500–2,300 at the very bottom of a thin market. The $150–300 band is not relevant for kits. There is no path here.

1.2 Plans: The One Thing That Fits in the Band

Plans DO fit in the $150–300 band. The plan itself — a dimensioned measured drawing of a historical instrument — is the one genuine in-band purchase for clavichord building. The plan does not build the instrument; it is the starting point for a materials-sourcing and fabrication project whose total cost is higher.

1.3 Specialty Components: Also (Partly) In-Band

When you build from plans, you source your own materials. Some of the specialty components — parts you cannot fabricate at home and cannot get at a hardware store — can be purchased in-band or near-band:

Component Source Price Notes
Clavichord tangents (brass, 3 sizes) Zuckermann Harpsichords (zhi.net) from $5.50 per set [ESTABLISHED] Small (0.16" W × 0.03" T), Medium (0.20" W × 0.05" T), Large (0.22" W × 0.07" T). A small fretted clavichord needs a mix of sizes; budget $12–20 for a complete set.
Music wire (raw spool) Zuckermann Harpsichords $22.59 (300" coil) / $66.50 (4 oz spool) [ESTABLISHED] A 4 oz spool covers most of a small fretted clavichord's stringing needs. Raw wire is significantly cheaper than pre-made string sets ($142+ for a single-choir set). Raw wire requires a stringing plan (Hekkelman's free online tool or Brauchli's tables) to calculate correct gauges.
Clavichord listing cloth (damping cloth) Zuckermann Harpsichords from $7.50 [ESTABLISHED] The woven cloth that damps the strings between the bridge and the hitchpins. Small amount needed; in-band.
Specialty components via Marc Vogel GmbH vogel-scheer.de Varies; ships internationally Tangents, strings, tuning pins, bridge pins, felt, cloth — all available. German language on some pages; products are clear from context. Comparable prices to Zuckermann for most items.

Non-specialty components (your sourcing problem): The wood is the expensive gap. A small fretted clavichord requires: - Case lumber (cherry, walnut, pine, or poplar): ~$35–80 depending on species and how it's milled. Pine and poplar are inexpensive; cherry adds $30–50+. - Soundboard (quarter-sawn spruce or solid pine): ~$20–50 from a specialty tonewood supplier (or pine from a hardware store as the adblom.net builder used, which is a deviation from the historical form but functional). - Key levers (basswood, lime, or similar): ~$15–30 for a blank. - Key coverings (boxwood, pear, ebony, or substitutes): ~$10–25. - Tuning pins (wrest pins): ~$20–35 for a complete set. - Balance and guide pins: small hardware; ~$10–20. - Hide glue: ~$10–15. - Finish (oil, shellac, or paint): ~$15–25. - Misc hardware (hinges, screws): ~$10–20.

1.4 The Complete-Build BOM Reality

Can a complete playable clavichord be built for $150–300?

Working through the numbers:

Category Low end High end Notes
Plans $54 $107 Marc Vogel ~€49–98
Case lumber (pine/poplar) $35 $60 Cherry adds $20–40
Soundboard (pine or spruce) $20 $50 Pine: cheap + functional; spruce: ~$35–50 from tonewood supplier
Key levers (basswood) $15 $30
Key coverings $10 $25
Wire spool (4 oz) $22 $67 4 oz Zuckermann spool ($66.50); raw wire only
Tuning/wrest pins $20 $35
Tangents $11 $20 2–3 sets at $5.50/set
Balance + guide pins $10 $20 Small hardware
Listing cloth + felt $15 $25
Hide glue + finish $20 $35
Misc hardware $10 $20
TOTAL ~$242 ~$494

Honest read: - The low end (~$242) requires: sourcing pine instead of cherry or spruce everywhere possible, using small raw-wire spools instead of pre-made string sets, minimal hardware spend, and a very small instrument (4-octave fretted form). - The high end (~$494) uses slightly better materials but is still quite economical. - The $150–300 band covers a complete build only at the very bottom of this estimate, and only if you already have lumber scraps, use the cheapest possible materials everywhere, and get the soundboard cheaply (pine or salvaged). - For most people, sourcing from scratch, the total lands $250–400+. The $300 ceiling clips the very bottom of a careful build. - No builder has published a documented BOM at under $300 for a complete playable clavichord. The adblom.net build does not include a cost breakdown. The absence of sub-$300 build reports is itself evidence that the threshold is real.

Confidence tag: [PLAUSIBLE] that a $250–280 total is achievable with excellent sourcing; [UNCERTAIN] that $150–220 works for a complete instrument; [ESTABLISHED] that $300+ is where most documented builds land or exceed.

1.5 Bottom Line: Clavichord

  • Plans fit in-band ($54–107 from Marc Vogel, Edinburgh, or Zuckermann). This is a real purchase.
  • Specialty components fit in-band (~$60–130 for wire + tangents + listing cloth + pins). These are real purchases.
  • Plans + specialty components = ~$120–240, which fits the $150–300 band. You can genuinely buy everything except the wood for under $300.
  • A complete functional instrument from scratch most likely lands $250–400+ with careful sourcing. The $300 ceiling catches only the very frugal end of this range.
  • The cheapest commercial kit is $1,500–2,329 — a full order of magnitude above this band.
  • The honest path for someone with $150–300: Buy the plans now (Marc Vogel Wahlstrom plan, ~€49–98) and the specialty components (wire, tangents, listing cloth, ~$65–100). Save the difference for the wood. Total project likely runs $280–400 when complete. This band gets you started.

Confidence: [ESTABLISHED] on kit prices; [ESTABLISHED] on plan/component prices; [PLAUSIBLE] on complete-instrument BOM total (no published sub-$300 build report found; estimates extrapolated from component prices and one documented build that omits a total).

Key resource: Maarten Hekkelman's free online clavichord stringing calculator at hekkelman.com/bouwershoek (Dutch; self-explanatory with instrument dimensions input). The adblom.net builder explicitly credits Hekkelman's personal guidance as critical; the tool automates the string-gauge planning that would otherwise require Brauchli's tables.

2. Harpsichord, Virginal, Spinet: Confirmed Over-Band

Nothing in the $150–300 range. This is said once and not expanded.

Floor for the harpsichord family: - Zuckermann Flemish Single kit (Stage 2, smallest harpsichord kit): $6,933 [ESTABLISHED] - TPW Delin Spinet (cheapest virginal/spinet kit): £5,195 (~$6,500) [ESTABLISHED] - Plans (Edinburgh, Marc Vogel): plans fit in-band at $49–109, but building a harpsichord from plans requires a soundboard, jacks, plectra, strings, wrestplank, case lumber (a bentside requires steam-bending or compound bending), and full voicing — materials totaling $800–2,000+, regardless of the plan cost. The plan is not the obstacle; the BOM is.

Is there any partial-component path at $150–300 for harpsichords? No. Unlike the clavichord (where tangents are cheap brass pins and strings are standard music wire), harpsichord jacks with plectra require voicing skill and either commercial jacks ($150+ for a set) or fabrication from scratch. A complete harpsichord jack set from Zuckermann exceeds the top of this band before any other components are purchased. There is no partial path that produces a playable instrument.

For full harpsichord/virginal/spinet kit and plan detail: see Historical and Mechanical Keyboard Kits and Plans.md (FFFFFFF).

3. Reed Organ / Harmonium: Cross-Reference

Reed organs, pump organs, and harmoniums are not covered in this fire. The free-reed keyboard family has its own entry in Build Catalog - Other Winds and Free Reed.md (OOOOOOOO), Section 2.4 and adjacent.

The short note from that file's findings: harmonium rebuild/restore from a donor instrument is the practical path (no build kit confirmed); melodica has no build path; accordion is overwhelmingly a rebuild/restore hobby with one niche UK kit far above $300. None of these have in-band ($150–300) build paths from scratch.

4. The Honest Call

Historical acoustic keyboards at $150–300: the tier barely exists, and here is why.

The structural reason is materials cost, not complexity cost. A clavichord can be built by a novice woodworker (the adblom.net build proves this). The barrier is not skill; it is that wood, wire, and specialty hardware for a keyboard instrument add up. Even the simplest historical keyboard — a 4-octave fretted clavichord — requires enough specialized materials that $150–300 covers only part of the build.

What this band actually buys you:

(a) The clavichord plans + specialty components (~$150–240): Buy the Marc Vogel Wahlstrom plan (~€49, the cheapest entry-level option) plus a 4 oz wire spool ($66.50), a set of tangents (~$12), and listing cloth (~$8). This gets you everything except the wood. Total: ~$155–200. The wood adds another $80–150+. This is a real in-band use of the budget that puts the build in motion.

(b) The digital/MIDI path (the actual cheap keyboard): If the goal is a playable keyboard instrument for $150–300, Build Catalog - Keyboard and Mechanical.md (CCCCCCCC) is the answer. A 25-key OEM keybed + Teensy + free firmware produces a velocity-sensitive MIDI keyboard for $50–100. It is not a historical keyboard, but it is a real keyboard instrument for a fraction of the clavichord's material cost.

(c) The over-band kit floor (when budget grows): The cheapest confirmed kit clavichord is the Zuckermann "King of Sweden" at $2,329 Stage 1. Budget target for that is $2,400–2,500 (Stage 1 kit + shipping + minor supplies). Everything below that is a from-plans build — achievable, documented, but more expensive in total than it looks from the plan price alone.

5. Confidence Audit

  • Evidence quality: Strong on commercial kit prices (Zuckermann, TPW via EMS and CBH all verified live June 2026); Strong on plan prices (Edinburgh, Vogel, Zuckermann drawings all confirmed); Moderate on from-scratch BOM totals (component prices are confirmed, but no published complete sub-$300 build account exists; the total is extrapolated from component prices); Weak on the low end of the $242–494 BOM range (the low end requires assumptions about sourcing that are not backed by a published build account).
  • Biggest confidence limiter: No builder has published a complete materials cost for a clavichord built from plans. The BOM estimate above is assembled from component prices only. The actual total for a specific builder may vary significantly depending on what wood they have on hand, what shipping costs they incur, and what small miscellaneous hardware they source locally. The $250–400 range is a reasonable estimate, not a verified figure.

PART ONE: NON-WESTERN ART STRINGS ($150-300)

1. Oud (Arabic/Ottoman Bowl-Back Lute) -- THE HEADLINE

Band win: Under $150, oud was a genuine void; the cheapest documented parts approach (from scratch) ran $400+ in materials just for the bowl. At $150-300, Ethnic Musical's pre-staved oud bowls from Izmir, Turkey unlock a real bowl-back oud build by skipping the hardest single step in oud making: bending and laminating the staves.

Path state: REAL BUILD (bowl + parts route; total lands approximately $250-$310 depending on bowl in-stock status)

Origin: Arab/Ottoman/North African/Hellenic tradition. Central melodic instrument of the Arab world. 5-double-course (typically 11 strings, 5 courses plus single bass string), fretless, plectrum-struck, deep bowl resonance.

Close-enough bar: What must transfer: the deep bowl-back resonance chamber, the fretless neck for microtonal playing, plectrum (risha) technique. What this parts build requires beyond the bowl: fitting and gluing a soundboard, installing tuning pegs, making or sourcing a neck, setting nut and bridge. This is a real luthiery project. The bowl is done; the instrument is not.

The bottleneck under $150: Stave-bending an oud bowl from kiln-dried tone wood requires bending irons, molds, and precision work. No kit bypassed this under $150. Ethnic Musical's pre-staved bowls remove that wall.

2. Erhu / Jinghu (Chinese Huqin Spike Fiddles) -- Real Instrument Tier

Band win: Under $150, the documented paths were tin-can builds and coconut builds at $5-25 in materials (Folk Strings Worldwide, Worker LLLLLLL). At $150-300, you can buy a genuine mid-grade student instrument with a real rosewood resonator, proper synthetic membrane (no CITES issues), a functioning bow, and factory setup. The step from improvised to instrument is real and audible.

Path state: BUY-FINISHED (step-up student instrument; no kit or self-build path exists at this level)

Origin: Chinese huqin family; erhu is the two-string soprano spike fiddle central to Chinese opera, folk, and classical music. Jinghu is the higher-pitched variant used in Beijing opera. (Full erhu context including CITES/python-skin background is in Folk Strings Worldwide, Worker LLLLLLL.)

Close-enough bar: What carries forward from the tin-can builds: bow-between-strings technique, two strings, same open-string tuning, same body-between-knees playing position. What the mid-grade instrument adds: real rosewood or sandalwood resonator (vs. tin can), proper bow tension and weight, factory-set bridge height, better intonation across the fingerboard, durable synthetic skin membrane that does not require humidity management.

CITES note first: Synthetic membrane instruments avoid the python-skin CITES documentation requirement entirely. No import paperwork needed. This is the primary selection criterion at this level, not acoustic preference; traditional python-skin instruments from China would require CITES permits for US import.

3. Guzheng (Chinese 21-String Zither)

Band win (limited): Under $150, the path was a build from GuzhengAlive free plans (~$85-150 in materials). At $150-300, the question is whether a finished student instrument is reachable. The answer is: technically yes at the price, but with serious quality caveats. The build path from the under-$150 catalog remains the better option.

Path state: BUY-FINISHED (toy-grade caveat; quality floor not met until ~$500; build path still superior)

Origin: Chinese classical tradition. 21-string movable-bridge zither, paulownia soundboard, steel strings with nylon wrap, right-hand finger picks, left-hand pressure bends for ornamentation and vibrato.

Close-enough bar: A finished budget guzheng vs. the GuzhengAlive build: same 21-string layout, same technique, same tuning system. The close-enough question is whether a $150-300 factory instrument is a genuine learnable instrument or a display piece. GuzhengAlive's own cost-of-ownership analysis answers this directly.

Honest assessment from GuzhengAlive (primary authority on this instrument): GuzhengAlive's pricing tier analysis states that instruments below $350-400 are typically what the site calls "decorative" or "toy-grade": thin paulownia soundboard that warps, poor string spacing, non-playable action out of the box, and tuning pegs that slip. The legitimate student tier in the US begins at approximately $500-700 from established vendors (Sound of China, GuzhengAlive-recommended sellers). Amazon listings at $150-250 are frequently in the toy-grade category. This is a genuine quality gap, not snobbery.

5. Tanpura / Tampura (Drone Lute) -- Better Electronic Substitute

Path state: SUBSTITUTE (electronic drone box; physical build remains a genuine void)

Origin: North and South Indian classical tradition. Open drone lute, 4-6 strings, no frets, only played as a continuous drone beneath a soloist. Gourd-body construction with GI (geographical indication) protection in Miraj.

Close-enough bar: The electronic substitute serves the musical function (drone reference pitch) completely. What it cannot replicate: the specific overtone bloom of a gourd-body tanpura, which is itself the aesthetic point of the instrument for raga performance. For a practitioner or student, the electronic box is the appropriate tool; for a purist performance context, nothing replaces the acoustic instrument.

PART TWO: ELECTRONIC AND SYNTH DIY ($150-300)

Sound-role labels are mandatory in this section. Every entry states what the device DOES, not just what it is called.

Band framing: The under-$150 Electronic and Synth DIY catalog (Worker SSSSSSS) covered: MFOS builds, mki x es.EDU module kits (~$74-85 each), AI Synthesis kits, Zlob, North Coast, HAGIWO, the Gakken SX-150, Music Thing Startup, Baby8 sequencer, theremin options (APC, bare-bones builds), and circuit bending. This file picks up where those items capped out: assembled no-solder semi-synths that landed above $150, the legitimate kit theremin options above the APC tier, Eurorack modules above the EDU/budget line, and multi-module rack strategies.

Tariff context (June 2026): Section 122 global tariff (15%) is in effect through approximately July 19, 2026, then likely lapses. EU and Swiss kits: approximately 15-20% total above the listed EUR/GBP price. Czech Republic (Bastl): same. UK (Thonk/Befaco): post-Brexit MFN plus S122, similar range. Verify before ordering; the tariff situation may change before you buy. All landed-cost estimates in this section are [PLAUSIBLE] unless otherwise tagged.

1. Korg Nu:Tekt NTS-1 mkII

Sound role: Digital synth voice. Two-oscillator digital synth with multi-mode filter, digital effects (reverb, delay, modulation), 16-step sequencer, and mini keyboard. Fully playable self-contained instrument. Plugin ecosystem extends it to a platform.

Origin: Japan (Korg, Tokyo). The NTS-1 concept is a complete synth sold in kit form, where "kit" means snapping four PCB units into a case with no soldering. It is fully assembled in 15-30 minutes. The mkII is the 2023-onward version with updated oscillator architecture and improved effects.

Close-enough bar: What you get: a real synth chain (oscillators plus filter plus effects plus keyboard) with sequencing and external MIDI control. What you trade: the oscillators and filter are digital rather than analog (important for some use cases, irrelevant for others); the keyboard is small and the keys are tiny for expressive playing. Still a real instrument, not a noise toy.

The plugin ecosystem is the differentiator: The NTS-1 platform (both mkI and mkII) supports community-developed oscillator and effect plugins via the logue SDK. Dozens of free plugins are available (search "NTS-1 user oscillator" on GitHub or the KVR Audio forum). This turns the device into a platform rather than a fixed architecture.

3. Open Theremin V4.5 (OpenTheremin Deluxe Bundle)

Sound role: Analog theremin pitch and volume. Proximity-controlled sine-wave pitch via RF heterodyning (right hand), proximity-controlled volume via separate antenna circuit (left hand). No physical contact with the instrument. CV pitch and gate outputs for Eurorack integration.

Origin: Switzerland (Urs Gaudenz, GaudiLabs, Zurich). Open-source hardware under GNU license. The most thoroughly documented, community-supported analog theremin kit available anywhere.

Band context: The under-$150 catalog noted the V4.5 was borderline over budget at approximately €129/$141. Current pricing for the Deluxe Bundle is €189-239, which puts it firmly in the $150-300 band (approximately $200-260 USD). This is the primary theremin kit recommendation in this catalog.

Close-enough bar: What transfers from a classic Moog-style theremin: true heterodyning (the pitch is generated by beating two RF oscillators, not sample playback or digital synthesis). What the Open Theremin is: a genuine analog theremin with the authentic playing behavior (proximity sensitivity, volume control, exponential response curve). What it is not: a digital theremin (pitch tracking via capacitance sensing with sampled tones). Setup requires calibration with trimmer pots. An enclosure is not included; plan to build or buy one.

The CV outputs are a significant differentiator: Pitch CV and gate outputs let the theremin control Eurorack modules as an expressive controller, turning it into a generative synthesis input beyond its standalone audio output.

Group 2: Build from open-source schematic (cheaper path)

The OpenTheremin design is GNU-licensed. Full schematic and Arduino firmware are on GitHub: github.com/GaudiLabs/OpenThereminV3. Order the PCB from JLCPCB (~$5-15), source components from Mouser or Tayda Electronics (~$40-60), use an Arduino UNO (~$25). Estimated parts total: $70-100. This is the from-schematic path that sits below the under-$150 floor for the DIY-comfortable builder; the Deluxe Bundle is for those who want pre-sourced parts and confirmed component values.

Calibration note: Budget 2-3 hours beyond assembly for calibration. Trimmer pots control pitch antenna sensitivity and volume antenna response. The open-theremin.com documentation walks through this; a chromatic tuner app and patience are sufficient.

Bottom line: This is the serious theremin kit for this band. The CV outputs (pitch plus gate) are a material differentiator for anyone also building Eurorack. Best documentation in the hobby, genuine analog heterodyning, and a strong community. Build from the GitHub schematic if you want to come in under $100 in parts.

4. PAiA Theremax -- HISTORICAL NOTE (currently unavailable)

Sound role: Analog theremin with CV/gate output. Was the primary recommendation for pitch-plus-volume theremin kits with the best CV integration in this band.

Critical status change (June 2026): Scott Lee, founder of PAiA Electronics (Edmond, Oklahoma), died April 21, 2026. paia.com is currently offline. Nathan Lee (his son) is evaluating whether and how to continue operations. The Theremax kit is not available for purchase as of this writing.

Historical context: The Theremax full kit (electronics, PCB, silkscreened faceplate, antennas, wooden lectern case) was historically priced under $200 shipped. It was well-reviewed for CV/gate output quality and praised in Tape Op's synthesizer coverage. The PAiA FatMan and Gnome kits were also notable catalog items from the same company.

The schematic: The Theremax schematic is documented in the PAiA archive; whether it remains accessible depends on whether paia.com comes back online. The Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) has partial PAiA archives; search for "PAiA Theremax schematic" to assess what was captured before the site went offline.

Flag for Mark: Check paia.com periodically. If PAiA resumes under Nathan Lee, the Theremax would be the preferred theremin kit in this band for Eurorack users (better CV quality than Open Theremin in reviewer assessments). If the company does not resume, Open Theremin V4.5 (above) is the replacement pick.

5. Moog Mavis -- OVER BAND (flag only)

Sound role: Complete patchable analog mono synth voice. One VCO (saw wave with variable pulse width), Moog ladder filter (VCF), VCA, envelope generator (ADSR), LFO, 48-point patchbay for modular routing. Fully self-contained; no rack, no case required. No-solder assembly.

Price: $349 MSRP [ESTABLISHED] -- $49 over the $300 ceiling.

The Mavis is listed because the brief explicitly flagged it and because it is the single most capable no-solder analog patchable synth kit available in or near this band. The 48-point patchbay transforms it from a fixed-architecture synth into an educational tool for modular synthesis concepts and semi-modular routing. It also accepts and outputs CV/gate for Eurorack integration.

If Mark can stretch $50 from the ceiling: this is the call. The gap between the NTS-1 mkII ($199.99, digital) and the Mavis ($349, fully analog patchable) is qualitative, not just price-proportional.

If the budget is firm at $300: The NTS-1 mkII is the next-best option. For the modular path, the EDU module cluster strategy (below) builds toward the same educational goal through modular construction rather than a self-contained instrument.

6. Eurorack DIY Module Kits -- Mid-Tier Makers and Starter Rack Strategy

Sound role: Module-dependent. A single Eurorack module does not make a musical instrument. A playable voice requires at minimum: an oscillator (tone source) plus a VCA (gating) plus a trigger or envelope generator. A case and power supply are required and not covered by any module kit below.

Band framing: The under-$150 catalog covered: mki x es.EDU series ($74-85 per module), AI Synthesis ($59-145 per module), Kassutronics PCB sets, HAGIWO from-schematic builds ($6-8 in parts per board), Music Thing Startup (~$85), Baby8 sequencer. This section covers module kits above $150 each and the strategy of combining multiple under-$150 modules into a playable rack within the $150-300 spend window.

6A. Starter Rack Strategy (spending $150-300 as a cluster of under-$150 modules)

The most practical $150-300 Eurorack strategy at this band is not one expensive module but two or three coordinated modules from the existing under-$150 catalog:

Minimal playable voice (from under-$150 modules):

mki x es.EDU VCO ($74) plus mki x es.EDU Dual VCA ($74-85) plus Music Thing Startup (~$82-88) = approximately $230-247 total

This combination yields: tone source (VCO), amplitude control (Dual VCA), clock, and headphone output. It is not a complete voice (no filter, no envelope shaping), but it generates musical sound and teaches the signal chain. Add the EDU Envelope ($74-85) to bring the total to approximately $304-$332 and you have a voice with dynamics -- just over the $300 ceiling.

The HAGIWO path (lowest absolute cost): PCBs from JLCPCB (~$5-15 per board), parts from Tayda Electronics, three to four HAGIWO modules (LFO, sequencer, VCO, VCA) = approximately $24-32 in parts plus $30-60 in PCBs = approximately $54-92 total in electronics. Add a case and power supply. This is the path for pure-budget Eurorack; the modules are simpler than the EDU series but functional.

Case and power (not covered by any kit listed here): A Eurorack case with power supply runs $70-200+ new (Intellijel Palette, Pittsburgh Modular Structure, Tiptop Mantis). DIY wood case + Tiptop uZeus power supply: approximately $80-120 in parts. Include this in total budget planning.

6B. Befaco Full DIY Kits (mid-tier quality, higher build complexity)

Befaco (Barcelona) makes arguably the best-quality beginner-to-intermediate Eurorack DIY kits available: through-hole assembly, thorough documentation, excellent audio quality. Their kits are a significant step up from the EDU series in complexity and an equally significant step up in audio performance.

6C. Music Thing Modular Turing Machine MkII

Sound role: Probabilistic 8-step CV sequencer. Generates semi-random melodic sequences that loop and evolve based on a probability/randomness control. One of the most musically generative Eurorack DIY modules ever designed.

7. Drum Machine, Sequencer, and Sampler Kits

Sound role: Rhythm pattern generator (drum machine), melody pattern driver (sequencer), or audio playback and manipulation (sampler).

Honest assessment: This is the thinnest section in the $150-300 band. Most dedicated drum-machine and sampler kits land either below $150 (Baby8 sequencer, MFOS builds) or above $300 (Isla Instruments S2400, Polyend Tracker Mini, Elektron machines). The $150-300 window for standalone (non-Eurorack) drum and sampler kits is genuinely sparse.

What does not exist in this band: A dedicated standalone drum machine kit with pads, pattern memory, and a rhythm-focused interface under $300. The drum-machine kit market below $300 is genuinely absent. The practical path to drum sounds in DIY is the Eurorack approach (individual drum voice modules: Erica Synths EDU drum set, Befaco Crush Delay, NLC drum modules) combined with a Baby8 or Turing Machine for patterning. This approach builds a drum section module-by-module rather than buying a drum machine.

Bastl Kastle 2 sound-role note: The Kastle 2 is a compact patchable synthesizer, not a drum machine. It can produce percussive sounds (the FX Wizard variant is particularly useful for noise and percussion textures), but its primary identity is a synth voice and generative instrument. The out-of-stock status as of June 2026 is worth monitoring.

Teenage Engineering Pocket Operators (assembled, not kits): PO-12 Rhythm (drum machine), PO-33 K.O. (sampler), PO-14 Sub (bass synth) are each ~$59 assembled -- not DIY kits, fully assembled. Three POs at $59 = $177, in-band, and the most capable drum-plus-sampler-plus-bass setup at this price point. They are not builds. Listed here because they frequently appear in conversations alongside DIY synths and they are the real answer to "I want drums and a sampler for under $300."
